That is a question we can actually investigate because it might be that the answer is that, in certain extreme cases, due to certain interfering factors, yes, it would be okay.
2.39: That brings me to a general principle, a general approach to ethics that's become popular and then radically unpopular and then popular again over the last century. This was the view that was very common, and in fact, maybe the dominant view in Anglo- American philosophy for the first half of the 20th century. Then it became so unpopular that people dismissed it in the first pages of their articles or books. I started getting interested in it back in the 1970s as a student, and the consensus then was that this theory is completely hopeless.
2.40: But then, over the past, say, 30 years, people have gotten very interested in it again. If you were charting the stock averages of philosophical positions, this would be a highly volatile one. But in any case, it's something that has a lot of affinity with some of the views we've talked about already, but takes them maybe even further. It's known as ethical intuitionism.
2.41: The idea is this. First of all, pluralism. There are different sources and different kinds of value. We care about different kinds of things. And so the goods, the values, the basic things we are concerned about in ethics, they differ in kind, and we have to take that into account. It's not all happiness. It's not all pleasure and pain. It's not all just good intentions, according to the intuitionist. It's a bunch of different things.
2.42: What makes this difficult is that these things sometimes conflict. So I can pursue this, but only at the cost of not pursuing that. I can't have everything. I can seek this good, but I realize I can't have both this good and that good. I have to make a choice. In some sense, this is a tragic vision. I cannot have everything I want. I've got to make choices, and I've got to make trade-offs. I've got to compromise.
2.43: Moreover, there are no universal rules for doing that. These conflicts are complicated, and I can't tell you in advance how you want to resolve them. As an individual, I might be concerned about, for example, success in my career as opposed to just relationships with my family and friends, and I've got a finite amount of time. These things conflict. If I spend more time working, I have less time for family and friends and vice versa, and I just have to find a good balance for myself. Is there a rule that will tell people, "Here's the right balance"? No. I've got to make some decisions. I've got to trade off one value against the others.
2.44: The same thing could happen in simple ways. I think I need a new car. I care about having money, but I also care about having a car. How much money should I be willing to spend on the car? I'd love to have the car and the money. Just give me a free car. But that's not going to happen. So I have to choose. And there's no rule that tells me, "You should spend this much on a car." It's something that I have to actually figure out for myself, balancing these different things I care about. In that sense, it is a tragic theory. You can't have everything.
2.45: Moreover, this is something W. D. Ross stresses: every decision is full of moral risk. Why? Because you are making a choice. You're making a compromise, and you have no idea whether it's the right compromise. You could be getting it wrong. There is no rule to tell you that you're doing good, you're getting it right. You've got to see how it works out. There's always the risk that you're going to be making a mistake.
2.46: After all, whether this is the right balance or not depends on all sorts of possible interfering factors. It's good, all other things equal. You have no idea whether other things are going to turn out to have been equal. By the end, maybe it will turn out that something unexpected happens. Then all of those decisions that seemed sensible at the time look pretty bad in retrospect. So every decision is full of risk.
2.47: W. D. Ross is the 20th century's most famous proponent of this intuitionist moral theory. He says, here are seven basic principles, but it's important to recognize they are principles. They have exceptions, and in fact, they can come into conflict. Here they are: "keep promises, make amends, be thankful, be just, don't hurt people," in fact, "help people and improve yourself."
2.48: He has an analysis of these. Sometimes I've done things that give me a moral obligation, like I've made a promise, so I should keep my promises. Sometimes, I've done bad things that now create an obligation, so I should make amends. I should try to fix what I screwed up. Sometimes other people have done kind things, and so I should be thankful. I should be grateful. And by the way, he's one of the few moral philosophers who stresses the importance of gratitude, which I think is a very important thing to have as part of the moral life. And then, I should be just. I should not hurt people. I should help people.
2.49: You might think that those are redundant. Why can't I just have one, like, help people? He says, "Well, here's the thing. I can help one person, but at the cost of hurting somebody else, and the primary one there should be avoiding hurt." So don't think of this as just on one scale. Then it looks like the hurts can be balanced by helpings. And he says it's not quite like that. Also, improve yourself. I should seek my own virtue. I should seek to become more knowledgeable and a better person.
2.50: Are those all the rules? No. There might be others. Those are the ones that he sees as fundamental. But he says that if you think we need to add to the list, feel free to add to the list. So maybe there are lots of others. When I've raised this with students, some of them are specific, like the golden rule: treat others as you'd want to be treated. Or tell the truth, don't steal, don't kill, don't cheat. He thinks these are all implicit, actually, in what he's already said. But also things like share, be nice, be kind, honor your parents, be true to yourself.
2.51: So there are many things we might add. In fact, we could keep going. If you have a large enough class, you can take up 45 minutes by just having people list these things that could be additional moral rules. Sometimes I say: What would you want to tell a class of kindergarteners? There are lots of things like this: do your best, be responsible, beware of strangers, and so on. We could go on and on. Maybe some of these are special cases of his principles, and maybe some of them aren't.
2.52: But in any case, he says that that's the heart of the moral life. It's common-sense moral principles like this, the things you would tell your kindergartener, the things you tell your kids as they're growing up. Those are the things that really form the heart of morality. But yes, they're all true only in general, for the most part, and they can come into conflict. So we just have to be sensitive to the ways in which they can be balanced and compromised.
2.53: Now, one more theory like this before we turn to the most famous deontological theory of Immanuel Kant. That's one that is part of contemporary psychology, in particular, Jonathan Haidt and a variety of his collaborators have developed this theory. It's an approach to ethics that he considers, by the way, a version of intuitionism. He calls it social intuitionism. Also, it's known as the moral foundations theory.
2.54: Here's the central idea. We can focus on morality in two different ways. We can think about the morality of the individual. For example, I think: What person should I be? That is a really important dimension of how to live. But I can also then start thinking about how I get along with others. That's the part he thinks virtue ethics tends to leave out. Yes, I should be a certain person, but now we also need certain principles, certain guidelines for our interactions with other people. Even if we're all good people, it doesn't necessarily follow automatically that the community ends up working well.
2.55: So there's a social aspect to this, he thinks, that is really important. Here's one way of thinking about it. I might be concerned with myself and being the right person, so not being the guy who takes a lollipop from a child. But I might also think about a team and what makes a team work well. Those are different questions. As a community, we are something like a large team. So one dimension of ethics, and a really important one, is how we build strong teams, how we build strong communities, how, in general, groups of people ought to interact and get along with each other.
2.56: He says that there are really two kinds of focuses that people have in ethics, and it's important to distinguish them. Some of them are individualizing. They're about freedom and respect. They're about individual people and protecting their individuality. Others are about binding people together into teams, into groups, into communities. He says that there are two fundamental things that ethics is doing: it's trying to shape people into the right people, but also shape communities into the right communities and bind them together.
2.57: He says that both matter, but it's very hard to actually put them all together and actually to figure out how to integrate them in a way that allows us to resolve conflicts that are bound to emerge between them. He started noticing this, again with some collaborators, thinking about how people on different parts of the political spectrum think about ethics and why they have some opinions that they do. He ended up concluding that liberals and conservatives rely on different sets of moral foundations.
2.58: Now, since he did this work, I'm not sure the political landscape is what it was, so I'm not sure the political side of this works quite the way he thought anymore. But I do think the basic idea that people identify these different dimensions of moral reasoning and assign them different weights is an important insight. I don't think there's anybody who just leaves some out and sets them to zero, but people do really differ in how much weight they put on each factor. That, I think, is really interesting.
2.59: Let's take a look directly at the dimensions of moral thinking. The first one is harm and care. This is something that reflects the principles in W. D. Ross: "don't hurt people." In fact, "care for them, help them." That is an important dimension, and I think we all recognize that as something that's pretty fundamental in ethics. We are not only to be a certain person; we're also to avoid harming other people, and if we can, helping other people, caring about other people. This involves not just charitable actions or that type of thing, generous actions, but also a general attitude of trying to be thoughtful about other people, being empathetic, sympathizing with others, thinking about what's good for them, and thinking about the effects of our actions on them.
2.60: A second one is fairness and reciprocity. This incorporates something like the "be just" part of W. D. Ross's theory, but it also goes beyond that to something like the golden rule: treat others as you would want to be treated. Also, trying to maintain balance in human relationships in such a way that I, for example, do something nice for you, then you are grateful to me or do something nice in return for me. There is a balance in relationships here, and that reciprocity seems important. Yes, we think it's unfair if this gets very far out of balance in a relationship.
2.61: He says what many people tend to discount and assign low ranks to, but others very high ranks to, are the next group that he calls the binding foundations. They're about teamwork and about binding communities together. So one is the idea of in-group and loyalty. It seems like an important part of ethics that you are part of certain groups.
2.62: Now, some of them you choose. You choose to join a club, for example, or you move to a community. Some of them you don't really choose. You don't choose your own family. But in any case, you're part of some of these groups, whether naturally or by choice, and you should be loyal to that group. The opposite of loyalty here is betrayal. Are you loyal to the group you're part of, or do you betray it? This might be an attitude toward a nation, toward your town, toward your neighbors, toward some group, whatever it is that you're part of.
2.63: Another dimension like that is authority and respect. This is something like the vertical relationships in Confucius, where there are hierarchies. Social arrangements are often somewhat hierarchical. That's certainly true in organizations of any kind. It's true in familiesbecause there are grandparents, parents, children, grandchildren, and so on. So you can think there is an authority and respect, not just respect in the absolute generalized way that I should respect all other human beings, but actually respecting the decision of those above me in the hierarchy and respecting those below me in the hierarchy, being willing to help them and nurture them to help them rise in that hierarchy.
2.64: Then, there's what he calls purity or sanctity. This is one that's maybe the hardest to describe. It's easiest to think about in religious terms, having a sense of the Holy or the spiritual, but it's not just that. The emotion that goes along with its violation is usually disgust. In biblical terms, it's a matter of certain things being unclean. But if you take that seriously, you realize, "Wait, there are a lot of things I think of as disgusting and it has nothing to do with religious reasons or spirituality." He says that that's part of ethics, too. We tend to prefer certain things that we view as pure.
2.65: Also, this is where virtue, he says, in general, comes in, because I can look at myself and value purity in myself and see certain things as morally staining me in some way. That's part of ethics, too. The idea is that people do put different weights on these. Everybody cares about these dimensions, I think, to some degree, but a lot of disagreements in ethics and in politics come down to different weights on these different dimensions of moral thinking. If you place a high value, for example, on in-group loyalty, you're going to think one way about things. If you assign a very low value, you're going to see other considerations as far more important. The same will be true in lots of others.
2.66: If we look at these in a little more detail—harm and care—that's going to lead, if we take that as fundamental to an ethic of care, I should be concerned about other people. Caring, nurturing, protecting vulnerable people, that's really central maybe to my moral vision. If I give this a higher weight than anything else.
2.67: Fairness and reciprocity—that leads to an ethic of justice: fairness, reciprocity, justice, reciprocal, altruism. You scratch my back, I'll scratch your back, all this type of thing. That's something that can be fundamental. Indeed, some thinkers think of that as the foundation for ethics.
2.68: In-group loyalty—that gives us an ethic of community. We're parts of a community, and we should sacrifice for the group, be loyal to the group, and we should watch out for traitors, try to protect the group as well as ourselves.
2.69: Then, there's the authority, respect. It's also part of the community, but in this case, the hierarchy is involved. There are going to be the virtues of subordinates and the virtues of the authorities or the people who are above others in the hierarchy. There's a lot written on that in evolutionary psychology. It does seem to be fundamental in a lot of the animal kingdoms.
2.70: Then, purity and sanctity—Haidt refers to that as giving us an ethic of divinity. It has to do with purity, pollution. There is a social function to all of this. Some things we think of as morally staining us. Other things as morally lifting us up. That can be religious; it can have another function as well. If you want something that isn't, that dramatically illustrates this, think about the ways in which we treat the dead. We speak about the dead, but also treat a dead body. There are ways in which we go about that. We take that as very serious, and there are certain things that would horrify us, disgust us, if they were done. That's just one indicator of the thing that might make you sensitive to this dimension of moral thinking.
2.71: Now I want to turn to the most famous and most influential version of deontological moral theory. That's the ethics of Immanuel Kant. It's also the most complicated of all of these. So apologies in advance. Even relatively simple works by Kant, if you feed them into a readability formula of the kind that they use in schools to determine what reading level this is, they come out at an 18th-grade reading level. So that's PhD level. And so he's hard to read.
2.72: I once made the mistake of asking students to read Kant the very first week of a course. I never did that again because it's hard. But it starts out seemingly easy. Here is the first sentence of the first part: "Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world or even out of it, which can be called good without qualification, except a good will." This might remind you of Abelard—intentions and good will. That's what's really fundamental.
2.73: But there are several things we can notice about this. "Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world or even out of it." Here's what you might be thinking about. He's thinking about what is going to apply, not just in this world. In other words, what's good for humanity, as human beings are constituted. He's after a bigger game.
2.74: He's saying, don't talk to me of human nature. Don't talk to me about, in fact, what seems to promote the welfare of human communities or human flourishing. Instead, I want to know what is good in itself. I'm thinking about what could be conceived as good, not just the way things are, but the way you could imagine them to be, and not just for human beings as they are, but for any rational being at all.
2.75: We might distinguish things that are good for something in some context, like all these instrumental goods. A hammer is good for some things in some contexts. Then, there are things that are good for human beings in general, things like health and prosperity and so forth. Those things are good, and they promote human flourishing. But Kant says, I'm after a more special good, something that is good for any rational agent at all. That is good, yes, for human beings, but would be good for Klingons and good for Ferengi and good for any other alien being and would be good for the angels, would be good no matter what.
2.76: So that leads him to say, I am interested in a certain core of ethics that is knowable a priori. That's a matter not of what we learn from experience, but instead what we can figure out through reflection or meditation alone. That is a priori, that is to say, independent of experience.
2.77: There can be additional parts of ethics that are a posteriori that do depend on experience. So, yes, we're going to learn what promotes human flourishing and so on in various ways. He's not meaning to say to throw away Aristotle, throw away all the rest. But he says that there is going to be a certain core that actually doesn't depend on any of that. You could know nothing about human beings except that they are rational agents and still derive these truths of ethics.
2.78: So these things are going to, maybe in some cases, conflict. If we're concerned with happiness, for example, maybe there are going to be times when we have to sacrifice happiness due to that a priori core. We're going to end up saying that we have to respect all rational agents, purely as rational agents, as ends in themselves. And that's sometimes going to be something that actually works against human flourishing. It might actually work against the achievement of happiness, but we have to do it anyway because it's something that is true necessarily, as part of just being a rational agent itself.
2.79: Here's the way he starts, and he's going back here to Stoic thinkers who think this way. Instead of distinguishing instrumental goods and intrinsic goods that might overlap because we could care about things both for the sake of something else and for their own sake, like walking, for example, Kant says, I'm interested in a different distinction. Some things are qualified goods. They're good for something under certain conditions. They're good if certain things are fulfilled. But unqualified goods are good unconditionally. They are good no matter what.
2.80: So his fundamental question here is: What is good without qualification? He's not asking what's good. Lots of things are good. He's saying: What is good without qualification? Good no matter what, good under all circumstances for any rational being at all. That's the question the Stoics asked, and their answer was virtue. So that's what's in the background here. Kant is really continuing a tradition that goes back not so much to Plato and Aristotle as to the Stoic thinkers that followed them and saying, let's ask that Stoic question: What is good without qualification in all circumstances, no matter what?
2.81: There can be, notice, no overlap between these things. If it's a qualified good, it's good only under limited circumstances. If it's good without qualification, it's good in all circumstances. You can't be both. So what is good without qualification? The Stoics had answered virtue, being the right person. Abelard would say having good intentions. Kant says something very much in that tradition, but slightly different: a good will.
2.82: Now, is a good will the same as having a good intention? Is it the same as having virtue? Yes and no. Similar? Not exactly. Here is how he goes through his argument. He says: What are some other candidates for this? What about virtues? For example, "Intelligence, wit, judgment, other talents of the mind, however they may be named,"—he's talking about Aristotle's intellectual virtues here—"or courage, resolution, perseverance, his qualities of temperament, moral virtues," according to Aristotle, "are undoubtedly good and desirable in many respects; but these gifts of nature may also become extremely bad and mischievous if the will which is to make use of them, and which, therefore, constitutes what is called character, is not good."
2.83: So now we have to think. Yeah, we've got a criminal who is devastating our whole community. Better if he's intelligent or if he's dumb. Ideas, his intelligence is not an improvement. It's not good to have an intelligent criminal who can avoid the police. How about courageous, resolute, persevering? Those are not good qualities for a criminal to have. We actually think that makes the criminal worse. And so those things aren't good if they are not coupled with a good will.
2.84: He says, "It's the same with gifts of fortune, power, riches, honor, even health, and the general well-being and contentment with one's condition, which is called happiness, inspire pride and often presumption, if there isn't a good will to correct the influence of these on the mind, and with this, also to rectify the whole principle of acting and adapted to its end."
2.85: In other words, he's saying being rich, being powerful, having everybody adore you, being healthy, and being happy—are these morally good things? Not necessarily. They can actually corrupt you. Here, think about almost any childhood star. Achieves fame, wealth, and so on very early in life and seemingly easily. I don't mean they don't work very hard to do it, but still, if, let's say, by the time you're 16, you're already a multimillionaire and already have a huge mansion and so on, you might think: What happens to those people later? All too often, their lives fall apart.
2.86: Kant predicts that. He says, that's right. It can corrupt you. It can make you think it's all easy and actually undermine that sense of a good will. Here's his test. "The sight of a being who is not adorned with a single feature of a pure and good will, enjoying unbroken prosperity, can never give pleasure to an impartial rational spectator. Thus, a good will appears to constitute the indispensable condition, even of being worthy of happiness."
2.87: Imagine watching a movie where there is somebody who has not one shred of a good will. Nobody likes this person. Nobody admires them. But as the movie goes, everything works out for them. They win all of these struggles. They become very wealthy. They get the girl, and it's a horrible person. There is not one shred of redeeming anything to this person. How does the impartial rational spectator, let's say you, as the moviegoer, feel about that movie?
2.88: Kant would say, you should think that's terrible. You don't want that person to be happy. Let's have an alternative history where Hitler ends up winning. It's like, "It's all great." No, that's really bad. That's not something where you end up saying, "That's a morally good situation." Happiness, in other words, he's saying, is not necessarily a good thing. Aristotle said that everybody seeks happiness. We all desire it for its own sake. Well, maybe we do for our ourselves. But do we think that it is actually a good thing without qualification? No, the happiness of somebody who is a terrible person, who has not one vestige of a good will, seems like a very bad thing to us.
2.89: This makes us ask the question, then: What is a good will? Here's his answer. It's somewhat surprising. You might think that it's caring about other people. It's being kind, being generous, and so on. But that's not his answer. He says that it acts on the basis of universal considerations. It is not influenced by subjective particular determinations. It "consists just in this the principle of action is free from all influence of contingent grounds."
2.90: Now, that is surprising because we might have thought it's a concern for human happiness or caring about other people. But instead, he says that those things are things that are contingent on, for example, the value of the person we care about. If I care deeply about somebody who's a moral monster, that caring might be a bad thing. In the end, here is what I have to think. I've got to say, "I've got to make my decisions on the basis of moral principle."
2.91: Think back to Confucius who said, I've got to be conversant, not with gain, not with self-interest, but instead purely with what is right. I think that's the idea here: I've got to focus on what is right. I've got to do the right thing because it is right, or you might say more precisely, for the reasons that make it right. I shouldn't be thinking about how much I care about that particular person. I shouldn't be thinking about these other subjective things: How much do I like that person? Or how good a person do I think they are? Even those things should not be driving my decision.
2.92: I should be thinking about what is right in a more general, more universal way. I should be thinking about my duty. I have good will and my actions have moral worth when I act from duty out of respect for the moral law. If I treat you kindly just because that's my natural disposition or because I like you, Kant says that that's fine. I'm not telling you to do something different. But on the other hand, that's not really the ideal of a good will. The good will is going to treat people well out of duty because it's the right thing to do.
2.93: In other words, the test isn't whether you treat your friends well; it's whether you treat your enemies well. The test is not going to be whether I do something because I care about this person or that person. Doing it for the person I really don't care about and don't like very much, that's going to be the test of my moral worth.
2.94: To formulate his principles, and after all, this is about moral principles, we need to think about imperatives. An imperative is something that says that you should do this or you shouldn't do that. It's going to say, "Do this, don't do that." It expresses a command or an obligation. These could be hypothetical or categorical. A hypothetical one says, "If you're in this circumstance or you have this desire, then you should do this." So it's conditioned. It says, under these circumstances, that's a good thing to do. But a categorical imperative applies across the board. It says, "Do this, don't do that."
2.95: So, hypotheticals, notice, are conditional. It's, "If you want that, if you're in this circumstance, if you're hungry and you find yourself in downtown Phoenix, then you should go to this particular place." That's a hypothetical imperative. Often these are imperatives of skill, imperatives that express knowledge of particular situations. "If you are walking by and you find somebody who suddenly falls down to the ground and appears to be having a heart attack, then you should do this." Those can be moral. They can be just things that have to do with knowledge of a particular thing.
2.96: Here's the thing that matters to us—they are suited for qualified goods. A qualified good is good under certain conditions. This says that under certain conditions, do that. So these apply to qualified goods. You need to drive in a nail? You should get a hammer. If you're in that circumstance, if you want to achieve that end, then this is what you ought to do. The hammer is a qualified good, and it's a means to an end. So this is appropriate for means and reasoning.
2.97: But a categorical imperative would go beyond that. It would just say, "Do this, don't do that," independent of goals, independent of desires, independent of circumstances. And so it would apply universally. Now, the question is: Is there anything like that? Is there anything that applies absolutely universally so I could always tell somebody, no matter who they are, what their circumstances are, "Do this, don't do that."
2.98: That would be appropriate, he says, only for unqualified goods. Because after all, qualified goods are good only under certain conditions or if you have certain desires. And so I can't give you a categorical imperative for that. I can't say, "Use a hammer, no matter what." That doesn't make any sense. But I can maybe find some things that are unqualified goods, things that are good without qualification, good no matter what, and say that we always pursue those goods. But there's only one unqualified good, he says: a good will.
2.99: Really, there's only one thing I can command, universally in this way, necessarily: you ought to have a good will. "Have a good will" is really the only possible categorical imperative. If there were other unqualified goods, we could have others, but he thinks there are not. I won't go into his argument for that. It has to be teased from the text, and a lot of people think there isn't an argument for that at all. But whatever you think about that, "you ought to have a good will" is really the only categorical imperative you could have.
2.100: Now, oddly, he never puts it that way. He says, what is a good will? It's one that acts on the basis of these universal considerations. We could frame it that way. You ought to act on universal considerations. Or in other words, act on principle. Don't act because you happen to like the person or you care about this or you want that. Instead, act because it's the right thing to do. Act on the basis of principle.
2.101: That is something that he then goes on to formulate more precisely in five different ways, and I'm only going to talk about a few of those, but the core idea of his Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals is to start with the good will, say, given what we've said, there can only be one categorical imperative, really, have a good will, but now we're going to formulate that in several different ways. I'll only talk about a few of them.
2.102: But what he does is say, here's one version. It implies the next version. That implies this version. That implies this one. This brings us back to this one, which implies the first. They all end up being equivalent. They're all equivalent formulations of that basic principle: have a good will.
2.103: Here's the first one. "Act only on that maxim [through which] you can at the same time will to be universal law." In other words, act on principle. Act on the basis of universal considerations. Act as if everyone were going to act on your maxim, that is to say, your principle of action. Don't make an exception for yourself. If I decide I'm going to do something, then I need to think: What if everybody did that? What if everybody acted on the basis of that principle? Here, it's not just looking at consequences. It's something deeper than consequences. We're going to say: Does that even make any sense?
2.104: Here's the test. We identify the principle on which you would be acting if you do this. Then you say, "Could everyone act on the basis of that?" Well, maybe the answer is no, in which case it's right out. Maybe the answer is yes, but we have one more question: "Could a rational being will that everyone act that way?" We've got to be able to answer yes to both of those questions for it to be a morally permissible action. If I say, "No, everyone couldn't act on it," wrong. Also, if I say, "Well, everyone could, but no rational being could want to be in that world," it doesn't work.
2.105: Here's a simple case. Should I steal? I think that maybe I could get away with it. Should I commit this theft? Well, here's my maxim: steal. Maybe more precisely: steal what I want. Could that be a universal law? His answer is no. Could everyone go around stealing from everyone else? No, there would be no such thing as property. But if there were no such thing as property, there'd be no such thing as stealing. So stealing is unjust.
2.106: Now, that's a weird form of argument. I can see several of you already going— it feels suspicious. But the idea is, wait a minute, in this situation, we're all going around taking each other's stuff, well, then nobody really owns anything. But if nobody owns anything, then nobody's stealing anything. They're taking. So you might think, wait a minute. It all depends on the word steal. Could we all go around taking everything from everybody else? Well, yeah, we could. There'd be no such thing as property, so there'd be no such thing as stealing.
2.107: But then we'd have to ask: Could a rational being want to live in that world where you couldn't rely on having anything around? Somebody else might have taken it? The answer would be no, because it would get in the way of you achieving your goals.
2.108: Here is the case he really considers, though. I'm going to skip the first because it's controversial and he makes the mistake of dealing with the hardest case first. Never do that. But anyway, here's what he does that's a bit pure, promising. Somebody finds himself in need of money. He wants to borrow some money. He knows he's never going to be able to repay it. Is it okay to promise to repay knowing he's never going to be able to do it?
2.109: Well, here would be his maxim: whenever I need money and need to borrow some, I'll promise to repay even though I know I'll never do it. Okay, maybe that'll work out. Maybe you'll get away with it. But is it right? He says, now we do the key thing. We make that a universal principle. We say, suppose that were a universal law. Everyone in need of money will go around borrowing, claiming they are going to pay it back, but never pay it back. What if that were a universal law?
2.110: And he says, "I see it once that it could never hold universally." It would contradict itself. Suppose everybody did that. "The promise itself would become impossible. No one would consider anything was promised to him, but would ridicule all such statements as vain pretenses." So the idea is, if there's a general principle, "Oh, you need money? You promise to repay, but never do it." Who's going to loan anybody any money out of those circumstances? There would be no such thing as borrowing and lending, no such thing as promising. People would laugh at you if promises were broken universally in that way.
2.111: Here would be the idea and outline. Here's my maxim: make false promises. What if everybody did that? There'd be no such thing as promising. In short, there couldn't be a situation where everybody did that because promising wouldn't even exist in that world. So making false promises is wrong. In fact, it's unjust.
2.112: Here's another one. Imagine that you have talents. You can develop your talents and work hard, but you think, "I'd rather indulge in pleasures rather than do that, and so I'm not going to improve my natural capacities." But is neglecting my natural gifts my duty? He sees that a system of nature could subsist like that. He imagines the South Sea Islands are like this. I guess he's never watched Survivor. But anyway, he imagines that this would be easy. "Can I just lay on the beach and be—"
2.113: He says, I could do that. I could devote my whole life to enjoyment, but I could never want that to be a universal law. It could be, but I, as a rational being, could not want it. Why? Because I necessarily will that my faculties be developed. They've been given to me for all sorts of possible purposes.
2.114: Here we're getting to a deep point in Kant, which is that I, as a rational being, necessarily value my own rationality and my own abilities because to be a rational being is to use means to obtain ends. I have to value my own ability to attain my ends. I value getting those ends, but I also have to value my own ability, my own rationality. I can't want my rationality, my abilities not to be developed. Yes, that could be the way people live; it is not the way I could want people to live. I am a rational being. I can't help willing my own survival. I can't help willing my own rationality, my own ability. I couldn't will to be stupid or irrational or ignorant or ineffective because I care about the things I want. I care about getting the things I want. So I necessarily want to be able to get them.
2.115: He thinks about that in connection with charity. Could there be a situation where we're all in it for ourselves and nobody tries to help anybody else? The answer is, yes. And maybe it would even be better than the actual world where we do care about people, but we as often hurt them as help them. He says that even though that's possible, a rational being couldn't want it. Why? We couldn't be willing to be part of that because we "need the love and sympathy of others."
2.116: This used to puzzle me a lot. Many cases could occur in which one could have the need of the love and sympathy of others. That seems cheap. But then I had a granddaughter, and I realized that we all need the love and sympathy of others when we're young, and then, of course, at various other points in our lives. But how could a child ever grow up if they didn't have the love and sympathy of others? So this gives us an obligation toward the person beaten on the side of the road. It gives us an obligation to other people because we've got to value their happiness as well.
2.117: This leads him now, crucially, to the formula that he says that even if you don't buy all the rest of it, this is the part that actually gives me your card to put in your pocket for how to live. The universal law test, that's tricky, complicated, hard to use, but this one's easy to use. He says, "Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or that of another, always as an end and never as a means only." So always treat other people as ends in themselves. Never simply use them as a means to your own end. In other words, you ought to respect moral agents, respect other people, don't use them. Treat people as ends, never merely as means. That, he says, is the key practical test.
2.118: It follows, he thinks, because I have to necessarily value my own rationality, my own abilities. But I'm not allowed to discriminate and make exceptions for myself. If I value my rationality and my abilities, I have to value your rationality and your abilities. But that means if I value my ability to make rational choices for myself, I have to value your ability to make rational choices for yourself. It's that that underlies this thought of the formula of humanity: I have to treat other people with fundamental respect.
2.119: Then it's very easy to see why I shouldn't make false promises. I'm using another person to gain an advantage. Why I should develop my talents; otherwise, I'm just using my own life for indulgence and pleasure. Why I should be charitable and generous toward others; otherwise, I'm not giving them full respect as rational agents.
2.120: He does go on to other considerations and other versions of this that I won't talk about because we're short on time, but a key factor is, because I value my own rationality and my own autonomy, I have to value your rationality and your autonomy, too. I have to respect your ability to make your own choices. I have to respect you as a rational agent. That means I have to value your ability to make choices for yourself. I cannot use you, manipulate you, exploit you. I have to treat you as equal to myself. In the end, all of this is supposed to be equivalent to, in a complicated philosophical way, the golden rule. I have to treat others as I want to be treated. The end.
2.121: You brought up intuitionism. In my opinion, and from what I can tell, it appears to be incredibly dangerous and could quickly dissolve into confusion and possibly even nihilism on a grand scale. What are your thoughts and how do you grapple with that challenge or create a foundational hierarchy of values?
2.122: A good question. Intuitionism might be thought to be so reasonable that it actually tells you nothing. It allows you to rule out nothing. Because once you say every principle has exceptions, then you can always say, "Yeah, I know it did that, but that's an exception." That can lead to a cynicism about moral rules. I mentioned that it implies that everything involves a moral risk, but it also involves, you're right, a deeper moral risk, not just the idea that, "Hey, in this case, I might be getting the balancing wrong, or I might be making an exception in the wrong place." It's like, I might think, "Oh, I can always make an exception for myself," to link it to Kant.
2.123: That is a scary thought because I, let's say, engage in a bit of violence. You say, "Wait a minute, that's wrong. You should not hurt other people." I say, "Well, that's true in general, but I am doing it in a quest for social justice," or "I'm doing it because I think it's actually helping this person." I say, "Oh, I'm doing it out of loyalty to my group, or I'm doing it—" All of a sudden, you start realizing, "Wait a minute. This is like having a get-it-out-of-jail free card." That is a very dangerous situation because once I start thinking that way about moral rules, maybe I can dispense with them altogether. So I agree with you, there is a danger there.
2.124: Now, if you're an intuitionist, how do you fight against that? I think part of it is to say— and this is the scary part, maybe—you have to say that normally, it works out that way. So yes, in this case or that case, there could be an exception. But normally it works this way. Normally, that would be the right thing to do, or normally, that would be the wrong thing to do, and the others have to be rare. If they start being used too often, you get suspicious and you begin to think, "Wait a minute, you're misinterpreting this."
2.125: How rare does it have to get? I don't know. If I saycats like fish, how many exceptions there have to be before you say, "Wait, I don't think that's true"? I don't know. Not every cat has to like fish, but enough do that we endorse that claim. Similarly, if I say that murder is wrong, but then go about justifying it in all sorts of special circumstances, and I do that routinely, you might think, "Wait a minute. I'm not so sure you actually agree anymore that murder is wrong." But that's a very squishy thing. When is that?
2.126: I think it's a real challenge. I myself don't feel as if it's impossible to guard against. But on the other hand, I think it's very difficult to guard against it. It can lead you into a situation where you think that there's nothing that will anchor any of this to anything firm. I think there is maybe some of the motivation for people appealing to natural law theory, as in Thomas Aquinas, saying that maybe there are certain things like seek the good and avoid evil that really are universal.
2.127: Now, if you're going to claim that your use of violence, let's say, is justified, you have to link that in some way. You have to say, "But look, I am avoiding evil by doing this." I am avoiding, let's say, a greater evil. Or you have to say, "I am achieving some great good." Then we just have to examine those claims. Is there really a greater evil? Are you really achieving this greater good? I think maybe if you go in that direction, you have some anchor. But even if you do, there's still a lot of room for disagreement. We seem to get thrown into facts like, "Hey, is it really doing that?"
2.128: It might be that when I think about the history of this, in the 20th century, the appeal of ethical intuitionism was at first something that came along with the decades just before and just after the First World War, where you might say there was starting to be a lot of cynicism. This was introduced as a way of actually combating nihilism and cynicism, but maybe it didn't go far enough. Indeed, after World War II, it lost popularity very quickly. You could argue it's because people saw sheer evil there and realized that it was justified in these kinds of ways. So maybe we really need a firmer anchor.
2.129: So I think part of the appeal was like, "Hey, this is reasonable," and a guard against cynicism, but maybe not nearly enough of a guard. I think it's fair enough to say it's the way a lot of moral rules might be, but if they're all that way, maybe we're in real trouble. Anyway, great question. Other questions?
2.130: This is maybe more about biographical details about the philosophers we've discussed so far. You'd mentioned earlier that if you're asking: What would a virtuous person do? If you don't have a role model, then who would that be? So look at Confucius, Aristotle. Did they have role models? I see a lot of influence around it, but under really what a worldview were they going at with saying, "This is my role model. Here's why I think— why I'm asserting what I'm asserting."
2.131: A great question. In Confucius, the real role model is something that he finds in The Book of History and The Book of Poetry. He refers constantly to earlier emperors from a long time before, more than a thousand years before, Yao and Shun. The idea is they showed us how to live, and so we have to get back to those old ways. In general, for him, it's very much past-looking, and in that case, the distant past.
2.132: It was like people knew how to live once. We've forgotten; we've become corrupted. But look at those earlier models. History has given us examples of people who were truly admirable. So don't just think: What would a virtuous person do? Think, what would Emperor Yao do? And there are these historic figures we can look up to. So for him, it's very much look at your history, learn history, figure out who were the characters in history you want to be like, and others you want to avoid.
2.133: In Aristotle, the name of the work is the Nicomachean Ethics, and it's named after his father. Actually, I think in his case, it was like, "I looked to my dad," and that seems to be another way of looking at it. Hey, I've inherited this. I have role models in my own family: in my own parents, maybe my own grandparents. There are people in my family I look up to and I want to be like. For him, I think it's a matter of looking at your elders and specifically those closest to you and saying, "I can ask, what would dad do, and what would grandpa do?" In this situation, "What would grandpa do?" That's how he thinks about it.
2.134: As I mentioned, I think if you're in a religious tradition, you can easily enough say: What would Jesus do? Or what would the Buddha do? I think the further away you get from a human or an ordinary human thing, though, model, the harder it is to apply. Because if I ask: What would Jesus do? I sometimes think, "Yeah, my friend's sick. Jesus would heal him. I'm just a philosopher. I can't really do that." Similarly, that's what the ancient emperor would have done. He would have made a law. "I can't make law."
2.135: I think that's why Aristotle thinks the closer the person is to you in your situation, the better, because the more directly applicable it is. The further they are from you or from your circumstances or from the human condition itself, the harder it is to apply what they would do because it may be just beyond your ability to do it.
2.136: Following up on his question, I was wondering, do you think humans crave religion because it does give them some form of structure or order to the possibilities of what could be considered good?
2.137: All right, that's a really deep question, and to some extent, beyond my abilities as a philosopher, since you're asking in part about human psychology and why people feel attracted to religion. But we've looked at enough already to maybe get a sense of that.
2.138: If I think there are rules, whether they are universal and necessary rules as Kant, for example, or Acquinas thinks, or whether they are just principles that are true all other things being equal, where do they come from? Now we can say that some of them might be rules about just promoting my flourishing. Some might be about binding communities together. They might have a variety of different sources. But you might think, "Is that really enough?" Here, psychologically, is it enough to motivate me and other people to do this?
2.139: Another problem is there's always this temptation to say, "What if I don't?" Sometimes you might get into real trouble, but all too often when we fail at our moral duty, we don't get into trouble. I at least do not have temptations to do things that are going to be getting me into trouble with the criminal law, at least I don't very often. But I do have temptations to not fulfill certain obligations.
2.140: In fact, confession time: near the end of my chairmanship, I was chairman of the philosophy department for 10 years. There were times when there were a lot of demands on me, and at times, I started feeling really overloaded. I would have two obligations that conflicted, two meetings I was supposed to be at happening at the same time. This is when I knew it was time to resign from that position. I would think, "I could use obligation A as an excuse for not fulfilling obligation B, and use B as an excuse for not fulfilling obligation A, and not go to either meeting, claiming I was the other. After I did that once or twice, I realized, "This is a bad sign. This is a very bad sign."
2.141: But notice there, it's not like I get in trouble in particular if people discovered this. I guess now they're about to. Instead, it's like, what makes me do my duty? What makes me actually put up with things that I'd rather not do. I think if you don't have a larger meaning to your life, you're going to find it very hard to find a reason for that.
2.142: Now, the larger meaning doesn't necessarily have to be religious. It might be based on a concern for humanity. But I think you need something higher than yourself. Dostoevsky lays this out very clearly at a certain point. In the end, what's central to your life? Either what is guiding you and giving your life meaning is just purely within you, or it's something you view as above you. That's a stark division. If it's all down here, then you are going to find yourself lost and your life without meaning. It has to be something you view as higher than you.
2.143: Dostoevsky thinks it has to be actually higher than humanity as a whole, because what you're going to substitute for humanity, since you don't know everybody else in the world or what would make them happy and make them flourish, it's going to be just you again. You're going to put your own image on humanity. In the end, he would say that if you're really to feel like your life has meaning, it's got to be through religion. But whether you like that conclusion or not, I do think it's compelling to say it has to be something higher than you.
2.144: If it's just about you—that, by the way, is a potential criticism of Socrates and Aristotle, though Aristotle, in other works, does talk about God. So it's not as if he ignores that. But in the Ethics, he doesn't really talk about that. And you could end up thinking that insofar as it's just about my flourishing, if I decide, "Enough flourishing." What do you really have to argue against that? So I like the idea that there must be something higher, or else all of it tends to fall apart. Lecture 3: On Consequentialism At a glance — On consequentialism.
3.1: In this lecture, I want to talk about an approach to ethical theory that is based on consequences. The idea here is to look at the effects of actions. Broadly speaking, an action is going to turn out to be good if it makes the world a better place, and it's going to be bad if it makes the world a worse place. That's very, very rough, but it gives you the feeling for what these theories are like. It says: forget, at least initially, forget intentions. Forget your motives. Forget the state of character of someone. What we're interested in is whether the action improves things or makes them worse.
3.2: Let's look at consequences. The consequences of an action are going to determine the value of the action itself. They're also going to indirectly tell us what the value of an intention is or a motive or a desire, because we're going to be able to say, "Intentions like that tend to lead you to perform actions like that, which tend to have certain consequences." But in the end, it is all driven by the consequences.
3.3: So theories like this are called consequentialist theories. They're theories that, as that name suggests, say that the moral value of actions, of motives, of intentions, of whatever, depends on consequences—on consequences in particular for the amount of good. We can be more precise than that. It's rather vague, like, what's good and what do we mean, the amount of good and so on? We're going to have to specify that.
3.4: Some of the key figures in this view are Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, together with his wife, Harriet Taylor, who developed this in the 19th century in England as an approach to ethical theory. It is mentioned in some of the dialogues of Plato, so it's not an altogether new theory, and there were a variety of British philosophers who were working in this general direction in the century before them.
3.5: But it was Bentham and Mill who really put this in a precise form, and a form that now has a huge influence, not only in philosophy, but also in politics, in economics. In fact, much of economics really rests on a theory of utility of the kind that they developed. You might see Mill, who was himself a great economist as well as a great philosopher, as giving key ideas for the analysis of social phenomena in general, including economic aspects of those.
3.6: Let's take a look at the general form of the theory. I think we could put it most generally this way. X is morally preferable to Y if X tends to lead to better consequences than Y does. What are X and Y? In the classic form: actions. So one action is morally preferable to another if it tends to lead to better consequences. But we could do the same thing with motives, intentions, even states of character, desires, and other things of that kind. We can think about their consequences, and so we could apply this very generally.
3.7: There are several things to notice about this. One is that it's about when one thing is preferable to another thing from a moral point of view. It's about better and worse. This makes it very different from most moral theories. The theories that Kant, for example, or Aquinas, or other people give you, are typically ones that say, "This is what you ought to do. These are things you should not do." They aren't about better and worse.
3.8: Directly, consequentialist theories aren't about good and bad or right and wrong at all. They have ways of building that in, and we'll talk about those, but fundamentally, they're theories about better and worse. What makes one thing better than another thing? That's something that, strangely, other ethical theorists don't tend to talk about. Look at Kant; you can say, "This violates the categorical imperative. You shouldn't do that. You're using someone else as a means." But if you say, "Here are two bad actions. Which one's worse?" There's no way to really think about that in terms of the theory.
3.9: Similarly, in Aristotle, if we say, "Here are two actions. They're both dishonest, but which one's worse?" There's no direct way of answering that question. Bentham and Mill, however, are saying, "Better and worse is the fundamental part of this. We want to know what's better than what." Then the question of what's right and what's wrong or what you have to do, that becomes a question of: How good does the action have to be to be acceptable? They start with a scale. They start with better and worse.
3.10: Well, let's talk a little bit about John Stuart Mill, who gives us, I think, the most elaborated version of this theory, though not necessarily, in all cases, the most precise version—Bentham maybe gets credit for that. It is striking, by the way, that all of these people knew each other. This is the house in London where John Milton, Jeremy Bentham, James Mill, the economist, John Stuart Mill, and then, later, William Hazlitt all lived at certain points—a black cap on the back, notice. But that's a striking fact. Those are some of the major figures of British literature and economics and philosophy; all happen to live in the same house.
3.11: That's what it looks like today, the white one on the corner. It's just a few blocks from Buckingham Palace, a rather nice location. But still, that's fascinating. James Mill, the economist, was best friends with Jeremy Bentham. The two of them home-schooled John Stuart Mill. There's a sense in which this theory emerged as a very strongly ingrown family affair, nevertheless, hugely significant.
3.12: The theory has its most powerful form and most developed form in a particular theory known as utilitarianism. That was a term given to it by Jeremy Bentham, and Mill follows in that. They're both utilitarians. Utilitarianism is a version of consequentialism, but it's not the only version, as we'll see.
3.13: What was Bentham doing in developing the theory? He was trying, first of all, to bring the methods of science to moral theory and to political theory. His greatest work was called The Principles of Morals and Legislation, and it's meant to be both. This is about morals. It's about human life, individually and as we live together, but also about legislation, about politics. It's meant to answer the question not only what should I do, but what should we do together as a political community? He thinks those are basicallyquestions that can receive the same answer. Not exactly the same question, but nevertheless, the same thing can answer both of them.
3.14: That's part of his motivation. He wants to bring science to this and say that there is a scientific method for answering that question of what I should do. Hence, we could see these theories as focusing on that third question of ethics I talked about, seen as fundamental: How should I decide? They're going to introduce a decision method, and they're going to say: What should you do? What that decision method tells you to do. What person should you be? The person who—well, in Bentham—uses the decision method, and in Mill, who at least acts in a way that corresponds to what that decision method would recommend.
3.15: That's a major motivation. What Bentham sees himself as trying to do is get rid of a lot of superstition, get rid of a lot of traditional ideas that may or may not have any foundation. If they have a foundation, he wants to say here's what it is. If they don't have a foundation, he wants to sweep them away. That includes not only views about morality and politics, but also about other things like death.
3.16: That is his body encased in the University College Library in London. It is said that he is wheeled out to preside at board meetings whenever they occur, even now, because he was a founder of that college. It is creepy. I agree with you. At one point, we actually had a conference in honor of Jeremy Bentham, and we had a telelink so we could talk directly to his body. I didn't love that part of that conference.
3.17: But in any case, Bentham was somebody who devoted his entire life to moral reform, political reform, legal reform. He graduated from Oxford with a law degree at age 19, so he was a child prodigy, but never practiced law. He instead started a group he called the Philosophical Radicals and a publication, The Westminster Review. And then he started writing huge numbers of texts on his own, only a few of which were published in his lifetime. It is thought that it's going to add up to 90 volumes once they're all fully compiled, edited, and published.
3.18: His fundamental question is, as I mentioned: How do I decide? I'm faced with decision problems like this all throughout my life, and we, as a political society, face problems like this. We have all sorts of things we might do, problems, and then proposals that are addressed to solving them. How do we make decisions about all of that? He says that, in the end, we care about effects. Sure, indirectly, we care, as Aristotle does and as Confucius does, about character. Yes, of course, we care about motives and intentions, as Abelard and Kant say. Yes, we can give principles and even maybe absolute rules for action. But in the end, what drives all of that, the utilitarian thinks, is effects.
3.19: If we're going to pursue a certain character, if that character makes the world a worse place and we're all worse off, then clearly we're doing something wrong. The same thing with motives. If our moral theory says this should be your motive, and in fact, that makes the world worse, something's fundamentally wrong with such an approach. In the end, where do we get these principles? They should be principles that make human life better. In the end, all of the value of our characters, of our motives, of our intentions, of our actions has to depend on effects.
3.20: Bentham frames all of this in terms of one principle he refers to as the principle of utility. He says it's "the principle that approves or disapproves of every action whatsoever, according to the tendency it appears to have to augment or diminish the happiness of the party whose interest is in question: or, what is the same thing in other words to promote or oppose that happiness." Bentham always writes like this, so if you find that somewhat unclear, you're not alone.
3.21: There are many things in that that are really very interesting, but I'm going to focus on the slightly simpler version that John Stuart Mill gives because it has the same features, and I think is Mill's way of trying to say exactly the same thing. Mill says, "The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness."
3.22: There are several things I want to focus on here. First of all, "in proportion as"—this is a theory of better and worse, as I mentioned. We're talking about proportionality. He is not talking about actions being right, period. Acts are right to a degree. They are" right in proportion as they promote happiness," so the degree of rightness of an action depends on the degree to which it promotes human happiness.
3.23: Well, I shouldn't say human because both Bentham and Mill think animal happiness is relevant here, too. Animals have a lesser degree, he thinks, but nevertheless have to be put into the calculation. At one point, Bentham says the key question is not does it reason, but does it suffer? If the answer is yes, then it's deserving of moral consideration. It's the total amount of happiness, period, that we are really talking about. So we've got this scale. As soon as we think about it that way, we realize that we're given here the outline, the core text, as it were, of a theory of better and worse. But now, how is that going to look?
3.24: Here's how Bentham and Mill think of it. Imagine a scale from best to worst, and things are in different positions. There should be something like a zero on that scale. That is to say, my action has no effect on happiness of anyone, whatever, and probably a lot of our actions are like that. I move my hand like this. Anybody happier? Anybody more unhappy? No, right? It's pretty much a zero. The action is right there; it does no effect, positive or negative. There are lots of things that are like that.
3.25: Imagine then that we've got four possible courses of action that we're facing: one, two, three, and four. Let's say they go on the scale like this. One is best, four is worst. Well, already we know a lot. But let's come back to that and figure out then what we have to do as a result of that.
3.26: The second thing I want to focus on in that definition or that principle isthe tendency talk. It's there in Bentham, too, "as they tend to promote happiness," or tend to promote unhappiness. That is an interesting way of framing it because Bentham and Mill are thinking about this primarily as a way of reaching decisions. It's a method for reaching decisions. I'm thinking about this before I act.
3.27: And now I think: What will the effects of this action be? Do we always know what the effects of our actions are going to be? No, in fact, often we don't. It's a matter of probabilities. And maybe sometimes we don't even have probabilities. We're just making vague guesses, thinking, "maybe this, maybe that." And so he says that we've got to focus on the tendencies of actions, not on their actual effects. We don't know those yet. If we have a method that says: see what it actually will do. Well, I won't know until I do it. That makes it a little tricky here.
3.28: Some actions have good tendencies and good effects. They tend to do this, and in this particular case, yes, that's the effect that happens. Good. Others have bad tendencies and indeed, in a particular case, bad effects. That's the normal case. But we can have actions that have a good tendency but produce a bad effect in a particular case. The doctor applies this treatment. It's normally the right treatment to give a patient with these symptoms. But in this particular case, that patient had a very unusual condition, and it was the wrong treatment to assign.
3.29: The doctor applying the method goes by the tendency, and that's the right thing to do in making the decision. Now, after the fact, we can say that it didn't work out very well in this case. Maybe it was the wrong thing to do. But we're interested in the before part, the context of deliberation about what to do, less the context of judgment after the fact. And so, as a decision method, we have to go about the tendency.
3.30: Similarly, some actions might have a bad tendency but have a good effect. For example, actually a medical example, again, I have for many, many years had high blood pressure and I'm on medication. I'm supposed to eat a low salt diet, but I actually also have low sodium. So I've got to actually consume a fair amount of salt. Now, normally, that would be a bad thing for someone with high blood pressure to consume a lot of salt— bad thing, bad tendency.
3.31: But in my weird case, it's actually good because my body gets rid of salt quickly, which is maybe part of my problem. But anyway, I'm a weird guy. I'm weird in that particular respect. If a doctor says, "Don't have much salt," that's the right thing to tell me to do until I pass out from low sodium, and then he says, "Okay, in your case, it's different."
3.32: Now, by the context of deliberation, as I mentioned, before the action, we have to go by tendencies. We don't know the actual effects. Once we have enough information after the fact, or maybe because something just like this happened before, or, "Hey, we know about your special medical condition," then we can judge according to the context of judgment. Maybe then we care about the actual effects, but that's after the fact. If we're thinking about how I decide, I have to decide on the basis of tendencies.
3.33: Let's go back to our scale. I've got these options ranked, better to worst. Now I think: What should I do? And what must I do? A lot of people think those are the same question, but some hear a difference. What should I do? That would be the best thing to do. But what do I have to do? What must I do? If you're like me, you hear that as a different question because maybe I really ought to do this, but this would be okay. I can do this. I got to do one or the other of these things, something in this range. That's the best one, but this would be okay. That is something that at least certain approaches to utilitarianism open up.
3.34: The real question comes down to this: Is there anything that would count as a supererogatory action? That's a fancy term derived from Latin. It means going above and beyond what is asked. Super-above-erogatory, what's asked. Can I go above and beyond the call of duty? If the answer is yes, there are actions that are above and beyond the call of duty, then that suggests I've done more than I really had to do. That suggests that I don't have to do the very best thing.
3.35: That brings us to these two different conceptions. I think in Bentham and Mill, there's actually a bit of waffling between them. For example, here, Bentham seems to express what is known as the satisficing concept, which means doing enough. Again, just Latin for doing enough. "An action may be conformable to the principle of utility, meaning with respect to the community at large, when the tendency it has to augment the happiness of the community is greater than it has to diminish it."
3.36: In other words, this action makes the world a better place. It makes people overall happier. It's okay. It conforms to my principle. If it makes the world worse, makes people unhappier, it does not conform. Essentially, here on this conception, the principle of utility says: choose the actions that tend to make the world a better place. There might be many such actions, but that's okay. As long as you do it in some way, you're good. You don't have to choose the best of all possible ones.
3.37: That would be like saying, "Hey, there, both options 1 and 2 are above zero. They make the world a better place." Now, you could say, "Well, maybe you should do option 1; it's the best. But option 2 is okay; it's acceptable." You have to do something that makes the world better. You certainly shouldn't choose 3 or 4, but it is possible to go above and beyond the call of duty. You're doing enough. You're doing, as it were, the least you can do by doing 2, but you can go above and beyond the call of duty by choosing option 1. That allows us to say that you should choose option 1, but what do you have to do? Choose 1 or 2. That makes utilitarianism fairly permissive. You get lots of choice about what you can do. You just have to make a positive contribution to the world.
3.38: Sometimes, Bentham, however, seems to talk as if you have to choose the best thing. That's a maximizing conception. Here in another work, the Constitutional Code, he's saying "the greatest happiness of the whole community ought to be the end or object of pursuit. The right and proper end of government in every political community is the greatest happiness of the individuals of which it's composed, say, in other words, the greatest happiness of the greatest number."
3.39: And there he's saying that our object should be the greatest amount. Actually, I'm not sure that contradicts the satisficing idea because it might be that you ought to aim at the best thing, but it's okay to settle without achieving it. So it's not exactly a contradiction. But on the other hand, he's talking here about the greatest happiness ought to be our goal, the greatest happiness of the greatest number. It certainly suggests, come on, we ought to be doing the best. At least we ought to be aiming at the best. If you have that maximizing idea, then you're going to say, "Oh, I should do option 1, and in fact, I must. I must be maximizing."
3.40: And by the way, I should add that even though I find Bentham and Mill ambiguous on this question, or if anything, talking like it's enough to do enough, most utilitarians thought the 20th century assumed everybody meant maximizing. So most people think you have to do the best possible thing. But then it becomes very demanding. I mean, what's the best possible thing for the world I could be doing right now? I don't know. Maybe this is it, but maybe it's not. I mean, maybe I should be out feeding children in Africa or something. I don't know what the best thing is. So it becomes a very difficult theory to apply.
3.41: However, if I can be doing something to make the world a better place, I don't have to worry, "Is there something that would make it even better than what I'm doing now?" This theory also, or that approach to the theory, I might say, also makes these supererogatory acts impossible. There's no way to go above and beyond the call of duty because the call of duty is always to do the best possible thing.
3.42: Here are some basic thoughts underlying this utilitarian approach, however you interpret it. One is that more is better than less. We want more happiness as opposed to less happiness. Obviously, I don't mean more is better than less of anything. More potato chips are better than fewer potato chips? Not always. But happiness, yes. In fact, the good, according to Bentham and Mill, is happiness. They identified that with pleasure in the absence of pain, but they have a very broad conception of pleasure and pain, so it's not as different from Aristotle as you might initially think.
3.43: Also, a very fundamental idea is that everyone counts equally. This is what distinguishes in part utilitarianism from other consequentialism. I could think, "Hey, I'm a consequentialist. I want the best consequences for me. I don't care about anybody else." That egoism would be a version of consequentialism, but it's not utilitarian. Utilitarianism says that you can't count your own happiness as worth any more than anybody else's happiness. Everybody's happiness counts and counts equally. "All count for one and no one more than one," Bentham says.
3.44: In one sense, we've got some very basic things that underlie utility theory in general in economics. This idea of optimizing—more value is better than less, assuming you've got the right value. "Why would any one, whether God or man, desire to make himself worse?" would desire something worse, writes Plato. Russell Hardin, a contemporary thinker, says "the simplest definition of rationality...is the one to choose more rather than less value." Here, value is being interpreted as in the end, happiness, and not just for yourself, but for everyone concerned.
3.45: But this is tricky because people choose under various constraints. If we start thinking about these two approaches—satisficing, settling for enough, as opposed to maximizing, insisting on the best—we realize this is a subtler thing to think about than you might initially think. Why? Because we're always choosing under constraints, and maybe what looks like settling for enough is really maximizing under those constraints. At a certain point, I decide, "I don't know if this is the best thing to do, but it seems like a good thing to do, so I'm going to do it."
3.46: Why don't I persist in thinking, "But wait, maybe I could think of something better." Partly because of constraints. I don't have an infinite amount of time. I don't have an infinite amount of energy. There are many sources of constraints. I have limited time. A lot of things that I do cost money or cost me something in other ways. I've got a limited amount of resources.
3.47: Sometimes it's a question of scope: I can't think about that many things all at once. I've got to focus on certain things. Sometimes it's a matter of quality. Let's say somebody comes in and says, "This is the best automobile you could buy." I might think that there are still many reasons why I'm not going to buy it. Maybe it costs too much.
3.48: Maybe, really, I'm willing to settle for lower quality because maybe that one really doesn't satisfy my needs in some other respect. Maybe I need to—I mean, I don't, but maybe I need to haul musical equipment around to lots of gigs, and then I need something that would enable me to do that. The fact that the Porsche is the best possible car, but I can't fit the drums in the back. There are lots of various constraints that I'm going to operate under.
3.49: Actually, that has been one of the main motives for people talking about satisficing, saying that once you recognize that our rationality is boundedby all these constraints we have to operate under, all the limitations that face us, then actually trying to do the best we can under those constraints is going to look like satisficing.
3.50: Herbert Simon and a variety of other people in economics have introduced that idea as a way of not conflicting with maximizing and choosing the best, but instead saying, really, in practice, that's what we do. We settle for good enough because in doing that, we're maximizing not the thing we're seeking—and if you're utilitarians, then global happiness—but instead we're maximizing that together, with meeting all of those constraints, saying, "That's the best I can do given these resources, given this time, given this scope," and so forth.
3.51: Now, so far, I've been pretty vague about how we figure out these consequences. So how do we really do it? Well, here is what Bentham describes as the moral or the felicific calculus, felicific meaning, having to do with happiness. So think about all the people your action might affect. In a lot of personal cases, this is a relatively small number of people. In some cases, it's more. In some cases, if you're a political agent of some kind, you're a legislator or a president, prime minister, it might be millions of people.
3.52: You've got to think about those people and then say, "What is the tendency toward pleasures for that particular person? What is the potential, the tendency for pain?" Think about the difference. I've got to think, "How will this affect you?" Then I realize thatI don't know what the outcome is, so I can't really assign a direct number to that. It might benefit you in this way. It might actually cost you something in this way. Now I've got to think, "What's the likelihood of that?"
