So, I've got to think about the possible range of outcomes and assign them probabilities and think what happens to you under each of those outcomes, and then do a calculation of expected utility.
3.53: This is actually a method that businesses use in cost-benefit analysis and that economists use in expected utility theory. This has now been developed into something of an art form, and there's a lot written about it mathematically. But the idea is really just that, and it gets complicated. I'm thinking, just focus on one person. "How does my action affect that person?" Well, it might be to their benefit, but I've got to think this through carefully. What are the possible outcomes of the action?
3.54: Let's say there are five of them. I've got to assign each of those outcomes a probability. Then I've got to think, " How does it affect person A under each of those outcomes?" Then I have to do a calculation, taking together the sum of all of those things, figuring out that's the expected pleasure for A. Now, sometimes this is something that's easy to do. Somebody says, "Hey, I'll bet you this coin will end up tails." I think, "What's my expected payoff for doing this?" We bet a certain amount of money. It's 50-50, assuming it's a fair coin. Pretty easy to figure out my expected benefit and my expected loss. In a game like that, it's usually zero. I mean, expected benefit will be the winning, whatever it is. The loss is whatever that is, and they balance out.
3.55: But that's a very simple case of what we'd have to do for each person who might be affected and each possible outcome. It becomes really complicated. We have to start by identifying the options we have. We've got a bunch of different options for our decision. Then we think in each case: Who might be affected by my undertaking that action? Those in some parts of the literature are called stakeholders.
3.56: Then we think, I've got to compute the expected benefits and the expected costs for each of those stakeholders under each of those possible actions. I've got to think about the probabilities and the outcomes and how it affects that person. Then I've got to assign the costs and benefits to each of the outcomes by doing that expected calculation, summing all these things up. Then I think, let's add it all up. Is there a net benefit to the whole? Is there a net cost? Then I do that for each option. I compare the options to put them on that scale.
3.57: All of that makes it sound nightmarishly complicated. It can be. It can be very difficult. If I've got a lot of options facing me and there are a lot of possible outcomes, I've got to assign them probabilities and think through all of this. It's really very difficult. Now, there are advantages to thinking of it this way.
3.58: One is objectivity. I've got to think about things from different points of view. If this is going to affect a number of different people, I have to think about how it affects them. And so I have to be empathetic. I have to see it from that person's point of view. What's the likelihood it will benefit them? What's the likelihood it will hurt them? So it forces me to confront externalities. I've got to think about how my actions affect others.
3.59: It also makes us think this through at a pretty sophisticated level of depth. I've got to think about the possible outcomes. We're bad at this, by the way. People tend to think about a few possible outcomes, often about the one they intend. They don't think about what if something goes wrong. It's important to think about those different possible outcomes. This theory forces us to do that, or at least strongly suggests that we do it.
3.60: Now, it does make certain assumptions in the calculation. We've got to be able to compare these effects. One of the tricky questions is whether pleasures and pains are really comparable in this way. I think Bentham and Mill both tend to assume, and economists, in applying this, tend to assume that pain is something like the opposite of pleasure. It's just the negative part of the scale, so we can put all of these on one scale. But if you doubt that, you start realizing that it becomes complicated.
3.61: Actually, at one point, Mill seems to concede that maybe they don't belong on the same scale. But then we have the pleasure scale, in other words, the benefit scale. We have the cost scale. We don't know how to put them together. It's actually rather bad if we can't compare them. If you're an economist and you're thinking it's all money, then they're all comparable. But if you are a moral theorist thinking about benefits and costs in the sense of pleasures and pains, it's not so clear we can do that.
3.62: The second assumption is that we've got to be able to compare short-term and long- term pleasures and pains. This is what Socrates thought we're all bad at and why we're often ignorant when we look weak of will. We're bad at calculating how my short-term benefit from eating that bag of cashews is going to compromise my long-term goal of losing weight. In the end, we find it hard to make the comparison.
3.63: Bentham and Mill are granting that it's hard, but we have to do it. And so what we have to do in this theory to compare them is to have something like a discount rate. In other words, how much better is it for me to have a pleasure now than to have it a year later? I care more about what happens to me now than a year later, typically. Would you rather have me slap you now or slap you in a year? Well, most of us would say, "I'll wait a year for the slap. I hope it never happens."
3.64: Similarly, "I'll give you $100 now or I'll give it to you a year from now." It's like, "I'll take it now." So there is something about the nearness of these that diminishes over time, and that will enable us to make these comparisons between the short-term and the long-term, but it's not obvious how we choose that discount rate. Bentham and Mill think that you just see what people do. Look at people's real choices. That's what economists tend to say as well: see the choices people really make. We can estimate, through experience, the discount rate.
3.65: The third assumption that's really important is interpersonal comparisons. How does the benefit to me compare to the benefit to you? We've said everybody counts for one and nobody counts more than one. But now we have to say: How much do my enjoyments track with yours? In other words, maybe I can bring out the point most clearly this way.
3.66: Maybe I care about this thing more than you do, so I'm going to actually be affected by it more. Maybe I'm just an excitable person. My happiness levels go like this. I'm really happy. "Oh, that's fantastic." Or, "Oh, this is terrible," and so on. Whereas you're much more mellow, even keel. Like, "This is nice. It could be better." How do we compare that? Actually, it becomes a tricky practical question to some extent.
3.67: We might think, hold on a second. It's the same thing that's happened. In fact, maybe we have similar incomes, similar levels of wealth, and we each lose $100. It really annoys you, and it doesn't annoy me so much. Well, what do we do? We've both lost $100, but one person is very upset about it, the other person, not so much. How do we make those comparisons?
3.68: Here, the problem is that it's hard enough to compare two things, two pleasures, two pains within my own head. You give me, let's say—I don't know if you have this decision problem, I do—you go into an ice cream place, they offer you to taste various flavors. You think, "Oh, the Dutch chocolate; that's quite good." How about the maple walnut? "Oh, that's really good, too." I've just experienced two pleasures, and now I have to compare them and decide which is better. I have a hard time. Even within myself, it's hard.
3.69: But now I'm looking at you and seeing you taste the ice creams. You say, "Oh, that's very good." I don't know how to compare your level of pleasure as a result of eating the ice creams to my level. It seems like it's hard enough to know in my own head. How do I know what's going on in your head? So a lot of economists give up on this. They just say, "Yeah, we can't do the interpersonal comparisons," and that's going to mean we can't calculate in the way of getting sums and having a simple scale of the kind the utilitarian wants. We can, under certain circumstances, still get some results. It's not like we give up entirely, but it changes and becomes considerably more complicated.
3.70: Now, another consideration is: How do we get to the cardinal numbers this theory requires? You say, "Which ice cream did you like better?" Let's say I say, "Oh, I guess the maple walnut." They say, "Well, how much better?" Give them numbers. On a scale of 0-10. Actually, let's go below zero because maybe an ice cream is terrible. From plus 10 to minus 10, where does this rank? "I don't know."
3.71: In hospitals, they will ask patients, "You're experiencing pain. On a scale of zero to 10, what's your level of pain?" There is something that people can say. People say, "I feel like I'm at a seven." But do people mean the same thing by that? They can probably rank pains pretty clearly according to how they're feeling, but how to put them on some general scale, that seems really hard.
3.72: Finally, something Mill worries about a lot, there are different kinds of pleasures. I come into some money—yay, it makes me feel good. I meet a friend that I haven't seen in a long time—that's good. I have some ice cream at the shop, choose the maple, all that—yummy. It's good. How do I compare those? They're very differentpleasures, and it's hard to say how we map them to some scale.
3.73: Here's one way of framing this set of problems, really: utility is subjective. It's happening within your head and within my head. How much pleasure and pain we're getting, how much happiness we're experiencing. That radical subjectivity is something that causes a problem. There might be a lot of interpersonal agreements. Here is Chateau Saint-Michel in France. Almost everyone is going to look at that and say, "Wow, that is beautiful."
3.74: So I don't mean to say that it's so subjective that people are going to radically disagree about everything. You'll probably agree that the bank is really ugly. In fact, that's the contrast between those two buildings. Who's going to say, "Oh, yeah, that's my thing"? I don't know. But nevertheless, there's a huge amount of subjective variation, and that's going to be a problem.
3.75: None of these objections, I think, are fatal, but they all point to ways in which the theory might have to be complicated, and we've got to be careful about how we apply it and where we apply it. But Bentham still would say, I'm telling you, this is the only way we can go about it. Really, in the end, these problems are just ones we have to cope with. He gives us certain arguments for this view.
3.76: One is common sense. He says that our common-sense moral judgments agree with the principle of utility. For example, take a look at some of the things in the Ten Commandments: Thou shalt not murder. What's wrong with murder? It makes people unhappy. Okay, very clear. Wiping out happiness, in general, detracts from the happiness of the community. What about stealing? The same thing. What about adultery? The same thing.
3.77: What about coveting your neighbor's goods? That's just internal. No effects, right? Well, it makes you less happy, and it leads you to do things that make other people unhappy. Honor your father and mother—it'll help you grow up better and give you role models, and so, consequently, make the world a better place. In short, he's going to say all of those things if you say, "Really, why is there such a rule?" The simplest thing to say is that it makes the world better. It promotes human happiness.
3.78: Another argument he gives is that any argument for a different theory really presupposes the principle of utility. Because suppose you say to Aristotle, "You think it's good for people to be witty. That's one of your virtues. Who cares about wit? I don't care if people are funny. I suggest that people be serious. Forget humor. There should be no fun in utilitarians."
3.79: If we say that, Bentham is going to say that that's going to make the world a worse place. Why is wit a good thing? Because it makes life more enjoyable. Because we laugh and we like to laugh. It adds to the pleasures of human existence. So what's justifying that as a virtue? What would make the person being somber all the time, wrong- headed about this is that you're going to be a lot less happy, and people in general are going to be a lot less happy. The same thing is going to be true with Kant's categorical imperative. Why should I treat other people with respect? Well, look, what happens if I don't? It's going to detract from human happiness.
3.80: The last one—and this is, I think, a very powerful argument: we can resolve conflicts. We've got to have a measure of value that allows us to do that. Here, Bentham is looking at other moral theories saying, I don't actually see how they help me make a decision. We talked about virtue theory and said that there's a puzzle. If I'm not already virtuous, I don't know what a virtuous person would do. So if you tell me, "Do what a virtuous person would do," it doesn't help me.
3.81: But he says, It's worse than that. Suppose you've got an action that actually is somewhat unkind, but it's honest. So you ask me a question, and I'm thinking of giving you a dishonest answer because I don't want to hurt your feelings. An honest answer will hurt your feelings. So I face a conflict. And I think, well, yes, I should be honest, but I should also be kind. But in this case, I can't really be both. So what should I do?
3.82: Aristotle's theory doesn't really help us settle that at all. What would a virtuous person do? Well, they'd be honest, but I can't be both. I don't know. I have no way of ranking or comparing those virtues or how they would apply in this particular case. So I still don't know what to do.
3.83: The same thing you might think is true of Kant's theory. I've got two people who are— really, I'm engaged in a conflict between them, and I find myself suddenly in the middle, and I'm thinking, "I want to treat both of you with respect, but you're treating each other with great disrespect, and I don't know how to do that. You both want me to choose a side. I don't want to choose a side, but that's starting to offend both of you." I don't know what to do.
3.84: You might think, "Kant doesn't really help me out there. Treat both of you with respect." Well, I'll try to do that, but on the other hand, I don't know what I should do being pulled in these different directions. So Bentham says, here's a way of doing it. We can calculate. Indeed, medieval thinkers had said that, faced with these moral conflicts, we need to choose the lesser evil. Bentham is, in effect, saying exactly that. I'm giving you a way of computing what is the lesser evil, or if it's a positive conflict, what's the greater good.
3.85: Now, there are complications to this. I've already mentioned qualities of pleasures. But since this gets more air time than it's worth, actually, I'll talk about it a little bit more directly here. Thomas Carlyle, a well-known Victorian writer, objected to Mill that he was really ignoring something very important in human existence. He wrote that utilitarianism was a philosophy fit for swine.
3.86: Why? Because it identified the good with feeling good. Insofar as the good is just happiness and pleasure in the absence of pain, the good is just feeling good, and evil is just feeling bad. He said: Where's virtue in this? Where's concern? Where's love? Where's thinking? Where's rationality? It looks like you're just saying, "Hey, feel as good as possible. Make other people feel as good as possible." This sounds like a "grab for all the gusto you can" philosophy. He said that maybe that works for pigs in the barnyard, but it doesn't work for human beings.
3.87: In the 1830s, there's an exchange of letters between Carlyle and Mill about this. In the 1830s, Mill's response is this: our goal is to maximize the good for all people. In fact, he says that we have to think about that over time because you need to think in terms of future people as well as people who exist right now. We should be thinking about mankind as a species and thinking about this developing over time. But that has a couple of important implications, he says.
3.88: First of all, I do, in general, do best at that by promoting my own good. He says that each of us, if we tend to our own self-interest, is actually usually going to be promoting the general welfare. I think he's influenced by Adam Smith here and the arguments in The Wealth of Nations, that in general, if I'm looking out for my welfare, you are for yours, we're going to be promoting each other, partly because I gain what I want by making other people around me happy, so that they will give me what I want. So there's going to be a tendency in which I don't have to think about the happiness of others a whole lot. Most of the time, thinking about my own is enough.
3.89: But the other aspect of this is that I have reason to develop my capacities, my abilities, my talents, my intellect, because they produce benefits for everyone. The whole idea is to make the world a better place. If I become virtuous, I'm going to be making it a better place. If I become more knowledgeable, if I become wiser, I'm going to be making the world a better place, and similarly, if I develop my talents.
3.90: So the idea here is that I'm going to have obligations to do all those things. I'm not going to be able to live like a pig because I want to make the world a better place. The pig isn't really doing that. The pig may be rolling around in the mud, and cavorting, and so on, but it's not really adding to the happiness of other pigs. It's helping itself. It's not helping anybody else. But as human beings, well, we're not just pigs. So we actually have an obligation to do these things.
3.91: Now, in utilitarianism, some 30 to 40 years later, he adds a different argument. He continues to affirm that argument. But he says that there's another point. Pleasure is different in quality as well as in quantity. Here, he doesn't just mean different kinds, like the pleasure of a pasta dish as opposed to the pleasure of ice cream as opposed to the pleasure of walking through the woods on a snowy evening and blah, blah, blah. It's not that. He says that there are things that are distinctively human. It's better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
3.92: Why? Well, it's better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied because human beings are capable of better pleasures than pigs are. It's not just that we have more pleasure, we have better pleasure. As soon as you get that idea, you can already maybe see the danger because now we have differentpleasures. Some are better than others. We all, in the end, have to map them onto a single scale, though. How is that all going to work? We've got to decide, for one thing, which pleasures are higher.
3.93: Mill says, no problem. See what the competent judges prefer. Well, who are the competent judges? Those who have experienced both, he says. You want to find out whether the pleasure of gorging yourself on a delicious meal is better than the pleasure of a good conversation with a friend. Lots of us have experienced both of those things. Which would we prefer? Then whatever we say makes that the better pleasure. If we disagree, that means they're roughly equal. That's the idea.
3.94: The way he thinks that goes is that intellectual pleasure is the best. Anybody acquainted with intellectual pleasures as well as the social pleasures of friendship and love, and then purely sensual pleasures like lying on the beach on a beautiful day, drinking a Corona—those things, they're going to say, no, the intellectual pleasure is better.
3.95: I mean, would you rather get a great new insight or would you rather drink a beer? He said that, obviously, get a great new insight. Would you rather hang out with friends and have a wonderful time talking together, or would you rather gorge yourself on this meal? You'd rather hang out with friends. So he thinks that people are overwhelmingly going to choose things in a certain direction.
3.96: Yeah, I sometimes say he's never met my students. So it worries me a bit. But his answer is, I realize a lot of people would not go along with this, but it's because they don't truly know the other side of things. They don't truly know. I mean, ask the pig what it prefers. It prefers pigish pleasures. But that's because it hasn't experienced these distinctively human pleasures. So you've got to ask those who are competent with both, who are familiar with both. Really, what it just means, if the students have a different view, that means the students don't really have acquaintance with those higher pleasures.
3.97: You may find this convincing. You may find it unconvincing. But in any case, Mill thinks that's how it goes. Bentham, interestingly, rejects this. The standard scholarly line is that Bentham ignores this question of qualities of pleasure. He dumps them all into one barrel. That is totally unfair. He has a chapter in which he discusses the different kinds and subkinds, and it's complicated. So he knows there are many different pleasures, many different qualities of pleasures.
3.98: In fact, in one place, he says that, of course, pleasures differ in quality as well as in quantity. In regard to well-being, quality as well as quantity has to be taken into account. But who gets to judge? He says, that you do. Quantity depends on general sensibility. In other words, how much pleasure are you experiencing? He thinks we can make these interpersonal comparisons.
3.99: I think in the end, his picture is neurophysiological. He thinks that if we just knew enough, we'd know how much certain brain pathways are being excited, and we'd be able to put a number to your level of pleasure, or conversely, your level of pain. He says, in the end, I think neurophysiology will take care of that problem.
3.100: But what about quality? He says that that's a matter of particular sensibility. Some people are more sensitive to pleasures and pains from a certain area. Would you rather read a philosophy book, go to a hockey game, or listen to a symphony? No reason why everybody has to agree. And Bentham is going to say, I'm not saying that that makes them all roughly equal. I'm saying it's absurd to think that people who have done all those things are going to agree or that it matters whether they agree. The point is: do you enjoy hockey? Go to the hockey game. You like the symphony? Go to the symphony. It's all fine.
3.101: So he sees this as fundamental to preserving liberty. Why? Because I've got to respect your ability to make these comparisons on your own. He says, I can know the quality for me just by reflecting and by experiencing things, but I can't tell what's a better pleasure for you except by seeing what you actually choose. So in the end, you get to be the judge of what's a better pleasure for you, and you get to be a judge of what's better for you, and so on. I shouldn't be in a position of saying that this one is generally better, because guess what? I and my friends would much rather read the philosophy book than go to the symphony or go to the hockey game.
3.102: Mill, on the other hand, says, I want to preserve liberty, too. But now he's going to do it in a different way because he thinks he can actually make judgments about better and worse in terms of these qualities of pleasures. However, he also has a principle that's often called the harm principle. The idea is that we should restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others.
3.103: So around each individual, there should be a sphere of self-regarding actions, things that either don't affect other people at all or at least do not violate their rights. And then you should be free to act however you want within that sphere. Does that follow from the principle of utility? Well, indirectly, he thinks the answer is yes, because we're all going to be happier if we respect those boundaries.
3.104: Say, if it affects just you, then I'm not going to tell you how to live. You get to make those choices on your own. You think the best possible pleasure for you would be sitting around in a drunken and stoned haze, then I shouldn't interfere with that as long as you don't hurt anybody else. If somebody else thinks, "I just want to go to the library and spend my life in the library." Okay, you go do your thing. Nobody else should tell you that that's okay or that that's required or that that's not okay.
3.105: Now, there are some objections to utilitarians I want to consider. One that Mill brings up himself is time. Am I not going to spend much of my life calculating? I mean, this sounds complicated. So what should I do for dinner? Well, gosh, mostly I'm affected, but other people might be affected, too. And so I've got to think through the possible effects on all those people and so on.
3.106: That sounds difficult. It's going to take me way longer than dinner time to do that. Are there times when we shouldn't, don't have to calculate? How can I tell? Do I have to calculate whether or not to calculate? Maybe I have to calculate about whether or not to calculate about whether or not to calculate. How do we know when we've calculated enough?
3.107: All these sound a little bit silly, but think about politics. When you get into that general framework, you start realizing that it does sometimes feel like we've all agreed for decades that this is a major social problem, and we still have committees and reports and commissions to study the problem. They produce proposals that are viewed by the committees. How can we tell when it's time to just do something? It's not a trivial question.
3.108: Now, Mill says that it's not a severe question as you might think either because the principle of utility is going to judge actions by their effects on happiness, making it better or worse. But it doesn't have to be our motivation. It doesn't even have to be a practical test. We usually apply it by relying on secondary principles.
3.109: I'm thinking, "Should I steal that car?" I don't have to think, "Let me calculate." I can just think, "Yeah, we've had the whole history of the human race to figure out that stealing is bad." I can rely on that. I can use those common-sense principles. They're supported by utility, and they generally give me the right answer. I don't have to do all the calculations ex nihilo.
3.110: The same thing is going to be true for a lot of other moral decisions I make, including ones where I just say, "I don't have to do a calculation. I don't have to worry about anybody else. I'm looking at the menu: What do I want? I should just choose what I want. I don't really have to do a calculation about the effects on other people." Those rules are justified by utility, and they let us take shortcuts. Really, we're only going to have to do calculations when we get into a situation of conflict and those moral rules conflict.
3.111: Then, I'll realize, other theories, he says, leave us far worse off. We got a conflict, we don't know what to do. Utilitarianism says, "I've got a method. Now we can do the calculation." Things like Ross's principles, they're all going to look like good principles from a utilitarian point of view. They all promote happiness, so it's easy to justify them. Then you say, "Oh, but wait a minute, I've got a situation of conflict. I can help this person only at the cost of hurting that person." Let's do the calculation. How much are you helping? How much are you hurting? If it's something like a tax law, it might be a lot of people; it'll get complicated, but still, that's how we need to think it through. When we get into a situation of conflict, calculate.
3.112: We're going to find that all over the place. We've already mentioned that there can be conflicts between various applications of Kant's principle, different virtues in Aristotle or Confucius, and there might be larger ones. Maybe I can get better results by actually disrespecting somebody by using them merely as a means. Or what if I can do something that gets better results by acting in a way that's really not very virtuous? There can be such situations, and we have to decide what we want to do.
3.113: In the end, the utilitarian says, "I'm going to do the calculation." I realize undermining that virtue is bad. I realize using someone as a means is bad. On the other hand, maybe sometimes I actually have to do it. And wartime gives us great examples of that: there are civilians there in that town, but we need to bomb the town to eliminate the munitions factory. Using those civilians may be merely as a means to do it, but maybe that's what we have to do.
3.114: Similarly, maybe we actually have to be vicious in this connection or in another. It is possible to say that we could be in situations like that. Could we ever know enough to know that we're in one? But I think the answer is that maybe sometimes we do know the consequences well enough.
3.115: One last point: many of the objections to utilitarians depend on rights. And Bentham is dismissive. He writes it's nonsense. Natural rights, as in John Locke, he says, that's nonsense on stilt. It's no use for human rights at all. But Mill says that's not right. "When we call something a person's right, all we mean is he has a valid claim on society to protect him in the possession of it, either by the force of law or of education and opinion."
3.116: In other words, if you say, "I have a right to property," what that means is society should help me protect my property. Why should it do that? Utility. In the end, we're all better off if society protects your possession of your property, or your possession of your life or your possession of your liberty. To say you have a right isn't some magical thing that comes out of the sky independently of human happiness. We protect certain rights because they make us all happier and make up communities where we protect and promote the happiness of the people in them. In the end, to have a right is to have something society ought to defend me in the possession of. Why? Utility. We'll all be better off if it protects those.
3.117: Well, there are many, many conflicts we could go through. I have a long part of the slideshow here that actually discusses this conflict, that conflict, and so on. But it's actually going to be the same answer to all of them. I will talk about one here just to illustrate the general point, one from Plato's Republic. "Suppose a friend in his right mind has deposited arms with me and he asks for them when he's not in his right mind, should I give them back?" So you've borrowed his knife. He wants the knife back when he's furious and angry and going crazy. Do you give him the knife back?
3.118: The utilitarian says no because the consequences of giving him the knife back are likely to be very, very bad. So you promised to give it back to him when he needed it. That's a promise you should break. Why? It's going to detract from happiness. Basically, that's going to be the utilitarian response to all of these conflicts. Some people are going to think it's the wrong response, in some cases. The utilitarian will insist that if you take into account the long-term consequences, it's going to be the right one. The end.
3.119: With utilitarianism, there's the premise that all people's good or happiness is equal. Do you see that as a weak point? Because there are those that have what would be considered a higher station, a general, perhaps, over a grunt, someone a leader over a standard civilian, where that could become very problematic or someone who employs 500 people compared to one of their employees, where that's not really an equal thing.
3.120: All right. A great question. How does this compare to those hierarchical structures I mentioned, where there are authority ranking relationships and subordinates and superiors? How do we think about it in that context? It's interesting what we do, actually, because we tend to think— suppose we're in a lifeboat scenario and we have people of different ages. Let's say it's all members of one family. It's clear that we have one more person than can actually survive in this lifeboat. One person has to go for the others to be able to survive, otherwise the boat sinks. Who do you throw overboard? Horrible question.
3.121: You might think, "Oh, well, the person who is superior—do we throw over the baby because it's the least in this social hierarchy?" No, usually we would say—I mean, there are some cultures that would say yes, but I think our culture would tend to say, "No, it has the most—" The utilitarian would say, "We're thinking about the future life wiped out. It has many more life years. It has a much greater potential for happiness. Throw over the old guy." That makes a certain amount of sense from a utilitarian point of view.
3.122: But now, if we transfer that to a different context, we say that a certain number of people have to be laid off in this company. Who should we lay off? There, we have to think, presumably, about the welfare. Usually, the company thinks about the welfare of the company. But if we think about this from a utilitarian point of view and we think we're concerned with everybody's happiness here. We do want the company to survive, so that's really important. But we have also got to think about the effects on people and who's going to be most vulnerable and so on.
3.123: I think it's unclear where that comes out. Sometimes we think, "We have to lay off the people at the bottom because these people's decisions are going to make the difference." Sometimes we think, "No, that's too awful. We shouldn't do that." I had a friend who was faced with this problem. He had to make a cut in his department's budget. As a result, he simply resigned because his salary was large enough to be the amount they had to cut. He could have cut maybe 10 to 20 people in his area, or he could just resign. He said, "I'd rather preserve those jobs, and I resign."
3.124: I think it's a noble action of his. Was that good for the company or bad for the company? I don't know. Was it overall good for people? Almost certainly, yes. The utilitarian would tend to applaud that. But now, to put it in a military context, and thinking about lives, the utilitarian wants to say that all lives are more important. On the other hand, if you're thinking about the objective, whose life matters more to that? The lives themselves are going to have equal value. But in terms of the larger scale picture, maybe the success of our army is going to save a lot of lives and add tremendously to happiness and avoid a huge negative. How best do we do that?
3.125: Maybe there we say that the general's life is worth more than that private's life simply because that person's decisions are going to make a huge impact on the overall outcome of the war; this person's won't. But it's not because this person's life is worth more than that one. It's because overall, making the decisions on that basis are going to lead to the best outcome.
3.126: I think it's going to be highly sensitive to the nature of this hierarchy, what's at stake, what the overall effects are. But we can't get away from the idea that a life is a life no matter whose it is. However, if one person is going to have a much greater effect on other lives than somebody else, they are going to indirectly, in that way, end up being more valuable as a result. What would be lives in the military can become money in a business context.
3.127: But then, in other contexts, for example, within a family, do you do what the kids want to do or do you do what the parents want to do? It may depend on how loud and obnoxious your kids are, because their decisions then and what they do might have a huge effect on the parents' happiness. The parents may be better able to say, "Yeah, we'll go to Chuck E. Cheese again for dinner," and be able to deal with that better than the kids will.
3.128: I think it's going to be sensitive to a lot of the things that are details of the situation. But that's exactly what the utilitarian would say. Sure, some people are going to have bigger effects on other people's happiness than other people will, and weneed to take all that into account. Lecture 4: On Realism At a glance — On realism.
4.1: Today, we're going to be talking about realism, and in particular, some of the foundational principles and foundational figures of Western philosophy. Alfred North Whitehead said that all of Western philosophy could be considered a footnote to Plato. I think that's a bit misleading. Really, Plato and Aristotle, in my view, give us two foundations and two traditions developed throughout Western philosophy. Some are footnotes to Plato, others are footnotes to Aristotle.
4.2: I had a teacher once who said the more he read Plato and Aristotle, the more he was convinced they were in agreement. I think that's totally wrong. I think they're in fundamental disagreement and that there are two traditions competing, sharing ideas, to be sure, but nevertheless really different in their fundamental assumptions.
4.3: For the first half of today, I'm going to talk about the Platonic tradition and its roots in Plato, and then we'll move on to Aristotle and try to get an understanding of how they think it's true that some things are independent of mind, but they're going to focus on different basic things. So it's important to recognize that what Plato takes as fundamental, Aristotle doesn't think exists at all. What Aristotle takes as fundamental, Plato considers merely a shadow. So we're going to see two very different ways of looking at the world. They both agree that there is a world independent of us, a world that's really out there. But their idea of what it consists in, is completely different.
4.4: Before we begin, let's think about the question of what there is. I've said that in philosophy, you could think of three basic questions: What is there? How do we know? Then what do we do, or how should we live? Let's focus on that first question: What is there? That question isn't raised in the context of saying thatthere are cameras and there are lecterns and there are glasses of water and so on. The question is really: What is fundamental?
4.5: Willard Van Orman Quine, a philosopher who taught for many years at Harvard, put it this way, "A curious thing about the ontological problem"— that question of what there is—"is its simplicity. It can be put in three Anglo-Saxon monosyllables: 'What is there?' It can be answered, moreover, in a word—'Everything' —and everyone will accept the answer as true. But that's merely to say that there is what there is. There remains room for disagreement over cases, and so the issue has stayed alive down the centuries." Indeed, there is a difference over the cases, the particular things that are fundamental.
4.6: In that context, let's go back to ancient Greece and look at Plato and Aristotle, think about the perspectives they have on what reality really is and how they differ. Aristotle is one of the foundational figures of Western philosophy. He was a student of Plato and a teacher of Alexander the Great. He gives us a simple argument for realism. He says, "In general, if only the sensible exists, there'd be nothing if animate things were not, for there'd be no faculty of sense."
4.7: In other words, he says, how do I know that there really is a world independent of my mind? He says, suppose that no sentient creatures existed. Suppose there were no human beings, no animals. It's not that distant a hypothesis to imagine a universe without any life in it at all. But if everything depends on a mind, then such a universe couldn't exist. There wouldn't be anything if there were no minds.
4.8: Yet it seems obvious that there could be a universe without any minds. In fact, we tend to think that the history of our own universe for millions of years consisted of things that existed, but there were no minds. And that hypothesis, if we deny realism, seems like a contradiction. He says that here's another way of looking at it. "For sensation isn't just a sensation of itself." It's not just a sensation of nothing. There's got to be something it's the sensation of. There's got to be something beyond that sensation.
4.9: If I look at a glass of water, for example, there must be something that actually causes my sense organs to have that sensation of a glass of water. It seems absurd to think that it's just a fantasy and that there's nothing there at all. So the idea is that sensations are sensations of something. Otherwise, they're nothing but dreams, nothing but fantasies or hallucinations. There must be something prior to the sensation itself. That, whatever it is, has to be a mind-independent cause of the sensation. Call it a thing in itself—that's Kant's term for this thing. But whatever you think of it as, it's going to be something that the sensation is actually a sensation of.
4.10: In order to understand the difference between Plato and Aristotle on what's really fundamental—on what there is—we need to draw a distinction that both of them would accept, though they have different attitudes about what's fundamental here. It's the distinction between particulars and universals.
4.11: What do I mean by a particular? It's a thing that can't have multiple instances. For example, Dan Bonevac. There's one of me. There can't be multiple instances of me. Even if you cloned me somehow and created a bunch of different copies, as in the movie Multiplicity, still, we'd be different beings, different particulars. We wouldn't be just a bunch of Dan Bonevacs. The same thing is true for anybody else. At the time, I was thinking of these examples. It was around the time of the beginning of the First World War, and I was teaching that. So, Gavrilo Princip or the Archduke Francis Ferdinand, those two are particular people.
4.12: Then, we can talk about various entities like the Empire State Building or the Perry- Castañeda Library, or a particular glass of water, or a beach ball, or a grain of sand. In other words, a particular thing. It can be a place. It could be Austin or Phoenix, Texas, Arizona, Sarajevo. Wherever it is, that's a particular place. It could be a particular time, a particular date. It could be an event. But anyway, these are particular things. There's one of them.
4.13: A universal, in contrast, is something that can have multiple instances. A lot of these are properties: red—lots of things are red. Triangular—lots of things are triangular in shape. Large—lots of things are large. And then relations. Between—here are many things that are between other things or things that are sitting on other things. Love is such a universal. It's a relation. But there are many instances of love, many instances of friendship.
4.14: And then, we can talk about kinds like tiger. There are lots of individual tigers or human beings, many humans, many buildings, many pencils, many short stops. There are lots of different instances of those particular universals. We can also talk about books this way. The Bible, for example. There are many different instances, many different translations, but they're all particular instances of the Bible. That would be true of any book. You take any novel, any non-fiction work, there can be many copies of it. It would be disappointing if Amazon could sell you only one copy, and once that copy was gone, it's gone. But no, there can be many copies of the same book. The same thing is true of musical works as well.
4.15: Artistic works, that's more controversial. If you have the Mona Lisa, the original, and then have many different copies of it, or, in a famous case, Duchamp submitted the Fountain to an artistic exhibit. It was just a urinal, and he wrote "R. Mutt, 1917" on it. Then he took it back to the plumbing supply place. He didn't think it had any particular significance, but it became very famous. And so what did he do? He bought a bunch more urinals, wrote "R. Mutt, 1917," and sold them all.
4.16: So maybe there are many copies of the Fountain, or maybe you say that it was the original one, so really, all of these are just duplicates. Well, I can't say duplicates, but maybe they're just imitators. In any case, artistic works are a bit different. However, a musical work or a literary work, those are things you could have multiple instances of.
4.17: The question that becomes controversial in philosophy is: Are these universals real? Properties like red or relations like friendship, are they real components of the world? Or are they just a matter of the way we think about or talk about the world? The realist says, "Yes, they are real, and they are independent of the mind." There is such a property as redness. There is such a relation as love or friendship. Those are things that have a real and independent existence.
4.18: The conceptualist says, "Yes, they're real, but they're mind-dependent." They're a matter of our concepts, organizing the world in a certain way. Those concepts really are constituents of the world, but on the other hand, they're dependent on a mind. So we classify certain human relationships as relations of love or relations of friendship. We categorize certain objects as red or blue. We think about certain things being between other things. That's a matter of our organizing the world. It's not a matter of things that are in the world independently of our mind.
4.19: The nominalist says, "No, they are not real at all." In fact, at one point, a famous nominalist simply said, they are flatus vocis. In other words, winds. Actually, it's rather vulgar in Latin. I will go into the literal translation. But really, they don't have any significance at all. They're just puffs of air. The idea in the nominalist's case is that everything is particular. They're individual red things, individual glasses of water. But some of them are similar to others, and so we group them together in language and apply the same word to them. But there's nothing corresponding to redness or triangularity or friendship. There's just a bunch of relations that we call friendship, or a bunch of objects we call red.
4.20: Let's go back to the realist idea here, which has its roots in Plato. He thinks of universals as real entities of the world, real and mind-independent entities. He is the paradigmatic realist in this sense in the entire Western tradition. He thinks there are what he calls Forms, these mind-independent universals. Redness, triangularity, or friendship or love —those things are fundamental constituents of the world, and they're independent of mind. They're not a matter of how we organize the world. They're not a matter of our concepts or our language. They are really in the world.
4.21: In fact, he thinks in a deeper sense than you and I are in the world. That's a bit shocking. Here is the analogy he uses, a famous allegory of the cave in The Republic. He says, imagine a bunch of people chained into—in a modern sense, this would be like a movie theater. There are no windows. It's all dark, but certain projections are up there on the screen, and you're chained in such a way that you can only look straight ahead, soall you can see are the projections on the screen. He imagines this in a cave with a fire behind and so on, but it's very much like a modern movie theater.
4.22: What would you think? Well, you would imagine that you were looking at reality. The only reality you would know is what's up there on that screen. You would think they were the real things, the real people, the real objects. But at some point, imagine that one of these prisoners locked in that theater manages to get loose a bit and starts looking around and realizing, "Wait a minute, there are other people here with me in this cave, and these things are being projected from behind me. Actually, those aren't the realities at all."
4.23: You can imagine the confusion. You've been thinking, you live in this world, this world projected on the screen, where those are the realities. And suddenly you start getting the sense, "Wait, this is fake." In his image, "These are the shadows of the things that are real back there." In the movie theater analogy, you think these are somehow representations of something being projected there, but I don't know what the reality is. So you get confused.
4.24: And imagine that you manage to get yourself freer and freer to the point where you can get rid of these chains holding you. And now you look around and think, "I want to get out of here. I want to find out what the real things are." So you see in the back an ascent, some stairs that seem to lead out of this theater. So what do you do? You go over, and you start going up that staircase. But it's difficult.
4.25: For one thing, you've been chained, right? Your muscles are atrophied, so it's hard to climb those stairs. Secondly, as you get up further and further, it becomes more and more light. Your eyes aren't used to that. You've been looking at this screen. It's as if you're in a dark theater and suddenly you come out into the sunlight of a summer day. It's painful. So at first, it's hard on your eyes. But finally, you get up above the cave, and you open the door, and it is blinding. At first, you can't see anything. But then your eyes gradually adapt, and you start looking around and you see trees and you see buildings and you see plants and maybe other people. Finally, you get to the point where you can look up, and you actually see the sun.
4.26: That's the image. He's thinking that we are like the prisoners in that cave. We are trapped in a world of sense with what Plato calls "the lovers of sights and sounds." We think those are the real things. But at some point, we start realizing, "Wait a minute, there is something more fundamental. What I've been looking at is merely the shadows, the reflections of the true realities." So what I have to do is force myself to think about what these true realities are. I've got to turn away from the objects of sense and think about the real things.
4.27: What are the real things? That he tries to explain. Because Socrates is giving this analogy in The Republic, and he's talking to someone who says, "How could they see anything but the shadows if they were never allowed to move their heads"—inside this theater or this cave—"and of the objects which are being carried in like manner, they would only see the shadows?" Yes, all we see in the world of sense are these shadows.
4.28: But now, "If they were able to converse with one another, wouldn't they suppose they were naming the things"— that were up there on the screen, the mere shadows? Yes, that's all they'd know. But imagine there was an echo. They'd hear these things, too, and they'd think that was reality. Yes. And so "the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images." And he thinks in our ordinary experience of the world, that's what it's like.
4.29: What we call the truth is nothing but the shadows of the images. So if we can get out of this cave, if we can get out of the theater, we start realizing there's something more. Now, how do we do it? Well, in my analogy here, it's a matter of leaving the theater. But he says that in reality, it's philosophy that can do this. Philosophy forces us to ask what there is, and in particular, what there really is.
4.30: We think about the world around us. It seems to be divided up into objects. We think they're the real things. But Plato says that they're just the shadows of the images. Instead, we have to see the true nature of the world, the true realities. They're not simply the things we see. There are deeper things. So the prisoner released is going to finally be able to look, maybe initially at just shadows and reflections of the real things up above, but then at the actual objects, and finally at the sun.
4.31: That, he says, is the progression of the mind as it begins to think more and more deeply about the world. We start with the objects around us, looking at what we see and what we hear, and then we begin to progress to more abstract things. He thinks the best way to do this is mathematics. Because when you're doing geometry, for example, you're thinking about triangles. You're not thinking about this particular triangle or that one. You're thinking about triangles in general, and it's not just the thing on the page.
4.32: When I was teaching my daughter geometry—and by the way, she ended up as a math major, so it worked out okay in the end. But initially, she was given a problem. There was an angle drawn there on the page and labeled with things and so on. There was a triangle, and she was asked to show that it was a right triangle. She took out a protractor, measured, and said, "See, 90 degrees!" Well, that's not a geometric proof. That reveals something about that particular triangle drawn on the page. But of course, that's not what you do in geometry. You have to take that as merely a representation, a shadow of the thing you're really trying to make the proof about. I had to explain that.
4.33: That's why Plato actually thinks math, and in particular, geometry, is really helpful because you have, in a sense, something that is sensible, but you are led to think not about that particular triangle, but about any triangle that fits a certain specification, about the nature of triangularity itself. So it leads you to abstract Forms. But now he thinks once you've done that, the ones that are directly linked to sense, like triangle or circle or something like that, you can then begin to progress to more and more abstract Forms, things like the good or the just.
4.34: So, he says, think of the world as divided up into realms like this. On the left of this diagram is the visible world. It consists partly of shadows and reflections and perceptions of shadows and reflections. There are the real objects of perception: the actual trees and buildings and animals, plants, human beings that we see. That is the realm, he says, of opinion.
4.35: But then we can move to this intellectual world. That's what you do when you stop thinking about that particular triangle on the page and start thinking about triangularity as such. You begin to move on to these Forms, at first, the Forms that correspond to shapes and number and other things like that in mathematics, and then you move on to the more abstract ones. That's really the realm of reason.
4.36: He says that gradually, as you learn, as you progress through school, you start out with the basic things, the things around you, the objects of sense, but then you move more and more in the direction of abstraction until you're thinking about things that are actually highly abstract and aren't found directly in the world at all. The visible world, he says, is a reflection of the intellectual world. It's the intellectual world that consists of the real realities.
4.37: So Socrates says, "This entire allegory,"—of the cave, that is—" you may now append to the previous argument: the prison house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun"—in my version, it's the theater and the projector—"you won't misapprehend me if you apprehend the journey upwards to be the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world, according to my poor belief, which at your desire I've expressed, whether rightly or wrongly God knows."
4.38: So Socrates, from one point of view, is humble here. He's saying, I don't know if I'm right. Maybe only God knows that. But here is the way I see it. The things around us aren't the ultimate realities. They're the shadows of the ultimate realities. So here is a way of thinking about Plato's philosophy of mind. These diagrams I learned from my teacher, Wilfrid Sellars. This is the way he understood Plato, and I think it's very revealing.
4.39: I have a thought. I'm looking at the thing on the page, as my daughter did, saying, "Okay, that's a triangle." There's a particular object, in this case, drawn on the page that I'm thinking about, but I also recognize it as a triangle. I recognize this as an instance of triangularity. My mind is focused both on that thing I'm perceiving, the actual triangle on the page, but also on triangularity, the form. I'm thinking about the universal at the same time I'm thinking about the particular when I classify the object as a triangle and say, "That's a triangle."
4.40: Now, here I think it's important to recognize that for Plato, I am seeing it as a triangle by seeing it as an instance of that more general form. I'm recognizing this is a particular case of something that actually has multiple instances. This is a triangle, meaning this is an instance of triangularity, or in his language, it participates in triangularity.
4.41: Now, why should we think these Forms exist at all? Why should we think they're the ultimate realities? Plato does give us some arguments for this, and I'm not sure they all work, but I think it's valuable to look at them and understand why he thinks this. Because at first glance, you might think, "What a weird view to think that you and I aren't the ultimate realities. We're just shadows of humanity. That's odd." But why would you think that? Well, he gives us, I think, five arguments.
4.42: Let's look at the first: general thoughts. I can think about triangles as such. I can think about horses. I can think about saguaro cacti. I can think about all sorts of things, and in doing that and thinking about these general thoughts, there must be something that the particular instances have in common that I'm really thinking about.
4.43: Let's say I think about horses. I'm thinking about horses as such, not just this particular horse or that particular horse. I'm thinking about horses and what horses are like. So there must be something I'm thinking about. That is the thing that all those particular horses have in common: their horsiness, I guess. That's something that is the character of being a horse that I'm reflecting on when I think about horses in general.
4.44: It seems possible to have those thoughts. I can think about triangles in general, circles in general, but then more abstract things like horses. Here I mean the kind, horses, the things that horses have in common. I can think about justice. I can think about all sorts of things that involve abstractions that aren't found directly in things themselves but are exemplified in the things themselves. A particular horse is an example of this. But insofar as I'm thinking about horses in general, having a general thought about horses, it seems as if I'm focusing on something that isn't just this or that particular horse.
4.45: Let's take the example of trees. I look at trees in various parts of the country, and in the past week, I've been in North Carolina and Texas and Arizona. Very different instances of trees in those three places, and yet I recognize them all as trees. I can talk about trees and what trees are like. It seems as if there must be something like being a tree that I'm able to reflect on. All these individual trees are instances of being a tree.
4.46: We're thinking in geometry, but in all of those cases, not of the particular trees or the particular horses or the particular triangles. We're thinking not of those, but of the ideals they resemble. That's Plato's point. We're thinking about triangularity or circularity or being a tree or being a horse as such. It seems possible to do that. In fact, it seems as if when I think about a particular horse or a particular triangle or a particular tree, I'm actually using that knowledge of what it is to be a tree or a triangle or a horse, and that's being activated, as it were, when I recognize that thing as a triangle or a tree or a horse.
4.47: He says that it looks as if those particulars are really something like reflections of the general thing: being a horse, being a triangle, and so on. Those are things that can only be seen by the eye of the mind. And that idea, that there's something like an eye of the mind that is capable of thinking about triangularity as such, or being a tree, or being a horse as such, is fundamental to the way Plato is thinking about this. I see individual trees; I don't see the abstraction of being a tree. Nevertheless, I got to be able to think about it. I must be able to perceive it with something like the eye of the mind.
4.48: Secondly, regularities. I can recognize regularities. Last night, there was lots of lightning that could be seen in the sky, occasionally, thunder along with it, and I might recognize that lightning seems to be followed by thunder. I'm not just thinking about that particular flash of lightning and that particular crash of thunder. I'm talking about a general pattern. But that means I'm linking being lightning to being thunder in a way that, to be fully general and to be a regularity, must involve thinking about the abstractions, not just the particular cases.
4.49: Third, the same thing is true in the case of laws. I have all sorts of things I call laws in science, and it looks as if in doing that, I'm not just talking about particular instances of mass or acceleration or motion or force or whatever it happens to be. I'm thinking about those as abstractions. I'm thinking about acceleration in general or velocity in general. Those things involve thinking not about the particular cases, but the things that have multiple instances. I can have a law, like force is mass times acceleration, and that's something that's about force as such, mass as such, acceleration as such. And then I have lots of instances of it when I look at things accelerated by the application of a force.
4.50: Fourth, we can think about communication or meaning. I'm able to use the word triangle, and you are too, and somehow we communicate with each other. If there's not something that anchors both of our ideas of triangularity, how is that even possible? I would have an idea, maybe of triangularity in my head, you'd have one in your head. How is it possible to actually have any confidence that the idea in your head is anything like the idea in my head?
4.51: I've got to be able to actually latch on to something that is going to represent something like the content of the word or the content of the thought. Those contents can't be just in your mind or my mind. Then it looks like we have different contents for every person. There must be something those contents actually link up to that gives our thoughts content outside of any individual mind.
4.52: One way of looking at it is to say that you and I communicate. I have an idea in my head. I manage to have confidence that that idea is being conveyed into your head. But why should I have that confidence? Or it doesn't even involve interpersonal things. What about me earlier and me later? I think about this yesterday, then I talk about it today. Why should I have any confidence that what I'm talking about today is what I was thinking about yesterday? Maybe it turns out I have totally different ideas yesterday and today.
4.53: The only reason I have for being confident that I'm thinking the same thought is that there's something outside of my head at a particular time that can be a content that I can somehow attach to on both occasions. Of course, it's not just at different times; it might be in different circumstances. Suppose instead of having a white background here, I had some other background. Would the entire content of what I'm saying be different? Well, of course not. But that means it isn't tied to a particular context, a particular surrounding, or anything like that. It's got to be attached to something independent of the particular circumstances.
4.54: Finally, I want to say that some thoughts are accurate, that sometimes I'm describing the world correctly, that I'm saying something true, for example, that my thought is veridical, meaning it matches the world. I want to think sometimes I'm stating the truth objectively. But how is that possible? How can we distinguish truth from falsehood, or correctness from incorrectness, or accuracy from inaccuracy?
4.55: There must be something that relates the content of what I say. Like, "That's a triangle"— that has a content, and somehow that content has to relate to the individual thing I'm describing. He refers to that relation as participation. We might call it simply being an instance of triangularity. But whatever term we use, we've got to have some relationship between the universal and the particular thing such that the particular really is an instance of that universal. Then I can say, good, my thought is true when I'm saying "this is a triangle," for example, and it really does exemplify triangularity. It gives me a way of accounting for the difference between truth and falsehood, accuracy and inaccuracy.
4.56: But now we face a serious problem. We don't perceive the Forms. I mean, I see individual triangles, I don't perceive triangularity. I see maybe instances of just and unjust behavior, but I don't see justice and injustice as such. So how is it possible to know anything about them? In the physics lab, I might accelerate a variety of objects, so I see particular instances of acceleration. Nevertheless, I draw conclusions about acceleration as such. But I don't see acceleration as such. I see particular instances. So how can I know anything about these universals?
4.57: Plato gives us some answers that aren't entirely satisfactory. In the Meno, he says, "I recollect them. Before I was born, my mind was united with the Forms. And then, being born, I was washed with something that caused me to forget them. And so I have to gradually remember them." Well, that's a pretty metaphorical account. I'm not saying there isn't some core there that we can resurrect, but by itself, that seems like a fable, not an account.
4.58: In The Republic, he says, "It's the Form of the Good." Just as the sun illumines the objects outside of the theater, so the Form of the Good illumines my mind and enables me to perceive the other Forms. But that, too, isn't a great account. After all, if the other Forms don't seem to have this power, why does the Form of the Good have that power? It looks as if that's an unsatisfying answer. Indeed, within a generation, most people in Plato's Academy, the school he founded, became skeptics. They decided, "Phooey, I don't see how we can know these Forms," and they gave up on the whole idea. It wasn't until much later that the idea got resurrected.
4.59: Because in Plato, the picture is something like this. I perceive the object, and that's a particular object, so I can talk about that in an ordinary way about causal relationships and my faculties of perception. But then what is this relation to the Form? Well, I somehow recollect it, maybe. The good serves as something like the sun to light this whole thing up and make it possible. That seems weird. There are three parts to that.
4.60: First of all, there is this metaphysical aspect having to do with the relation between the Form and the object and the role of the sun here or the good. That seems odd. Then, there is the semantic question of my idea or my sentence, my thought, having a relation to this abstract Form. So there's something about content or meaning there. Then, I've got to have something I say about the theory of knowledge. How is it that I recollect or know these Forms? There are a lot of parts here that are remaining to be explained.
4.61: There are different strategies. The realist says, "I take for granted that there really are these things that serve as our contents and that objects really do exemplify them. So I now have to give you a theory of knowledge. I have to explain how we can know the Forms." That's one way of trying to solve this problem. A second way that the conceptualist uses is say, "Let's stick those Forms inside your mind, and then they're just concepts. So now it's not complicated to say how you know them. They're right there in your mind." Then, the nominalist says, "I'm going to erase them altogether. All I need now is to explain a theory of meaning in such a way that I don't need to have these contents outside of anybody's head."
4.62: That is a set of problems that we're going to come back to. But on the other hand, it was enough to make people give up on Platonism for hundreds of years. Really, it wasn't until Jewish and Christian thinkers came along and said, "The Form of the Good —it does all this? I don't see how that's possible, but God could do it." If you replace the Form of the Good with God, then, aha, problem solved. God can do anything. That's actually a pretty stable solution, and it lasts for about a thousand years, as we'll see. But that's a story for a little bit in the future.
4.63: Let's turn to that other tradition I was talking about in Aristotle. Aristotle starts out with a purely grammatical account. He says, I want to account for what there is, but let's look at language. Let's see what language actually commits us to and what we actually think about and talk about. Well, he says, "Expressions that aren't composite,"—so aren't complex, simple expressions, signify the following things. They "signify substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, or affection."
4.64: Here's an example. Substance: things like man or horse or Socrates. Quantity: like 6 feet tall or 235 square miles. Quality: like white, tall, angry, wise, red, triangular. Relations: like double or greater than or loves or is a friend of. Then, there are places: at the market or in Austin. Times: today, at noon, for a week. Position: like lying, sitting, standing, talking. States: like being armed or puzzled or impressed. Actions: like hit, smile, do, walk, thank. Then affection, passive forms of those: like to be hit or to be thanked.
4.65: Anyway, you can see that they look very grammatical. We've got nouns, we've got adjectives, we've got prepositional phrases of various kinds. Then we've got gerunds and gerundives and verbs in active and passive forms. At first glance, it seems likethis is just grammar, really. And in one sense, that's where he's starting. He's saying, you want to know what's in the world? We talk about the world all the time. Let's see how we talk about it. What are we talking about? Let's turn to language.
4.66: That's not the only way of thinking about categories. There is a tradition in India, the Vaisheshika tradition, that says there are only three basic categories, really. We can simplify that picture. There are substances like a pot or a cloth or Socrates. There are qualities, and there are motions, actions like moving, eating, throwing. Those are things that Aristotle would recognize.
4.67: But then, the Indian thinkers in the Vaisheshika tradition say that that's really all we need. Those are the existent things. Then, relations and places and times, we can put them into one of those three categories. Maybe we can simplify Aristotle's scheme. As that tradition in India progresses, people begin to think, wait, what about other things?
4.68: I want to mention this just to indicate Aristotle is making choices, and they're not necessarily the obvious choices. One thing is something Plato would insist on: What about universality? What about, in other words, triangularity or friendship as such? Plato would add those as fundamental. In fact, they're thinking they're more fundamental than the others. But what about things like "the pots being blue"? What the thinkers in this tradition call the inherence. That's something like Plato's relation of participation. So maybe we need that, and Plato would agree, yeah, we need that. But then what about individualizers?
4.69: Let's say you go to visit the Dixie Cup factory. Not sure anybody's ever done that. But if you did that, you'd see all these Dixie Cups being produced. They all look alike. Nevertheless, they're all different. They all exemplify Dixie Cupness. But there's this one, this one, this one. What makes them different? Well, there must be something that makes them different. So the Vaisheshika tradition evolves to the point where people say, "I need an individualizer, something that makes this one different from that one, even though their shapes are exactly the same, the matter in them is exactly the same and so on."
4.70: And then, what about absences, like the elephant right here? There's no elephant right here. But if I say, "There is no elephant here." What makes that true? You might think I need absences or lacks. And by the way, there's a very funny paper by David and Stephanie Lewis called Holes, about whether holes are real constituents of the world. It's entertaining, but it's addressing this issue. Do we have to talk not only about what's here, but what's missing? And maybe to give a full account of reality we do.
4.71: In any case, I want to mention those to indicate that Aristotle's way isn't the only way of setting it up like this. What are these categories, categories of? You might think, "It's a matter of grammar. He's just listing the parts of speech." Or you might think, "I don't know, there are these different things that we talk about, so maybe there are different constituents of reality."
4.72: Here's how he thinks of it. He says, "There's a science that investigates being as being and the attributes that belong to this in virtue of its own nature." In other words, he's thinking of metaphysics, this part of philosophy that answers the question, what is there, as being the science of being, qua being. That's an odd phrase, but the idea is that when we think about what there is, we're thinking about what is being and what is being as such. In other words, what is it to be something? He thinks that's really the fundamental question.
4.73: Because I could say, "What is there?" and start listing a bunch of things. I could think, "What are the basic things?" and then start listing things like substances, qualities, quantities, relations. But I could also say, "What is it to be?" You're asking me what there is. I want to know more about "what this is" business is involving. What is it to be something? And he thinks that's the most fundamental question in metaphysics.
4.74: The moment he raises that, he says that here's why it's complicated. There are many different ways in which things are said to be, but all of them are related to one central point. So what are the categories? There are ways in which a thing can be said to be. You can be a horse, you can be brown, you can be in Austin, you can be between this thing and that thing, you can be lying down, you can be running, and so on. All of those are ways in which something can be something.
4.75: He says they're all related to one central sense. From one point of view, the categories are just the ways you can be something, the ways in which you can be, but they all relate to one thing, namely, substance. Because what we have are quantities of substance, relations between substances, qualities of substance, places where a substance can be, times at which a substance can be, things a substance can do or have done to it, and so on. They all relate to substance in the end. So all the other categories depend on substance. Everything is really a quantity-quality relation, et cetera, of a substance or of substances.
4.76: That means, yes, there are many senses in which a thing can be said to be, but in the end, there is one thing that is really fundamental. He calls it—well, he doesn't call it; scholars call it a focal meaning of being. The central meaning of being is substance. So the best answer to what there is is that there is substance. Or maybe we should say there are substances.
4.77: Now, what is a substance? He says it's of a kind, so it has a species, and that species is a specific kind that falls under a certain genus. So I, for example, am a substance. I am of a certain kind. I am a human being, and that falls under a more general kind: I am an animal, and so on and so forth. So all substances are of a kind, but moreover, I'm a particular instance of that kind.
4.78: So one way Aristotle puts it is, "I am a this such," and that's to say, I am a particular instance of a kind. I am this particular instance of humanity. And that's true of any substance. That particular horse is a particular horse of a kind. It's a horse, so it's this horse or that triangle. Notice here: there is a difference from Plato because he's saying that the fundamental things aren't things like triangularity or being a horse or being a human being or humanity. The fundamental things are substances: that horse, this human being, and so on. Now, those are the primary substances.
4.79: There are secondary substances, kinds, because I can also talk about horses, human beings, triangles in general. That's true. But I don't need any abstraction like triangularity or humanity to be able to do that because I can focus on kinds of things. If I say, "Cats meow," I'm not referring necessarily to each individual cat. There might be cats that don't meow, but I'm talking about the kind and predicating something of the kind. In this secondary way, we also have to recognize these substances as being kinds of things.
4.80: But the primary substances are the particular instances of those kinds, the individual cats. Then I can generalize about the kind cat. But that's not an abstract form as in Plato, because it exists only in the individual cats. We see this in what linguists call bear plurals, things like cat's meow or tigers are striped, philosophy majors are smart, whatever—these are things that talk about a kind, and there can be exceptions. Not every cat has to meow, not every tiger has to be striped, not every philosophy major is smart.
4.81: Now, let's go back to that core idea: a substance is a this such. It's this particular thing of a certain kind. How do we tell that something is a substance? First of all, there are no degrees of it. Think about hot and cold. Those are qualities, and there are degrees of that: something could be hotter or colder. But there aren't degrees of substance. If you're a horse, there's no such thing as being more of a horse or less of a horse. You're just a horse, period. Similarly, you're a triangle. You're a triangle or you're not. There's no, well, it's a little bit more of a triangle. No.
4.82: Secondly, there's no contrary. We can have contraries like hot and cold or black and white, but we don't have contraries like being human versus what exactly? I mean, we can make one up: nonhuman. But the fact is, there's no natural contrary. There's no natural opposite to being a human or being a horse or being a tree.
4.83: Then, substances can admit contrary qualities. I can be asleep at one time and awake at another time. I can be speaking at one time and silent at another time. The same thing is true of that individual horse or that tree. The tree might have leaves on it now, but later in winter might lose its leaves. Contrary qualities can be had by the same substance. That's not going to be true of other kinds of things, like qualities themselves. It's not as if being hot, let's say, can sometimes be cold. No, it's being hot.
