4.84: I've said that ontology is the science of what there is. It is really the central part, you might say, of metaphysics. It's the examination of that question, what there is. Aristotle says that now we know how to answer that question. In the primary sense, what is there? Substance. The basic question then, if you ask what is being, what is it to be? In that primary sense, it's just to ask: What is substance? We've already said that in a sense. We've said it's to be a particular instance of a kind, to be that particular human being or that particular triangle or that particular horse.
4.85: But now, in the most difficult book of the Metaphysics, Book Zeta, he starts examining this question more carefully, and I tread on it now nervously because it's difficult and because it represents the only incomplete I ever took in graduate school. I thought I was going to come up with a grand explanation of what Aristotle had in mind in Metaphysics Zeta. After working on it all summer, I realized I got nothing, and so I changed my topic entirely. But I now think I understand it better.
4.86: What he's doing there is he says, I want to understand what it is to be a this such. A particular human being, that's a primary substance. But let's dig a little deeper. What is that? Because after all, Plato is going to insist that I'm merely a shadow. I'm merely a shadow of humanity. I'm a reflection of this more general thing, this abstract concept or this abstract Form— I shouldn't say concept because it's really supposed to be independent of mind in Plato.
4.87: He's thinking, what could a substance then really be? He's concerned to not say that it's a Form. Here, he says that there are four things we could describe as substance. There is the essence and the universal. In other words, we could say, as Plato does, that humanity is the ultimate substance; I'm just a particular instance participating in it. Or we could say it's the genus. We could say the substratum. We could say the individual thing, just me, individual human beings, for example. We'll get to what he means by the substratum.
4.88: Let's start with this idea that substances are individual things. I think that's what Aristotle thinks is closest to our idea of substance. It's particular people, particular pens, particular horses and trees. Here are some of the criteria he mentions. These aren't things that are predicable of anything else. I can talk about red, and many things are red, but I can't talk about many things being Socrates or many things being Sarajevo. These are particular things.
4.89: Being a particular, not predicable of anything else, well, individual things are like that, so good. Substances underlie everything else. It does seem as if everything in the world is a particular this or that, so that seems good. A substance is supposed to be an individual thing. Well, individual things are individual, so that's good. They shouldn't have contraries, and individual things have no contraries. There's no opposite to being Dan Bonevac. They don't have degrees. There's no more or less of being me. They admit contrary qualities. Yes, I can be speaking, I can be silenced.
4.90: But now, am I really primary? Here, Aristotle starts to worry because he thinks that we can distinguish matter from form. That's a pretty fundamental divide in Aristotle. He thinks everything has matter. I am flesh and blood, as Aquinas later describes it, but I'm also that in a particular form. So I can distinguish the matter, the things that make me up from the particular form they take in me. That suggests that maybe substance isn't really primary. Maybe I have to distinguish it into matter and form. That worries him. That's a strike against thinking of individual things as substances.
4.91: What about compounds in general? For example, matter and shape. Let's get away from an individual human being, partly because I don't want to imagine the same matter in a different form, like toss me in a blender and see what happens. Let's get away from that thought and think about a statue instead.
4.92: I've got a particular statue. Somebody makes up a statue of Hercules, and it looks like it's got a matter in it, let's say we've made it of bronze. And it's also got a particular shape, so I can distinguish the matter of the statue from the form of the statue. They are separable. I could melt it down and make that bronze into something else, or I could make the same form out of something else. I could maybe make a cast of it and then do it in clay or something else. So I can distinguish the matter from the shape of that compound, that statue.
4.93: But that makes me think, then, that it's not really primary, is it? I don't want to say the statue is really a fundamental thing. It looks like there's the bronze of which it's made, then it's in a particular shape. But it seems like if anything's fundamental there, it's the bronze. That could lead me to think, "What if substances just matter?" It's the bronze of the statue, or it's the flesh and blood of the human being, or it's the, I don't know, the various parts out of which the piano is made. Take an individual object and start thinking it's the matter that is involved in it.
4.94: Well, he says, here's the worry. It's obscure what matter really is. If matter isn't substance, it's hard to say what else is. But if we strip everything off, evidently nothing but matter remains. Here's what worries him. We start taking away qualities. What is it that is in this shape? Well, the bronze. We could stop there and just say it's the bronze.
4.95: Or we could push further in science and say, ultimately, maybe it's microparticles, or it's a string, or it's an electromagnetic field. Or whatever our favorite theory of physics is, we say, ultimately, it's really that. Or we could do what John Locke does and keep saying, what is it that is the bronze? What is it that is an electron? What is it that is a particular field? In the end, we're going to end up saying, "I have no idea what it is," and we'll talk about that a bit later.
4.96: He says, here's part of the problem. If it's this matter that's substance, that seems bizarre because, first of all, we want substances to be separable. I want to be able to talk about this substance and that substance. If we end up with just matter, it looks like it doesn't have a natural separation in that way.
4.97: We just talked about the matter comprising the universe, but it's hard to divide it. Maybe there are particles, and we could think what particle physics tells us, that in the end, those things are divided. But what if it's something like a field or a string? Then we have something that isn't separable at all. He says that separability, thisness, we attach that to our idea of substance, and matter isn't going to give us that. So it seems like matter can't really be substance.
4.98: Well, then what about the shape or the form or the universal? What about the shape of the statue? Maybe that's fundamental, but that doesn't really seem fundamental either. I mean, it's a universal that might make Plato happy. But on the other hand, that can't be the name of a substance. The substance is individual. And so the name of the substance should indicate what's unique about it. But to just say it's something bronze doesn't indicate anything unique about it. The universal is what things have in common. All of those individual horses are instances of being a horse, maybe, but you don't want to say being a horse is the substance. That doesn't seem right.
4.99: No universal attribute can be a substance. Here really is part of his argument against Plato, because we think of substances as the things that I can say, "this substance or that substance," that I refer to in my speech and that I think about. It really isn't primarily these abstract universals. That just gives us the such part, not the this. Matter would give us maybe the this, maybe not even if it's not separable, but it's not going to give us the such. So they can't be right. So universals are going to flunk several of these tests. They are predicable over a variety of things. They're not individual, they're not primary, they don't admit contrary qualities. So it looks like that's a problem.
4.100: What about the substratum? What even is the substratum? It's maybe just what everything else could be predicated of. It's not predicated of anything else. That seems to work in some ways, but on the other hand, that looks like in the end, if you really think about what's that root, it's going to end up being either matter or form or some compound. So it just throws us back into the circle at some other part. Consequently, it looks like at best that's going to be something that doesn't give us universality.
4.101: What about a kind? Those are supposed to be secondary substances, he says. They are predicable of other things. There can be many human beings or many tigers, many trees, so kinds can't be the fundamental thing. They're not individual.
4.102: Here is now, I think, the moral of that book, Zeta. He says, in the end, nothing really satisfies all the criteria for being a substance. When we think intuitively about what a substance is, what would be fundamental in the world, there are a number of criteria we have, a number of things we associate with that. The thing that comes closest isthe individual object of a certain kind: you, me, a particular horse, a particular tree. Those are the things that come closest to our idea of substance.
4.103: But I think in the end, what he's saying there is nothing exactly satisfies it. Maybe our intuitive idea of a substance is actually not entirely coherent. That could be. It may be that we start with language and start with the way we think. We say, "What's really fundamental to our thinking? What's primary in our thinking and talking about things?" It looks like, well, individual objects.
4.104: But then, when we examine carefully what we think about that, we realize that the idea is actually a little bit confused. We've got to clean it up a bit. When we clean it up, we realize the closest thing we have to a substance is, in a sense, a compound. It does consist of matter and form. It is "a this" and "a such." That makes it sound compound and therefore derivative and not fundamental. But he says that actually, that's the closest we can come to reflecting this idea of what's basic in the world. The moment we say that it's just the such part or it's just the this part, that leads us into big trouble.
4.105: I now think he's basically saying, "I wish I could have it all. I wish substance could be all of these things." It turns out there's nothing that's really like all of those things, but the closest thing we have, and the thing we most naturally talk about, are the particular things around us. So, where Plato starts and says, in the end, reflections or shadows, Aristotle says that maybe it doesn't satisfy everything we would like as a foundational object, that is what the world really consists in, but it's the closest thing we have. That is really what we have to think of the world as consisting of.
4.106: Now, he does admit that in a certain sense, you could use substance in two ways then. You could talk about each individual thing: the this, such, that horse, that tree. Or you could mean the ultimate substratum, the thing not predicated of anything else, just the stuff out of which everything is made. They both might be legitimate uses of the word substance. Neither one gives you all the criteria, but nevertheless, they come as close as anything else. They come closer, really, than all the competitors.
4.107: We think about the statue and we think, there's that particular statue, and then there's the stuff out of which it's made. You could call either one of them substance. But I think he prefers to think of substance in the primary sense as the statue, the this such, that particular thing.
4.108: Now, one more important distinction in Aristotle. We can distinguish essential from accidental properties. Things are said to be in an accidental sense or by their own nature. So you have certain properties, essentially. Without them, you wouldn't be you. Other things are accidental. You could change them and you'd still be you. So the essence of a thing is what it is said to be, propter se—in the Greek, it's kath’ auto, "by virtue of itself." There are things you have inherently by virtue of being you. So what are things like that?
4.109: Consider these candles. They can be solid or they can melt under heat, but it's still the same candle. Being liquid or being solid is not an essential property of the candle. It could be either one. They are contingent. The object might or might not have them. I could be awake, I could be asleep. I could be lying down, I could be standing up. Those are accidental properties of me. I can change those properties; I'm still me.
4.110: On the other hand, essential properties, they're different. Without an essential property, the thing would not be what it is. That candle wouldn't be that candle. Maybe it wouldn't be a candle at all if it didn't have those properties. They're necessary to being the thing. They have them by virtue of what they are. So maybe what is essential to the candle is being made of wax. What's essential to me as a human being, maybe it's to have a certain DNA, it's to have a certain biological property.
4.111: Being musical is an example he uses. Is being musical something that is essential to someone? Well, no. You could stop being musical or start being musical—you're still you. You could learn to play the piano or play the drums. It's something that doesn't change who you are. It's only things by your nature that you are essentially.
4.112: One way of thinking about this is to say, suppose we could define something, then that definition would give you the essence. It's the formula of the essence. Now, the essence then is precisely what something is, and that means we have essences only of things we could define.
4.113: So he says, really, you can define kinds. I can't define individual people. I could define human being, maybe if I knew enough biology, but I can't define Dan Bonevac. I can't define Socrates in the same way because the such part I could give a definition of, but the this part can't really be defined.
4.114: The essential property—what is it? It's what it is to be the thing, what it is by virtue of itself, what it is by its very nature, what would be expressed by a definition of it. Those are all ways of thinking about what the essential properties of a thing are. Those are things that are necessary for being a thing of that kind. Particulars? He thinks about whether there is an essence of a particular thing. It's complicated, but in the end, not really, because I can't define the this part.
4.115: Now, one last thought. There are natural kinds, and those natural kinds push us in a certain direction. What's the essence of water? Well, it's what it is to be water, what's necessary for being water. In a modern sense, we say that's being H₂O. But of course, that's something we learned only around 1750. Before that, we were still talking about water, what was essential to it.
4.116: That's going to be something that motivates later philosophers to think, actually, there are two ways of talking about essence. There's the nominal essence, the set of properties we ordinarily associate with the kind, and then there's the real essence, the scientific account of what that kind is. It's going to apply only to these natural kinds like water or gold. It won't apply to things like philosopher or writing implement or something like that. Those are artificial kinds. But a natural kind, we're going to see that the concept of the essence starts dividing in two. But that's for a later part of the story. Thank you. Questions?
4.117: Hopefully, I can express this. Based on what we were just talking about, it seems like a lot of the difficulty in defining everything does come down to a lot of grammar and a lot of linguistic subtleties, especially between the implicit and the explicit. I'm wondering, are you able to comment on, linguistically, some of the different philosophy, the evolution of philosophy between, say, Aristotle and Plato with more of a Greek, the original Greek, and then, say, Confucius with Chinese, and I forget the one from India, just how the linguistics plays into the evolution of these philosophical ideas?
4.118: That's a great question. Yes, conceptual schemes are expressed in language, and so differences between languages are really going to lead people to have different ideas about what's fundamental in this way. In some sense, every language has something like a noun, or at least those languages have something like a noun. So the idea of substance is something that persists across all of those different cultures and all those philosophical traditions.
4.119: But you're right to say that language differences matter. For example, in India, part of the reason things go in a slightly different direction is that Sanskrit is even more highly inflected and more complex a language than Greek. Greek is much more complicated than English. In English, we're happy to say, yeah, there are things. Everything exists. Just focus on what nouns refer to, and you're good, really.
4.120: In Greek, you've got all sorts of grammatical cases and verb conjugations and so on that are much more complex, even than in Latin. Those of us who started learning Latin and then learn Greek, it's like, "Oh, Greek is miserable." The people who start out with Greek, then turn to Latin and say, "Oh, all this stuff is missing."
4.121: Greek is complicated, but Sanskrit is even more complex. There's a lot of subtlety that some of the Indian thinkers conceive of that is missing from Greek philosophy, like this idea of absences. It's something that's natural to express in Sanskrit, not so much in Greek or English. We don't tend to think about holes or the absence of elephants as things we have to worry about. But in Sanskrit, that's a pretty natural thing to think.
4.122: Now, in Chinese, here, classical Chinese has so few case markings or connectives that it's highly ambiguous. For example, there is a verse in The Analects that simply says— it's usually translated as something like, "If Confucius's mat was not straight, he would not sit on it," or "If the seat isn't right for you, don't sit in it." But Chinese is literally just, "Seat no right, no sit." That's it. We have to figure out, how do we express that? What does that mean?
4.123: In particular, in classical Chinese, there is no word for "if." There is no "and." There's a big difference between "If that's a cat, it might scratch you," and "That's a cat, and it might scratch you." It's just "cat might scratch." That means that what we think of as logical structure—something that is investigated a lot in Indian philosophy and in Greek philosophy—is missing from Chinese philosophy. There just isn't the language to express those distinctions.
4.124: So I think you're right. If we started with a language that actually was agglomerative or in some way didn't have something like a noun, suppose that it basically took adjectives or verbs as its foundational thing, and there really weren't any nouns.
4.125: Jorge Luis Borges thinks about a language like this in one of his stories, Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, that we'll refer to later. Then we'd say, "Oh, then it's going to look like maybe events or qualities are fundamental and not substances." So I agree with you. Language is intimately tied up with these questions. Lecture 5: On Skepticism At a glance — On skepticism.
5.1: In this lecture, I'm going to talk about skepticism. I'm going to try to convince you you know nothing at all. In fact, not only that you know nothing, it's not even reasonable to have any beliefs. So I intend to reduce you to intellectual rubble—or at least I will give you the arguments that people have used to try to reduce people to intellectual rubble.
5.2: I mentioned last time that within a generation, Plato's students in the Academy had given up on his idea because they saw no way to explain how it was possible for us to know the Forms. So they became skeptics. And skepticism remained throughout the entire Hellenistic period— and really up until about the year 500, say—a major influence, one of the three main schools of Western philosophy.
5.3: Then, throughout the medieval period, it went into the background. Many of the texts were lost, but they were rediscovered during the Renaissance. So skepticism became very powerful again back in the, say, 15th and 16th centuries. Throughout the early modern period, philosophers are constantly battling the skeptics, trying to show how it's possible for us to have some knowledge.
5.4: Throughout the whole history of philosophy, whether you're talking about Western philosophy or Indian philosophy, Chinese philosophy, there have been skeptics. They've always been a small minority, but on the other hand, they bother everyone else rather intensely because they realize, "If I'm to convince you that I know anything and that you have any reason to believe anything, I have to in some way refute the skeptics." It's a challenge that most people see merely as a challenge. They're not convinced, but they also have a hard time explaining what's wrong with this view.
5.5: Modern skeptics usually have the view that knowledge is impossible. In fact, they define skepticism in many ways as the view that knowledge is impossible. But ancient skepticism tended to be more sweeping. It's not just that you know nothing. There is no reason to believe anything. Many of the ancient skeptics say, "Take any proposition, there is every bit as much reason to believe it as to disbelieve it." You're always in this balance of reasons. There's always evidence on one side, evidence against. There is ultimately no reason to believe anything.
5.6: So the skeptic holds, if you take that modern view about knowledge, you think that beliefs are unjustified or unreliable, depending on how you view knowledge, whether it requires justification, as Plato, for example, tended to think, or whether it requires reliability, as people in the Indian tradition and some more modern philosophers have thought. But in either case, knowledge is impossible.
5.7: Now, if you have skepticism about a particular area, that's not so shocking. People argue considerably in physics and in popular culture about whether there's life on other planets, somewhere else in the universe. Well, you might be a skeptic about that. You might say, "I don't think there's any reason to believe that there is. I don't see any reason to believe that there isn't. It's just an open question. So I suspend judgment." And that's not a shocking thing. Nobody thinks, "Oh, my, this is Earth-shattering." You could just say, "Yeah, I don't think that." And there are people who are skeptics like that about, let's say, what is really fundamental in the universe, or about the existence of God, or all sorts of questions. You might be a skeptic about this or that.
5.8: But what's interesting from a philosophical point of view is mostly an extreme form—a global skepticism. What if all of our beliefs are unjustified or unreliable? What if there's never any reason to believe anything? What if all knowledge about anything at all is impossible? Socrates is reported to have said, "All I know is that I know nothing." If you reflect on that a minute, you can think, "That's a very strange thing to have said"—if he said it. Plato doesn't report him as saying that. Diogenes Laërtius does, and Diogenes is not entirely reliable himself. But anyway, he says, Socrates said, "All I know is that I know nothing."
5.9: Now, this is taken to be characteristic of a view known as Academic skepticism, the skepticism that emerges in Plato's Academy after Plato's death. You might think it's self-refuting. "I know only that I know nothing." Well, if you know nothing, how do you know that you know nothing? It seems like a self-contradictory. Now, maybe there's a way of patching it up. Suppose Socrates meant, "I know only this." What, Socrates? "Well, what I just said, this is all I know, period."
5.10: Now, that's a bizarre thing to think. I mean, maybe it's self-consistent, but on the other hand, how would you know that? You couldn't deduce it from something else that you knew, because then it wouldn't be true that you knew only this. It couldn't follow from anything because then you'd presumably have to know that it followed, and you don't know anything else. There's something that would be very strange about that view, even if it could be made consistent.
5.11: There's a deeper problem that Gisela Striker has talked about. If I say, "I know nothing or I know only this," so what? I can say, "Well, okay, you're not very smart, are you?" The skeptic usually doesn't just say knowledge is impossible or there's no reason to believe anything; they then draw a certain conclusion, they make a recommendation. For example, "It's impossible to know anything, so suspend judgment." Or, "It's impossible to have knowledge, so make room for faith." Or, "You can't have any knowledge, so just pursue peace of mind. Try for tranquility, whatever that takes." In other words, they usually tell you to do something or draw some conclusion from their skepticism.
5.12: But that's very strange, too. Where does that recommendation come from? After all, you would have to follow from this idea that you don't know anything, but they claim you don't know anything. So how could you know that's the right response? If you have no reasonable beliefs, there's no reason to believe in their recommendation or take it seriously. So it's not so clear that one can really express skepticism in an entirely coherent way. At least that seems to be true of Academic Skepticism.
5.13: Now, that became part of the motivation for a deeper kind of skepticism known as Pyrrhonian skepticism. Pyrrho was the first to really take things this far. He went so far, in fact, as to conclude that the evidence of his senses gave him no reason to believe anything. And his students had to lead him around because he would just walk out on the street in front of chariots and so on. And they would say, "Pyrrho, what are you doing?" And his answer was, "That I perceive a chariot racing toward me is no reason to believe it's really there." He got to the point where he decided, "There's no reason to believe that I understand what anyone is saying at all." So he simply refused to speak. And when he wouldn't speak and wouldn't answer, the students began to think, "He's gone deaf." So they started shouting things, thinking he's hard of hearing now. And so he had to start wiggling his finger to indicate, "I hear you."
5.14: In any event, the Pyrrhonian skeptic says, "I don't know anything. I don't even know whether I know anything. Okay? So don't get trapped in this Socratic idea of, 'I know that I know nothing.' No, no, no—I don't even know that." So typically the Pyrrhonian skeptic argues, but they deny knowing whether skepticism follows, and they make no recommendations. They essentially just attack other people's views. So you claim you know something, the Pyrrhonian will say, "I bet you don't know it," and they'll start challenging you and trying to convince you you don't know it. But if you say, "Well, what about you, Pyrrho? What do you know?" "I don't know."
5.15: That's one way of looking at the difference between these two branches of ancient skepticism. If I say, "What do you know?" The Academic skeptic says, "Nothing." And the Pyrrhonian skeptic says, "I don't know"—which does seem consistent, if entirely unhelpful.
5.16: Now, what kinds of arguments could you have for skepticism? How could you be convinced there's no reason to believe anything? Well, Cicero writes a work on Academic skepticism. Cicero, in fact, is our source for a great deal of information about ancient Stoicism, ancient skepticism. He himself says, "I'm contributing only a few original ideas of my own, mostly I'm reporting the ideas of others." And many of those texts he's reporting on have since been lost. So he's our best source for what some of these people were thinking.
5.17: In any case, he divides things into five arguments. And then Descartes, as we'll next time, adds a new argument that's quite dramatic. But in Cicero, they're what he refers to as "inapprehensibility"—or might be referred to as just the argument from illusion. There's the argument from "comparison," from "variability." There is what's now known as the "problem of the criterion," and then there are "paradoxes." I want to talk about each of those five in turn and try to understand what those arguments are like. They all have a certain amount of modern appeal as well. I don't think there's anyone here that we can just discard and say, "Oh, well, now we know there's some problem with this." They're all to be taken quite seriously.
5.18: They start with maybe the most primitive and earliest version of an argument from illusion. It's found in Zeno's paradoxes. They date from the fifth century BC, and they're arguments against the possibility of motion. Aristotle gives us an account of what this is. "The first argument asserts the non-existence of motion on the ground that that which is in locomotion must arrive at the half-way stage before it arrives at the goal." I say, "I think I can move. I think I can move across this room." Zeno says, "No, you can't."
5.19: Why not? Well, before you'd get to the other side, you'd have to go halfway. Before you could get to the other side now, you'd have to go halfway again. And halfway again. And halfway again. You'll never get there. Because in each case, you can only get there by first going halfway, it would require infinite number of motions to actually get to the other side of the room. Surely it would take you forever to get to the other side of the room. You could never achieve it.
5.20: Now, it certainly looks as if I can walk over, I say, "Aha, I refute you, Zeno!" But Zeno is going to say, "What does that show me? It does look like you've refuted me, but I've proved that motion is impossible. Conclusion is: motion is an illusion. What you've just done is perform an illusion. You didn't really move at all. Somehow, you tricked me into thinking you did." Okay, that's wild.
5.21: Here's a second argument Zeno gives: Achilles and the Tortoise. In a race, the quickest runner can never overtake the slowest since the pursuer must first reach the point where the pursuit started. Okay, so here's the idea. Tortoise challenges Achilles to a race. Achilles says, "Yeah, sure. I'll give you a head start." Here's Achilles, and the tortoise is starting from there. Well, in order to overtake the tortoise, Achilles first has to go to where the tortoise was. But by now, the tortoise has moved forward a little bit. Well, to overtake him, he's got to get to that point. But by then, the tortoise has moved a little further. He's got to then get to that point. But the tortoise has moved on. He can never catch the tortoise. So the tortoise, of course, will win the race.
5.22: Now, that's absurd, right? You could, again, give that turtle a little bit of a head start; you can clearly run past it. Zeno's conclusion, "But I proved to you that it would take you an infinite amount of time to catch the tortoise." Actually, sorry, what you just did: an illusion. It couldn't possibly have happened.
5.23: Now, he takes it further than this. Some of these arguments are really pretty amusing. So one is from unity. It seems like there are different things in the universe. But he says, "Look, that can't be right because I might think I have two hands—right hand, left hand. Well, then, there must be something in between, separating them. Anytime you've got two objects, there must be something in between that divides them. Okay, so there's stuff in between. But now, what's between the hand and the stuff in between? There must be something in there that divides them. But then, take whatever that is, there must be something between it and the hand that divides it from the hand. And so there have to be infinitely many things between my two hands. But that's absurd.
5.24: Okay, so what that shows us: there can't be different things in the universe. There's got to be only one thing in the universe. But it sure seems like they're different things. It's an illusion. Now, my joke is: a friend once said about my house—which didn't look as bad as what's pictured there, but nevertheless, I did at one point have 30 cats. And it really did seem as if between any two cats in my house, there's another cat. But of course, that would imply that there are infinitely many cats, and there are not infinitely many cats in my house or anywhere else. So it follows that, well, what? All these cats are an illusion. I wish that were—well, I don't wish that were true. But litter boxes would have been easier to deal with if it were true.
5.25: Now, those arguments go on to other things. He considers whether: if there can't be more than one thing in the universe, it must be very, very big. But no, there would have to be something dividing its sides. If there's anything in between that divides the sides, there would have to be infinitely many, so the sides can't be divided; so the universe consists of one thing, and it's actually just a point. That, too, is bizarre. It certainly doesn't seem like that's the way things are, so the world is an illusion. Well, that's one form of the argument from illusion.
5.26: There are other somewhat more convincing forms. And by the way, before putting down Zeno, I should say it was not until the 19th century—when we had a theory of infinite sequences and infinite limits, and the modern reconstruction of the calculus— that we could really say what's wrong with Zeno's arguments. So these were things that were puzzling to people for a very, very long time.
5.27: Now, some of the ancient arguments are expressed nicely by Philo of Alexandria, who was the first person to try to reconcile Jewish religion with Greek philosophy. And he writes a number of works on biblical passages and then begins to reflect on philosophical themes in them. So he's somebody who is often ignored in philosophy because it seems as if he's talking just about Noah or about Lot or about whoever it is. You don't realize after a while that this is really a work of philosophy introduced with a certain interpretation of a biblical story.
5.28: But anyway, he talks a lot about skeptical arguments in a work called On Drunkenness, where the idea is, well, the world looks pretty different when you're really drunk. Now, here's the argument from illusion as he presents it. We often misperceive things. We think we usually get the world right, but often we do suffer illusions. We get things wrong. But here's the thing: there's no way to tell in a particular case whether we are misperceiving things or not. So on any given occasion, we might be misperceiving things. We could always be subject to an illusion.
5.29: Descartes says, "Hey, to be sure, 'Whatever I've so far admitted as most true I've learned either from the senses or through the senses. But sometimes I've caught them deceiving me. It's prudent never to trust fully anything that's once deceived me." Sometimes I fall prey to illusions, and sometimes maybe I can see through them, but sometimes it's really due to the nature of my perceptual system. I can't see it any other way.
5.30: Here's a classic case discussed a lot in cognitive psychology: the Müller-Lyer illusion. You can look at a line like that, and it looks to anyone as if the left part is longer than the right-hand part. And yet, you can see in terms of the measurements, they're exactly the same length. And yet even knowing they are the same length, I can't see them as the same length. I see the one on the left as longer. Our visual systems are simply set up to see it that way, and we can't see it any other way. Even though we know that the left-hand part and the right-hand part are the same length. I cannot force myself to see it that way.
5.31: Take a look at this. Which is larger of those two orange dots? They're exactly the same size. But even knowing that, I cannot make myself see it as the same size. I'm comparing it to what's around it in each case. And so the one around big things I see as smaller, the one around smaller things I see as larger, and I can't unsee that. The same thing is true no matter what the background is here.
5.32: What about that? I tend to see that as weird things spiraling in, but in fact, it's just squares embedded within one another. Or here, those lines are all parallel. But even knowing that, I can't make myself see it that way. How about this café? It's the same thing. Those lines are actually parallel, but the bricks are arranged in such a way as to trick your sense organs and make you think it's jumbled and actually almost Escher-like. Confusing visually. Here, line AC and AB, which looks longer? AC, right? But in fact, they're exactly the same length.
5.33: We're used to seeing things in perspective, and we discount for that. But it's easy to trick our visual apparatus by relying on that. The same thing is true of the two blue lines. The one on the left looks longer than the one on the right, but it is not. They are the same length. Here, A and B, they look— well, they don't look the same size, but actually they are. What about that shape in the middle? It looks distorted, but in fact, it's a perfect circle. This looks like a spiral, but it's not. It's actually just a bunch of ellipses embedded within one another. Same thing is true of that. In fact, that one, even knowing that—and if I can trace them around and see that that's true— but even so, I can't believe it.
5.34: That, too, a bunch of perfect circles. But it doesn't look like that. There, it looks like that part in the middle is larger, it's magnified in some way, but it's not. Now, look at squares A and B. They're the same color, exactly the same shade. But that doesn't look like it's true at all. Again, even knowing that, I can't make myself see it that way. The same thing is true of the gray column on the left and on the right. They are the same color. You can look at this without the interference. It looks like that gets darker on one side. But if I put it against a solid background, you see, no, it's all the same color. It's the background that makes us perceive it differently. That looks like it's in motion, but it's not. It's stationary. Same thing is true of this, or of that. Now, there: count the white dots.
5.35: Well, all of those are cases where we suffer illusions, but there are also cases of ambiguity where you can just see it in different ways. This is Wittgenstein's famous duck-rabbit. You can see it as a duck or you can see it as a rabbit. Usually there, it's not very hard to switch from one view to the other view. The Necker cube is another example. You might see one side as projected out toward the front, but you could also flip your perception and see it the other way. I tend to see first that lower square as the one facing me, but if I think about it, I can switch it so that it's in the back and the top one is actually the one facing me.
5.36: Now, people have thought a lot in the tradition of skepticism about those sorts of arguments from illusion. It looks like we're often able to be misled, and we can't really trust our perceptions on certain things. And that's a serious matter, by the way; a serious matter in courts of law, for example, we rely a lot on eyewitness testimony. But eyewitness testimony is not very reliable, and it's somewhat depressing that it's not. Can you recognize a face that you had never seen before, and now several days, or weeks, or even months, or years later, you're asked to identify that person? People are actually pretty unreliable about doing that, which should disturb us if we're ever accused of a criminal offense. But it's not just things like that.
5.37: If you look at the interviews of the witnesses in Dealey Plaza on November 22nd, 1963, of the assassination of President Kennedy, and you ask people, as the FBI did, "How many shots were fired? How many shots did you hear?" The answers range from 3 to 17. Now, that's an astounding range. The vast majority of people say either 3 or 4 or 5. But then you have a few people reporting these, and one guy was convinced there were 17 shots. How you would even count 17 shots in a short time, I don't know. Maybe that's really his way of just saying, "Well, a lot."
5.38: They might not be totally wrong. It might have been echoes and other things that made people confused about how many shots were fired. But that seems like a very fundamental thing. How many shots were there? And yet, eyewitnesses are all over the place in answering that sort of question. And so really, that argument from illusion— that we can't trust our perceptions very well—is a serious matter.
5.39: Now, there is an additional problem that I think philosophers haven't thought nearly enough about, but psychologists are beginning to examine. We're capable of missing a great deal if we're paying attention to something else. This is called the problem of inattention. Our brains have limited capacity. They ignore most of the evidence we receive through the senses. Actually, our optic nerves only transmit to the brain a small subset of what's there on the retina, and most of that the brain discards as irrelevant.
5.40: That's why we're astounded when we read, let's say, the Sherlock Holmes stories, or Agatha Christie's stories about Hercule Poirot, because we look at it and we think, "How does he notice all this?" Well, it's unimaginable to most of us because we're discarding most of the information we receive, and we need to. If we kept all that information around, our heads would have to be the size of dump trucks in order to process all of that. It's important that we do that, but it means we can miss a great deal.
5.41: Let me talk a little bit about some of the experiments. It started with things that were taking place in a university setting. Students would come in—they were the subjects of the experiments— and they would ask for a certain form in an office. Someone would say, "Oh, I'll get you the form." They would bend down like this to get the form. Another person would pop up and hand them the form. The students never noticed. Now, you might say, "Well, one bureaucrat is like another bureaucrat. It doesn't matter who hands you the form."
5.42: Then people began to do this in more extreme ways. There are some famous instances of this. A bunch of students are around bouncing basketballs and passing basketballs to one another. You're asked to count the number of times they pass. And as that happens, something comes into the scene. In one instance, it's someone with an umbrella, in another case, it's someone dressed in a gorilla costume. But if you're counting the basketballs, you don't notice. Most people do not notice. I know the first time I saw one of these, I didn't see this.
5.43: Then we were told, "All right, forget about the counting. Now—" and a few people laughed halfway through this video. "What are you laughing at?" But then you're reshown the video without the distraction of counting, and you realize, "Oh, yes, this guy comes in in a gorilla costume, stares right at the camera, goes [grunts], and then walks off." Almost no one saw it. Astounding.
5.44: You can change things in the background. You're watching people sitting there at a café —and it happens slowly—you see nothing change beyond they're drinking their coffee. But then, if you speed it up or just show you the beginning and the end, you realize, wait, the color of the café wall behind them went from red to blue, and no one noticed. There are a variety of these things that have been taking place.
5.45: Derren Brown has done some experiments showing that people can mistake even radical changes. For example, he started with him asking for directions, then someone coming in with a large poster—of him, by the way—interrupting this, and then someone else popping up, and then receiving the directions. But okay, if it's people who look kind of alike, you might think, "Sure, people aren't paying attention." But then he was replaced by a very tall Jamaican fellow, and a very short Asian woman, and so on.
5.46: Again, almost no one notices. A few people do, but almost no one sees the difference. It's astounding. We just ignore this. You can replace people in the scene, and nobody seems to notice, or at least very few do. That's disturbing, too. Because you might think it relates to the absence of the elephant in the room. "Did you see such and such happen? Was there a gorilla in that video?" 90% are going to say no, because they were paying attention to something else, even though there was.
5.47: Now, a form that this can take is to talk about the possibility of dreaming. How do I know that right now I am not asleep and dreaming this? Maybe I fell asleep. I'm supposed to be lecturing on skepticism, but instead, my alarm didn't go off, and I am sleeping, but somewhere my brain is saying, "Aren't you supposed to be discussing skepticism?" And so I'm dreaming that I'm giving this lecture when I'm really not. Or maybe somebody in my morning coffee slipped in some LSD, and I'm hallucinating that I'm giving this lecture, even though I'm really not. Well, how do I know that's not the case?
5.48: Descartes is worried about this. He says, "In my sleep, I experience the same things as madmen do when they're awake, sometimes even less probable things. How often have I been persuaded in the quiet of the night of familiar things that I was here in my robe sitting near the fire, when in fact I was lying disrobed beneath the sheets." He says, "It seems to me now I'm looking at the paper with waking eyes. My head, I can move it—it's not asleep. I deliberately and knowingly extend my hand and feel it. What happens in sleep isn't so distinct, no doubt. But as if I don't remember being tricked while asleep by similar things on other occasions." In other words, it seems to me when I'm awake, that when I'm dreaming, yeah, things are funny and they're vague and weird things happen. But when I'm asleep, I totally believe in them. And so the fact that I totally believe right now that I'm awake isn't actually very good evidence that I'm awake.
5.49: He says, "When I think about this more carefully, I see so plainly that there are no certain indications by which we may clearly distinguish being awake from being asleep that I'm dumbfounded. My astonishment almost persuades me that I'm asleep." Now, I want to focus on that phrase, "There are no certain indications to allow us to distinguish that we're awake here." That in other words, we're perceiving things accurately instead of misperceiving.
5.50: This is why Cicero calls this inapprehensibility. What he means is there's no mark, there's no sign, there's nothing in the perception itself that says, "I'm a veridical perception. I'm depicting the world accurately. You are awake. This is really happening. You are perceiving it accurately." There's nothing like that. When we are in a certain perceptual state, there is nothing that marks that state as accurate or inaccurate.
5.51: Indeed, if I showed you most of those illusions in a different context—and wasn't talking about illusions, just giving you a test of visual perception, for example, saying, "Which line do you perceive to be longer?"—you would have said, "Oh, AB is longer than AC." It would never have occurred to you that maybe you were misperceiving. There was nothing in the experience itself that cried out and told you, "You're being tricked. You're being tricked." Or, "No, you're getting things right."
5.52: Now, Zhuangzi was an ancient Chinese Daoist philosopher who was a skeptic and puts these kinds of arguments in a really memorable way. He says, "Those who dream at the banquet, wake to lamentation and sorrow. Those who dream of lamentation and sorrow, wake to join the hunt. While they dream, they don't know that they dream. Some will even interpret the very dream they're dreaming. And only when they're awake, do they know it was a dream." Indeed, I think he's observing something interesting here. Sometimes, maybe in a slightly—a state that's somewhere between being awake and being asleep, you start being aware of this.
5.53: I had the sensation, for example, last night in a dream that I had opened an email and clicked yes when I meant to click no, and I realized that was a fishing attempt. I'm in big trouble, okay? I dreamt that. But then later I started feeling terrible like, "Oh, my gosh, I've got to do this. I've got to do that. I better call the university and blah, blah, blah, blah, blah." Then I started—but still within this dreaming state— thinking, "But I dreamt that. I don't really have to do that." But then my brain starts to say, "But yes, you do. You're in big trouble." And then I said, "No, it was just a dream." But I was still dreaming. So sometimes you can be dreaming that you're dreaming and have dreams within dreams. Maybe that doesn't happen very often, but it does happen sometimes, and clearly it happened to Zhuangzi.
5.54: Now, I think his most memorable instance of this, and it's really beautifully done, is about Zhuangzi and the Butterfly. It inspires art like the one you're seeing there because it's a story that people can remember for years. My own daughter took my intro philosophy class many, many years ago, and she later told me there was only one thing she really remembered clearly—which depresses me. But anyway, it was this. It was Zhuangzi and the Butterfly.
5.55: Here's the passage. "Once upon a time, I, Zhuangzi, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I don't know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I'm a man." That's a creepy thought, in a way, but it's a very powerful thought.
5.56: There is, incidentally, a Star Trek: The Next Generation episode that's a bit like this involving Commander Riker, who is being held by aliens and being convinced he's in an insane asylum. It's like, "Wait, am I mad? Is this reality? What is happening?" It's very much like the dreaming thing. They're giving him drugs to simulate psychotic episodes, but it's the same kind of thing. "Am I a madman dreaming of a commander of a spaceship? Or on the other hand, am I a commander of a spaceship who is enduring some weird psychological state?" He goes back and forth and really has no idea which is the accurate one.
5.57: Well, let's move on to the argument from comparison. This is an argument advanced especially by Philo of Alexandria, but also by Sextus Empiricus. It's in a way a very deep argument that inspires quite a few developments in early modern philosophy. Here's the way it goes. We know not things in themselves, but things in relation to other things, and in particular in relation to us.
5.58: Now, that's a bit nerve-wracking in a way, because how do we distinguish what's really in the object itself, from what is being supplied by our own faculties? After all, I've got perceptual faculties, I've got cognitive faculties that are taking place in my brain, so I'm processing this information. Here, it seems like I've got a clicker in my hand, but what is the clicker really like? What are its true properties? What about my experiences is really there in reality, and what is being supplied by my own perceptual faculties, by my own cognition in the way my brain is organizing the information it receives from my sense organs?
5.59: Something, presumably in the world, is causing me to have these sensations—let's go with Aristotle on that. But still, how much of what I perceive here—that it's gray and black, for example, that it has a certain shape and a certain feel to it—how much of that is being supplied by my own brain, and how much of that is truly in the thing in itself, the ultimate cause of those sensations?
5.60: The fact is, I have no way of knowing. I can't step outside of my own brain, my own sense organs, and see what it's really like in reality. It's as if I'm in the matrix and I can't take the pill that takes me out of the matrix and see what's really going on. By definition, I've got to rely on my sense organs and my brain to understand the world. As a result, there's no way to distinguish what's really in the object itself from what I'm contributing. But if that's right, I look at an object and I think, "Oh, I know all sorts of things about it. But do I really? There's nothing I know for sure is about the object itself rather than just being supplied by my own sense organs, by my own brain." And that's a rather frightening thought.
5.61: Zhuangzi, I think, has this idea, too. He says, "Intellectual distinctions in general correspond to nothing in reality." Or at least it might be safer to say, we have no idea which of them might correspond to things in reality. It looks to me like parts of this are gray and parts of this are black. Well, I draw a distinction between the gray parts and the black parts. But does that correspond to a difference in reality? How would I know?
5.62: Now, Zhuangzi, it said, took this to an extreme. He said, "Well, then there's no reason to believe anything. There's no point to doing anything." Zhu Xi, a Neo-Confucian philosopher, said, "Laozi still wanted to do something—he's the founder of Daoism— but Zhuangzi didn't want to do anything at all." Well, maybe. One thing he does say is that subjectivity and objectivity are all wrapped up together.
5.63: I think it's his way of expressing the argument from comparison. He says, "I don't know which of my perceptions of this, which of my thoughts about it, are objectively true of the thing itself, and which are really subjective reactions based on my own cognitive apparatus. I can't tell. Objectivity and subjectivity are all intertwined. They depend on each other. After all, I've got to rely on my own perceptions, on my own subjectivity to determine what this thing is like, which means that any distinction I make that I claim to be objective, really relies on my own subjective reactions.
5.64: And yet subjectivity also seems to be something I could describe objectively. I can say, "Well, it seems to me that parts of this are gray. It seems to me that parts of this are black." And there I seem to be objective. And yet I'm not being objective about the thing in itself; I'm being objective about my own subjective states of mind. So he says, in the end, "I don't see how we achieve true objectivity and know anything for sure about the way the world really is. So knowledge seems to be impossible. Even a reasonable belief about the way the world truly is independently of our cognitive apparatus, that seems impossible."
5.65: So he concludes, "That means I can't trust any distinctions I draw, any distinctions I perceive, any conclusions I reach. I should just reject this. At most, I can say how things seem to me. There, I'm on pretty safe ground. But how things are, I can't say anything." So he says, "Just place yourself in subjective relation to things." Meaning: just say how things seem to you. There's nothing more you can say. Don't pretend to know how things are.
5.66: And he tells some stories about subjectivity. This is another memorable one. "A keeper of monkeys said with regard to the ration of chestnuts that each monkey was to have three in the morning and four at night. At this the monkeys were very angry, so the keeper said they might have four in the morning and three at night, with which arrangement they were all well-pleased." It was the same number of chestnuts, the same thing in reality, but subjectively it seemed really different to them. And so the point is, in a way, that it's the subjectivity that ultimately matters. Forget about the claims to objectivity. It doesn't matter to the monkeys that it was really just seven chestnuts a day.
5.67: Okay, this brings us to the argument from variability. Really, I think you could see the argument from illusion and maybe even the argument from comparison as special cases of this. Here's the idea, and again, I'll stay with Zhuangzi because he does such a beautiful job of expressing these arguments. "Men admire Mao Ch'iang and Li Chi, at the sight of whom fishes plunge deep down the water, birds soar high in the air, and deer hurry away. Who shall say what's the correct standard of beauty?"
5.68: Well, here's the general mode, as Sextus puts it. "We find that undecidable dissension about a matter proposed has come about in ordinary life and among philosophers." In other words, people disagree all over the place. They perceive things differently. They don't see things the same way. They disagree about things. They have different opinions. Here's the problem: we can't choose or rule out anything on any neutral grounds, so we have to suspend judgment.
5.69: Here's the way we might frame the argument in general: Things are perceived differently by different beings at different times. Now there are a bunch of different versions in Sextus—for example, as I recall, you have six different modes, all of which have this form. Different people see things different ways. Beings of different species perceive things different ways. Bats see things very differently from cats, and they see things differently from the way we perceive them and so on.
5.70: Here's the problem: there's no neutral way to determine which perceptions are right. There's no way to say, "All right, now I'm imagining that I'm not a bat or a cat or a human being. I want to see what the world is really like." There's no way to do that. We can't step outside. There is no neutral way to determine this. So, conclusion: knowledge is impossible. Or even more radically, in the ancient world: there's no reason to believe that any perception is trustworthy. There's always another alternative, and there's no neutral way to tell that this is likely to be better than that one.
5.71: Consequently, given the differences and no way of telling, what should we do? Well, the best we can do is suspend judgment. We have no reason to trust any of them. Sometimes this is a matter of different species. Sometimes it's a matter of different people. It can even be me at different times. I may feel differently about something or have a different opinion at different times. How do I know which portrays reality accurately, which should be trusted?
5.72: There's an example like this in Dostoevsky of a young man who realizes, "I'm going to inherit a great fortune. I'm undoubtedly at age 50, going to see things very differently from the way I see things at age 20. But what should I trust? My 20-year-old self or my 50-year-old self? And how would we tell? What's a neutral way? If only we had a way of not being any particular age at all." Well, there's no way to do that. We can't tell which of those is more reliable.
5.73: Now, the problem of the criterion, our fourth argument. You might think, "Hey, wait a minute. I know how to solve this problem. Let's have a neutral arbiter. Let's have a fact checker. Let's have somebody come in who's neutral, who can tell us what is really trustworthy." Okay, let's have an arbiter between us. Now, Sextus says, "That's not going to work. If we get somebody who agrees with me, he'll side with me. If we get somebody who is on your side, he'll side with you. How could anybody like that arbitrate between us? If I employ somebody who differs from both of us, who doesn't agree with either, he's not going to be able to decide between us."
5.74: In short, there's no such thing as a neutral arbiter. There's no way of going to neutral arbitration. If that's right, well, we seem to face this problem of finding a criterion. If only we had a criterion that would tell us which perception was accurate, or at least which perceptions were more reliable than others. But there's no such neutral criterion.
5.75: Now, suppose you propose one. Suppose you say, "I think there is a criterion. Here it is." I can say, "How do you know that's the right criterion?" There could be other criteria that would do this. Why is that the right one? Say, "Well, I don't know. I guess I need a criterion of criteria." Well, but okay, you propose one. That's the right criterion. How do you know that's the right one? Okay, there could be multiple criteria of criteria, and it looks like we get led into an infinite regress.
5.76: So either we can't find a neutral one at all, or somebody proposes a neutral one, and then I say, "How do you know that's neutral?" We need a criterion for neutrality, and we get led up into this infinite regress. A suspension of judgment, he says, is the only thing that's rational in response to that. There is no neutral ground to stand on. So that's the problem. There's no neutral way to tell which perceptions ought to be trusted or which opinions ought to be trusted. It would be nice to have a criterion for doing that, but we'd need a criterion for telling us which perceptions to trust, and then a criterion of the possible criteria for doing that. In the end, we could never justify a criterion.
5.77: We would end up either arguing circularly, like, "Here's my criterion. Why is it the right one? It says it's the right one." That's not very convincing. Or I'd get led into this infinite regress. This is the right criterion because—How do you know that's the right and neutral fact checker? Well, this guy says he is. How do you know that guy's neutral? Well, that person says he is, and so on. We would face an infinite regress. We get into trouble.
5.78: Now, this isn't just, I think, a philosophical curiosity, as you might think Zeno's paradoxes are. What do you mean? There aren't things in the universe that take up any space and that nothing moves, etc. Here, they're real problems. People worry a lot about gerrymandering, for example, dividing up political districts in a way to advantage one party or another. Often people will say, "We need a neutral way to do that." But what would be the neutral way? People say, "We need a neutral bipartisan commission." But the moment it makes a recommendation, people will say, "Well, that commission was biased!" You would need a criterion of determining what are neutral arbiters for doing the gerrymandering and dividing up the areas into districts. And it looks like the moment you do that, you face this infinite regress, or you just have circularity. You have the commission saying, "We're trustworthy." Well, why should you believe them? That's a problem.
5.79: Similarly, with a political debate, people often complain, "I don't like the moderator of that debate. I think they were on this side or on that side. We need a neutral moderator." But where do we find a neutral moderator? Maybe these people propose that moderator, these propose that one. We need a criterion for determining who would be neutral. But the moment I propose a criterion, somebody on the other side is going to say, "No, no. no. That would be my favorite criterion." Now we need a criterion of criteria, and we go up into the infinite regress.
5.80: Or finally, something that's been talked about a lot over the last few years, the problem of bad information—misinformation, disinformation, whatever you want to call it. Yeah, it would be great if we had a neutral way of deciding what's true, and hence the fact checker and so on. But the problem is there's no neutral ground on which to stand to do that. Really, who could tell you what's accurate information, what's inaccurate information? Now, if God were to pronounce, let's say God knows all, and God says, "I'll tell you, okay, I've just read the New York Times this morning, and here's what you could trust, here's what you can't," or something, then great.
5.81: But how would we know that anybody trying to tell us this is themselves neutral? There's no way to do it. There is no neutral way. The moment somebody says, "Here would be a neutral way," somebody else would say, "No, this is a better neutral way." Again, we get laid into the infinite regress. This, in short, isn't just a philosophical problem. It's a real practical problem.
5.82: Now, the last problem. What if the whole thing is completely misleading? That is to say, what if there is no way to trust anything in our surroundings and say, "This is reality." I've been assuming that there is a real thing in itself underlying, for example, my perception of this clicker. And I perceive parts of it as gray, parts of it is black, I perceive it as having a certain shape. But the skeptic says, "Well, what is it really like, independently of your faculty of perception, independently of the cognitive processing of your brain, what is the thing in itself truly like?" We've worried that, well, we're not sure.
5.83: But now, what if it's worse than that? Because we've been assuming something like realism and the difficulty of reaching out and actually talking about the underlying reality. But what if there isn't one, or at least isn't one on anything like our plane of existence? What if this is all a computer simulation? What if we're all just avatars— we're all just characters in a video game? Elon Musk is reported to have said the chance we're not living in a computer simulation is one in billions. He's convinced the world is a matrix-like world. There's no way to get out of that. There's no way to actually break the simulation, take the red pill, and somehow get to the true reality. Well, what then?
5.84: Now, different people disagree about this, right? Here, again, we have an instance of variability. Here's one report, "There's only a 20% chance that we're all sims." That's not really that reassuring to me. Bank of America—why they're discussing this, I'm not sure—but they say, "There's a 20% to 50% chance we're inside the matrix and reality is just a simulation." That seems puzzling. Here's another article, "Elon Musk is wrong. We aren't living in a simulation." How would we possibly know?
5.85: Now, here is a good case then of people seeing this differently. Some say, "Actually, I think we are living inside some computer simulation. But that too is puzzling because who simulated us?" Even if I'm just a sim, even if I'm just an avatar, I'm some beings avatar, aren't I? So there must be some other plane of existence in which people are just playing this as a video game. I don't know, but we can't access that. What would that be like? Is there any likelihood at all that we're actually in such a simulation? How would we know?
5.86: When we face a question like this, that problem of variability and the problem of finding neutral grounds becomes really acute. How would I tell whether Elon Musk is right that there's a 99.999% chance that we're in a simulation or other people saying, no, it's very remote. Some people saying 20%, 50%. On what basis? How could we possibly be in a position to neutrally decide a question like that? If we can't, what does that mean?
5.87: The skeptic says, it means not that we should be terribly worried in our personal lives about a simulation. Like, "Oh, sure, I'm going to walk in front of that car because it's just a simulation. The guy will just press the button, reset, and I'll be back to being alive." No, it's not like that. It doesn't really make any difference to me one way or another from one point of view. But from another point of view, you could say, "That's a pretty deep question. Is there anything like a reality of the form we think there is— and we have no way to tell?" Scary.
5.88: Now, let me talk about the problem that Cicero focuses on. Interestingly, Zhuangzi, Sextus, and a variety of other skeptics tend to ignore this problem, but Cicero takes it quite seriously, and I think there's good reason to take it seriously. Here is the classic liar paradox. The reason Cicero is interested is that he thinks this implies we don't even understand what truth is. We've been talking about, do we know anything? Is it reasonable to believe anything? Should we ever think our states of mind correspond to reality and are actually true? But what if we don't even know what truth means? Then there's a deeper puzzle. We don't even know what it means for something to be true.
5.89: Here, from the New Testament, Paul's letter to Titus, "One of them,"—Epimenides—"a prophet of their own, said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.'" So someone from Crete says, "Cretans are always liars." Well, it seems to imply that they're lying in saying that, right, if they're always liars? Now, that itself is not a paradox because if the person is telling the truth, well, then it looks like they're lying, they're saying something false. So suppose what they're saying is false, that Cretans are always liars, well, then some Cretans don't lie. And so actually, that's not a paradox.
5.90: But we can put it into a more paradoxical form. If we imagine the Cretan saying, "I am lying right now," or a purer form, just, "This sentence is false." Suppose it's true, then it's false. But suppose it's false. Well, it says it's false, so it must be true. I mean, that can seem odd. Maybe there's something wrong with such sentences like, "I am lying," or, "This sentence is false." But there is one simple way out, which is to say, well, it can't be true, it can't be false. Maybe it's just neither true nor false. We might think that's a way to solve it. Maybe other sentences are neither true nor false. But we can fix that problem.
5.91: The strong liar paradox says, "This sentence isn't true." Suppose it's true, then it's not true. Suppose it's not true, then it's true. Now it doesn't seem so easy to get out of. We can't really say it's neither true nor not true. It looks like now we're really trapped. Maybe it's both true and not true. Some people have said that, but that's disturbing. Otherwise, what do we do? How do we deal with that? Now, you might think it's because there's this weird self-reference, "I am lying," or, "This sentence is false, this sentence is not true."
5.92: But we can get rid of that problem. For example, John says, "Everything Bill says is false." Bill says, "Everything John says is true." Neither sentence actually is by itself self- referential. On the other hand, we put them together and we realize, oh, we're led into a paradox. John says everything Bill says is false. Bill says everything John says is true. It looks like Bill is saying everything John says is true. One of those things is what Bill says is false. That implies what Bill says is false. But then, well, it's false that everything John says is true. So something Bill says must be true. But if we imagine Bill saying only that one thing, we have a paradox. We can make that as big as we want. "What Mary tells you is true. What Carol tells you is true. Carol says what Alice tells you is false." We can make these loops big and get paradoxes as long as people just say this.
5.93: Here's another paradox like this, and it's about knowledge itself. "This sentence isn't known by anyone." Well, that's a weird thing, but suppose I say it's false. Well, then somebody must know it, right? But if they know it, it must be true because you can't know what isn't true. But we've just shown that if it's false, it would have to be true. So it's true. But now we know it, so it's false. Okay, that's actually a pretty deep paradox, and it's hard to get out of that one. It seems to suggest that it's not just truth and falsehood we don't understand. We don't understand even the basics of the logic of knowledge.
5.94: This one is related; it's called Fitch's paradox, because Frederic Fitch, a logician, thought of this. Suppose you think every true sentence can be known. It's knowable. But some true sentences aren't known—surely there are things we don't know. Now, his argument is those can't both be true. That sounds a little surprising. Suppose P is true but isn't known. Well, then it's possible to know that P is true but unknown. I just told you that. But then we'd know P, but also know we didn't know it. But if we know we don't know it, we don't know it, so we'd know it and not know it. He takes that as an argument that you cannot say every true sentence can be known. So he thinks that means there are some unknowable truths. And so this isn't exactly a paradox. It might be that we can prove, logically, there are truths you cannot possibly know. But it seems surprising that we could just prove that outright.
5.95: So far, whatever you think about those logical paradoxes, let's come to the question of recommendations, because we've heard all these arguments on the basis of which we're supposed to conclude we can't have any reasonable beliefs, and we can't know anything. So what? So what do we do? The skeptic gives us all these arguments, and we might, like David Hume, say, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, I'm going to go back and have my dinner. So forget about it." Interesting for the philosophy classroom, but I'm not interested in taking this any further. I'm going to go on and live my life. So who cares?
5.96: Well, here's what Sextus Empiricus says, "The result of all this should be suspension of judgment, and suspending judgment leads me to peace of mind." So I might worry about increasing political polarization and the collapse of bipartisanship. I might think some people are arguing this very vehemently, and others disagree and argue that very vehemently. If I get torn between these partisan battles, I get all upset. I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to suspend judgment. I'm going to say, "These guys say that, these guys say that. I don't know. I suspend judgment." Who knows? Who knows who's right? In that way, I can attain peace of mind.
5.97: Here is the idea: give up your claims to knowledge. Give up your fervent beliefs. Just admit, "I don't know. It seems to me this way, but who knows?" If you do that, you can be tranquil. You can have peace of mind. You can say, "Am I going to watch the news? Am I going to read the paper? Am I going to follow that particular person? No, I don't care. I just log on for pictures of cats, and that gives me peace of mind. That's enough for me."
5.98: Now, you could take this as an argument. Here's Gisela Striker's worry: Wait a minute, it doesn't follow that you should suspend judgment—or, for that matter, that suspending judgment will lead you to peace of mind. After all, you've said you can't know anything. You have no reason to believe anything. So you have no reason to believe that this is a reasonable recommendation.
5.99: But now, Sextus says, "You're right. I can't actually assert that." I can't say this follows. I can't claim that if you suspend judgment, you will have peace of mind. But let me tell you, it just happens. And so here is his response, "The skeptic had the same experience, which is said to have befallen the painter Apelles. Once, they say, when he was painting a horse and wished to represent in the painting the horse's foam [after running really hard], he was so unsuccessful that he gave up the attempt and flung at the picture the sponge he used to wipe the paints off the brush."
5.100: Imagine him, he's been trying this, keeps getting rid of it, can't do it. Finally, he says, "I give up," throws the sponge, and poof. What happened? "The mar of the sponge produced the effect of the horse's foam. So too," he says, "the skeptics were in hopes of gaining quietude," peace of mind, in other words, "by means of a decision regarding the disparity of the objects of sense and of thought." In other words, don't worry about whether the way it seems to you is really the way it is. Give up on worrying about that.
5.101: "And being unable to effect this they suspended judgment; they found the quietude, as if by chance, followed on their suspense, even as a shadow follows its substance." So he's saying, "Am I in a position to claim that if you suspend judgment, you will have peace of mind? No, that would be an assertion. I realize I can't defend an assertion. I've just told you there's no reason to believe anything. But try it and see what happens. It'll happen." There's the effect of the horse's foam, done by just throwing the sponge. You don't make any claims, it just happens.
5.102: In the end, what can I say about these recommendations? Can I assert that they follow? No. Can I say this is a reasonable thing to do in response to your worry that maybe your perception of the world is really off base? No. I'm just telling you, relax. Suspend judgment. Don't insist that you're getting the world right. And you'll just, by surprise, find that you're way happier. Will I claim this is the way to happiness? No. Just try it. See what happens. The end.
5.103: You mentioned at the outset that skepticism disappeared from like 500 to the Middle Ages. Why? Do we know?
5.104: That's a great question. Why does skepticism disappear for about a thousand years? Partly, it's just that the texts are lost. And so people aren't reading Sextus or Philo; and certainly in the West, they were never reading Zhuangzi or some other skeptics. There is a fascinating report, however, of a meeting between Greek philosophers and Indian philosophers after Alexander's conquest, because Alexander conquered most of what is today the Middle East, bringing Greek and Greek culture all the way to the boundaries of India. But there he stopped. And so there were Greek philosophers who came and actually met with Indian philosophers. They described them as the naked philosophers because they just wore loin cloths, I guess. But in any event—
5.105: There was a very strong tradition in India of skepticism that I didn't actually talk about here. But Madhyamaka Buddhism is heavily skeptical and is similarly quietistic about what the skeptic can say. The skeptic argues against others, but makes no propositions himself. And so simply says, "You claim to know, you don't." But otherwise, puts forward no recommendations, no theses. It's after that that Greek philosophers start taking these skeptical arguments seriously. So it may well be an Indian influence.
5.106: But in any case, it becomes a really important school that lasts all the way from about 300 BC up to the time of Augustine. Now, Augustine wrote a work called Against the Academics, where he is trying to say skeptical arguments can be refuted. What it amounts to is that in Western philosophy, his refutations were actually thought to be devastating. I think the real reason it starts in Greece was due to the Indian, and specifically Buddhist, influence.
5.107: But I think the reason it dies out for a thousand years is not only that the texts are lost, it's because Augustine seems to give the right answer. It's an answer, by the way, that just gets copied by Descartes. Now, Descartes does add some dimensions to it. I don't want to say there's no originality, but the, "I think, I am," that we're going to be discussing next time, he's just ripping that off from Augustine in Against the Skeptics.
