5.108: I think what it amounts to is that Augustine was able to take Platonism and express it in a form by replacing the Form of the Good with God that people actually found compelling. They thought, "Okay, wait a minute. There are things I know. As long as I'm convinced that I know even one thing, then the skeptical arguments have to be wrong." And so now the question becomes: What's wrong with them? So as long as I've got anything— I would like to say I know a lot about the world—but as long as I know anything, I know these arguments can't be right.
5.109: And so then for a thousand years, people proceed merrily thinking, "All right, that's settled. We don't have to worry about this." And it's not until Descartes comes along that he realizes, "Wait a minute, that Augustinian solution has an instability built into it," and that begins to worry him. It's when he puts the skeptical arguments in a much more powerful form than even the ancient skeptics did, that he realizes, "We'll start with Augustine's solution, but we have to do something better than that." Lecture 6: On Rationalism At a glance — On rationalism.
6.1: I've mentioned that there are two grand traditions in the Western philosophical heritage, one of them stemming from Plato, that is, in some sense, a series of footnotes to Plato, the other stemming from Aristotle, that we could describe as a bunch of footnotes to Aristotle. I want to talk today about the rationalist tradition.
6.2: Rationalism is a specific philosophical view. You find it in Plato. I think throughout the rationalist tradition, Plato remains the chief inspiration. Really, this is a lecture on footnotes to Plato. But in the modern context, as we'll see, this also becomes a battle against the skeptic because the skeptics were thought to be submerged for many years, for reasons I'll mention.
6.3: Then it reemerges in the Renaissance and early modern period and presents a new challenge. The rationalists of that period have a different problem from the one Plato faced, and therefore advanced things, in some ways, considerably beyond where Plato left them. From another point of view, you could say, they actually stage that revival by also staging a retreat.
6.4: The key figure here is René Descartes. Descartes was famous as a philosopher, but also as a physicist, as a mathematician. He himself was mostly a private tutor, and he carried on a long correspondence with Princess Elizabeth of Bohemia, who was really the leading classicist of her age—we'll talk a little bit more about that later. But Descartes, in short, was accomplished in a variety of intellectual areas. The fact that we still talk about Cartesian products and Cartesian graphs, and representations of all sorts of things, indicates that he really was of fundamental significance in the development of mathematics.
6.5: In the context of skepticism and rationalism more generally, he does make a significant contribution. He repeats arguments from dreaming, arguments from illusion, arguments of various kinds that we've looked at in the skeptical tradition. But he adds one of his own that's similar to the argument I considered about the possibility of living in a simulation. But if anything, it's even more radical than that.
6.6: He says, imagine that there is not a good God, but an evil deceiver who is out to trick us. He says, "I shall suppose not that God who is supremely good and is the fountain of truth, but some evil genius of the greatest power and cunning who has employed all his energies to deceive me." Why is that so devastating? He imagines an all-powerful but evil being out to trick all of us.
6.7: Imagine that this being makes our mind skip every time we have a thought, every time we try to draw an inference, every time we reach a conclusion. So anytime I'm about to think anything, the evil deceiver goes [makes a popping sound], and my mind skips a beat, and I come to the wrong conclusion; I think the wrong thing. In other words, this being is all-powerful but is not good as God on the classical conception; instead is evil and sets up the universe to deceive us.
6.8: Here is why that is such a shocking contribution and makes an advance over the ancient skeptical arguments. They may apply to things we perceive by our senses, but they don't really apply to logic. They don't apply to mathematics. You could think 2 + 2 = 4. That's true even in my dreams. That's true even if I'm suffering illusions; still, 2 + 2 = 4. But if the evil deceiver is tricking me, then maybe my mind is making some mistake when I do that. Maybe 2 + 2 = 3.9999 something. Maybe something else is going wrong.
6.9: In other words, every time I try to draw a logical inference, every time I think I know something in math, no matter how basic it is, maybe it's all an illusion. My mind might be getting everything wrong. That would be true even in the matrix. Even in the matrix or even if this world is a simulation, it seems like that doesn't affect logic, that doesn't affect mathematics. But if there's an evil being controlling my mind, then, actually, everything is in question, not just the things I learn through my senses, not just things that I hear from someone else or derive in some other way from experience—no, this challenges all my knowledge, even what's independent of experience. That challenges the classical rationalist conception that ended up submerging skeptical arguments for a while.
6.10: Here's the idea. The classic rationalist—here's someone like Philo of Alexandria. Even though he reports all these skeptical arguments, in the end, he's not on the side of the skeptics. He is on the side of the rationalists. He thinks it is possible to have knowledge of the world independently of experience. That really is the definition of rationalism. I can have knowledge of the world even apart from my experience of it. I can do that just through meditation or reflection alone. Why is that even possible? His answer is that the structure of the mind matches the structure of the world.
6.11: The empiricist, which we'll study next time, thinks, "I learn about the world through experience. That's why I think what's in my mind matches the world. It's caused by the world. I experience the things in the world. So I'm hoping there's enough of a match as a result of that." An idealist that we'll look at later says, "Actually, my mind is constituting the world. So of course, there's a match between my mind and the world because my mind is constructing the world."
6.12: But the rationalist has to give a more sophisticated account. "I think I know some things," says the rationalist, "that I'm not relying just on experience for. But how could I be sure I know them? How could I be sure I'm getting them right? I must think that there's some match." Here is how Philo explains it. This is the answer given later by Origen and then by Augustine. For a long time, it presides as dominant throughout Jewish and Christian philosophy, at least.
6.13: The idea is that these Forms that Plato had talked about seem puzzling. How could I know about them? They seem to be in some ghostly realm. They're not in space and time. It's not clear how I could causally interact with them. How could I possibly know about them? But Philo says, "Wait a minute. My concept, for example, of triangularity, is supposed to be grounded in this form of triangularity. Well, what could an idea actually match or be grounded in? It would be simplest if it was another idea?"
6.14: We can talk about ideas matching other ideas. If I say an idea matches something I know not what, it's not clear how I would explain that or justify it. So what if the Forms are just ideas in the mind of God? Then, instead of talking about the Form of the Good and its mystical power to shed light on the realm of the Forms in my mind, what if I just say that God has these ideas that he uses in creating the world, and both my mind and the world are stamped with the word of God? There is the logos in the world, there is the logos in my mind, and so the structure matches. They both reflect the logos, that basic order or structure that applies to the world and applies to my mind.
6.15: Here is why Descartes's thought experiment about the evil deceiver is so challenging and changes things fundamentally. He says that a good God would stamp my mind and your mind and the world with the same stamp. But what if we have an evil deceiver? Then that deceiver might stamp your mind or my mind with a different stamp from the one he uses to create the world: "Here's how I structure the world. Here's how I structure your mind. So there's a complete mismatch. Your mind consists of square pegs and the world consists of round holes, and none of them match." You think you have knowledge of the world after experience or before experience? Ha, you don't. Your mind is systematically mismatched to the world."
6.16: In that case, there is the logos, let's say, that informs the structure of the world. Your mind has the pseudo logos, this cheap imitation that doesn't match at all. "Haha, you can't know anything." It's one thing if it's just maybe intertranslatable, but if they're radically different stamps that can't even be translated into one another, like the square pegs and round holes, then what happens? Maybe everything we think is wrong.
6.17: Well, that challenge is a very serious challenge, and it really disrupts not only Plato's picture of the good, happily shedding light over the entire thing and making it possible for us to know the Forms. If we go the way of Philo and Augustine, we say, "No, don't talk about the good there. Talk about God." God can do anything. It's not clear the Form of the Good can do anything at all, but God can do anything.
6.18: God can illuminate our mind. Augustine has this theory of illumination, that God sheds light. He turns the light of the mind, as it were, and allows for us to have access to at least some of the ideas of God. That would help to explain how we can know things about humanity or justice or triangularity or the good.
6.19: But now, if we have an evil deceiver, we've got, in effect, a fake form. It's not the Form in which objects participate. It's not the Form that structures the world. Our minds are structured with a different set of things, and there is just a fundamental mismatch. In this case, the evil deceiver, instead of shedding a light on the mind—actually, I don't know what the right analogy is—keeps it in darkness, or maybe even better, puts you in a fun house so that nothing looks the way it really is.
6.20: The result of that would seem to be, yes, radical skepticism, more radical actually than we find in Zhuangzi, or in Sextus or in Philo or in any other ancient thinker, because it affects logic, it affects mathematics, it affects absolutely everything. We are utterly lost in a forest where we're convinced that nothing we think is right.
6.21: It's in the face of that that Descartes goes back to Augustine. Augustine had defeated the skeptic by saying, wait a minute. First of all, I may not know how the world is, but I know how it seems to me. I know that the clicker looks gray to me and looks black to me, different parts being different colors. He says, "Is it really that way? I don't know, but at least I know it seems that way to me." He says, "But there's something more that I know: I know that I am. I know that I think."
6.22: Because after all, suppose I were wrong, that I am. Well, who's wrong? I have to be, I have to exist in order to even be wrong about that. "I think"— well, that gives me some basis for knowledge. I know that I think. How can I be sure? Well, suppose I doubt it. Who's doubting it? Doubting is a form of thinking. And so Descartes goes back to Augustine and says, good. He's right about that. "I think"—that's something I can know. Every time it's thought or uttered, it has to be true. The same thing with the "I am."
6.23: So here is Descartes' solution. He says, I'm going to start with Augustine's starting point, and I'm going to prove that God exists. Now, actually, Augustine tried to do the same thing. He went from "I am, I think," to "there is a God," and then "I have knowledge of all these things." But how does he do it? It's something known as the argument from truth. I actually think it's a really good and interesting argument, but no one throughout the medieval period thought that. I have been trying to dig it out after 1,500 years and say, "Hey, this argument is worth taking seriously."
6.24: But Descartes doesn't really do it quite that way. He is going to try to prove that God is responsible for the ideas in my mind, that God did create the world and gave it a structure, and that God is good and would not deceive us. In a way, he's trying to resurrect that Augustinian solution, the solution of Philo of Alexandria, and he's going to do it with what he calls the new way of ideas. He's going to put the Forms inside us.
6.25: So instead of having this independent realm as Plato did, that we have to access, he's going to say, look at Philo's solution, in a way. He's putting the logos both in the mind and in the world. I don't have to talk about some otherworldly area, the realm of Forms. My mind is structured that way. The Forms are in us. They are these innate ideas, the ideas I'm born with. So think about that platonic image. Instead of having an independent realm of Forms and then creating the puzzle that I have to solve through illumination or recollection or something, how do I know this independent realm? Put the ideas in our own minds.
6.26: But then, wait a minute: What if my idea is very different from yours? Don't talk about directly the ideas that are coming from experience. You and I might have different experiences and have different ideas there. Let's talk about the ideas that we're born with. We're all human. We're born with the same set of ideas. Then we have different experiences and learn things, so we get different ideas, different experiences. But we start with the same body of things that are innate. They're inborn. So focus on those, those innate ideas or an aspect of the logos that God gives us. They match the world because God is good. God is not an evil deceiver.
6.27: Now, this way out, of course, means I've got to get from the "I am" to "God is." That's a bit of heavy philosophical lifting, so it's not going to be easy to do that. But that's the idea. If there's an evil deceiver, I could be wrong about everything. However, if God is good, if God created me, if God created the world, if God wouldn't, being good, want to deceive me, then, hey, maybe there are some things I cannot reasonably doubt. There are some things I know for sure.
6.28: So the first one is "I am." And here he goes back to Augustine. He says, "But let's say there is some deceiver or other, very powerful, very cunning, who ever employs his ingenuity in deceiving me, then without doubt, I exist also if he deceives me. I have to be in order to be deceived. And let him deceive me as much as he will. He can never cause me to be nothing so long as I think that I am something." In order to be deceived, I have to be. I have to exist. So I can know that I exist.
6.29: "We come to the definite conclusion that this proposition: I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time I pronounce it or mentally conceive it." Every time I say, I exist or think I am, I've got to be right. Who else is thinking it? Now, incidentally, Buddhist logicians would disagree with this. They would say, "At most, I'm entitled to 'there is thinking.'" But I think ultimately, it's not going to matter because as long as there's something that is definitely true, every time it's thought or uttered, whatever that is, it's going to be enough to defeat the skeptic.
6.30: The same thing he says is true of "I think." "What of thinking? I find here that thought is an attribute that belongs to me; it can't be separated from me." I think, and I realize, suppose I'm wrong about that. But wait, I'm thinking that I might be wrong. So I'm thinking. So I've got to be thinking. I've got to exist even in order to think.
6.31: So he says, "To speak accurately, I'm not more than a thing that thinks. That is to say, a mind or a soul or an understanding or a reason,"—which are terms whose significance was formerly unknown to me. "But I'm a real thing. I really exist."—I couldn't be wrong about that—"And what thing? I've answered a thing that thinks." Why? Because as soon as I say, "I think," I've got to be right about that because thinking, I think, is thinking.
6.32: If I say, "I think, I think," well, then I think. I'm thinking. That's a thinking. So I can't be wrong. If I say, "Oh, I don't know. I doubt whether I think." Doubting is thinking. So I'm good. I'm thinking. That has to be right. Now, again, even if we say, "What do you mean this I?" As long as I say there is thinking, as long as I say something exists, and I know those things for sure, then there is something the skeptic is undermined by. There is something I know, something I not only find reason to believe, I find no reason at all to reject.
6.33: So he says, "I think, I am." They're true every time they thought or uttered. That means they are things I can know. So the skeptic cannot be right. It is possible to have knowledge. Not only can I have knowledge, now I know some things that could belong in the foundation of knowledge. He starts out with a method of doubt.
6.34: He says, "I'm going to try to doubt everything I can doubt." Can I doubt that I'm actually speaking right now? Yes, I could be dreaming. Can I doubt that I am actually wearing a blue jacket? Yeah, I might be in a mental hospital in a straitjacket. Can I doubt that I'm a human being? Well, yeah, maybe I'm a butterfly dreaming I'm a human being. Can I doubt that I am? No. Why? Because doubting that I am—who's doubting? I must exist in order to even doubt something. Can I doubt whether I think? Doubting is thinking. So I cannot doubt those things.
6.35: So there we have some foundation for the rest of the knowledge. Not only do I know them, I couldn't be wrong about them. Anytime I think them, they have to be true. But now, is there anything else? Here's the trap. You might think he's painted himself into a corner. He said, I'm going to doubt everything. And now he says, the "I am," the "I think." I've got this little corner on which I can stand. But what if that's all?
6.36: He says, "I'm certain that I'm a thinking thing." I couldn't be wrong about that. But now, don't I know what's required to make me certain of something? Here, he gives us a fancy argument. It's about the possibility of something. It's known as a transcendental argument. It's about the possibility of things and the necessary conditions for the very possibility of something. So he says, "I am certain that I am. I am certain that I think. What would have to be true in order for it even to be possible for me to be certain?"
6.37: Well, something must be true. And moreover, that thing has to necessarily be true. It is a necessary condition for the very possibility of my knowing that I think and knowing that I am. So he says, here is what it is. "In this first knowledge"—that I think that I am —"there is nothing that assures me of its truth except the clear and distinct perception of what I state." In other words, it seems to me clearly and distinctly that I am, that I think, and that I couldn't be wrong about that.
6.38: He says, that's enough to guarantee the truth of these things, but "it seems to me now I can also establish a general rule." For me to be, for it even to be possible for me to know with certainty that I think and that I am, it must be that "all things that I perceive very clearly and very distinctly are true."
6.39: He's generalizing in a way, but he says, I'm not just saying I know these two things, so on the basis of two instances, I suppose all. That would be a terrible argument. I know this, I know that. I happen to clearly and distinctly perceive them. So yay, I can know everything I clearly and distinctly perceive. That would seem like a terrible argument. And some people interpret him that way and think, Yeah, it's a terrible argument.
6.40: But here's what I think is going on. He's saying, somehow, it is possible for me to have certainty. Under what conditions could I possibly be certain about anything? The answer is, what makes me certain of those things? There's a clear and distinct perception. I try to imagine doubting them, and I find I'm led right back into affirming them. So think of that as a clear and distinct perception. I start to doubt, and I realize I can't even doubt it. Then, I can conclude that the method must be right. That must work for it even to be possible for me to have certainty here.
6.41: So that tells him he can necessarily trust what he clearly and distinctly perceives. That's going to get him out of that little corner he's painted himself into. You might worry about that argument, even if we say it's not some inductive argument, two cases to everything. It's this sophisticated argument about the necessary conditions for the possibility of certainty, which is what I think he's doing.
6.42: But now you might still worry: Can't I doubt the premises? Well, I can't doubt that I think, and I can't doubt that I am. But what about the fact that the path to that is a clear and distinct perception? Couldn't I doubt that? Now, it is interesting that in the Latin version here, he says "seems" instead of just "is." That's a hint that maybe he realizes, "You could doubt what I'm doing here." But still, he thinks he's got a necessary condition for the possibility of being certain about anything. That jump, at least, he's willing to make.
6.43: Now, notice this does lead him to a certain conception of what is essential to me. When I was talking about Aristotle, I distinguished essential from accidental properties. I said the essence is what a thing is of its very nature, the thing that is necessary to being it. Well, notice I've concluded that I exist and that I think, and I couldn't be wrong about those things. In other words, those things are necessary. For me to be at all, I have to be. That's trivial. But for me to be at all, I have to think—that's not trivial.
6.44: So he says, "What am I? A thing that thinks. What's a thing that thinks?" His conception of thinking is very broad. "It's a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, that also imagines and feels." You'll notice there I've got "conceives" in brackets. The reason is that he publishes this work, the Meditations, in both Latin and French.
6.45: There are a few interesting differences: in the French version, he adds conceives; it's not there in the Latin. There are a few other interesting divergences, by the way, that I'll note as we go along, but that's one of them. He adds that in. Imagining, but also just thinking of something, conceiving of something, is something that counts as thinking.
6.46: Here is what he concludes. "What am I? I'm a thing that thinks." Moreover, I'm essentially a thing that thinks. That's necessary to me. Now he makes a bit of a leap. He says, "I think I can know my own mind more securely than I can know anything else." Why? Because I can't doubt my own existence. I can doubt your existence. I can doubt your existence. I can doubt the existence of this clicker. I can even doubt, in some sense, the whole of this perceptible universe. I could imagine that I'm living in a simulation. But can I doubt my own existence or that I think? No.
6.47: So there is something about my mind that I can know with certainty in a way I can't know anything else with absolute certainty. I see clearly that there's nothing easier for me to know than my mind. Now, this leads him to some radical conclusions. If I'm essentially a thing that thinks, well, what about my body? Is my body something that is essentially a thing that thinks? His answer is no. It's easy for my body to stop thinking. I fall asleep, maybe, and I'm in deep sleep, I'm not thinking at all. My body isn't essentially a thing that thinks, but my mind is. So I am a thing that thinks, essentially. My body isn't. So I am not to be identified with my body.
6.48: That means my mind and my body are distinct things. This makes him a dualist. He thinks there are two fundamental kinds of things. There are physical bodies, and there are minds, and those are independent. Still, they're intermingled. He says, I feel hunger, I feel thirst, I feel pain. That tells me there's some relationship between my mind and my body. There is a union and apparent intermingling. So if I'm going to say they're distinct and possibly separate, I've got to explain how they actually communicate, how they're intermingled.
6.49: So he says, "I am lodged in my body as a pilot in a vessel"—here, that's what the French says. In Latin, it says "as a sailor in a ship." I find that a really interesting difference. What's the difference between being the pilot of a vessel and being a sailor in a ship? Well, imagine yourself on a boat or on an airplane. There's a difference between flying it and just being a passenger. That's the difference between being the pilot of the ship and being a sailor on the ship. It's an interesting difference.
6.50: But now, "I'm very closely united to it and intermingled with it, so I seem to compose one whole." So he says, I have a clear and distinct idea of myself as a thinking being and as an extended being. My thoughts don't seem to be in space in the way that my body is in space. But I've got a distinct idea of my body as an extended and unthinking thing, or at least potentially unthinking. It's not necessarily thinking.
6.51: So I'm entirely and absolutely distinct from my body, and I can exist without it. Consequently, my mind, my soul, can exist without my body. This is, he thinks, a very important conclusion. I've got a clear and distinct idea of my mind as being this thing, a clear and distinct idea, actually, just a distinct idea of my body as being another thing, so they can't be the same. They've got to be distinct and separable.
6.52: Saul Kripke, a contemporary philosopher who just died recently, gives us a version of this: suppose I've got a pain and then a brain state, which might be a good example of a bodily correlate to that. Being in pain is essential to a state of pain, a mental state. But is being in pain essential to a certain state of my brain? He thinks the answer is no. So you can't identify the pain with a certain state of my brain.
6.53: However you think about that, I want to focus on Princess Elizabeth's criticisms. I've mentioned that she had a long correspondence with Descartes, and in her letters, she raises some problems. One is already, in a sense, admitted because he's saying they're distinct, but there is a union and apparent intermingling. And she says, wait a minute. I want to know more about the apparent intermingling. I'm a thing that thinks, but I also have a body. How does my mind relate to my body? How is this union and apparent intermingling possible?
6.54: Now, it goes in two ways. There is an effect of my body on my mind through sensation. I am aware of things. I see things, for example, it affects the state of my mind. Something might happen to my body, and I feel pain or feel pleasure. That affects my mind. But also, my mind can affect my body through what is known as mental causation. I can say, "I will now raise my hand," and my body obeys. Amazing. I mean, my children don't obey me, but my body obeys me. It looks like my mind can affect my body.
6.55: So how is that possible? If they're the same, I don't really have much to say. Sure, it's all just physical processes. But if they're distinct, I've got to give an account. So she says to Descartes, "I ask you to tell me how man's soul, being only a thinking substance, can determine animal spirits so as to cause voluntary actions." How is it possible for this mind, which is not really located in space, to actually have effects in space? It seems at first rather puzzling.
6.56: For one thing, the causes of bodily motions must be in space. They must contact the object to move it. If I say, "I'm going to move my hand," and I do it, well, something in space must have done that. But my mental acts aren't in space. They aren't extended in space. They're acts of a mind. So how does something outside of space affect something in space? She says, "I don't see how that's possible. You owe us an account of how that causation is even possible."
6.57: There's another problem she raises. It seems like physics is, at least, it pretends to be, complete. You want to know something about the motions of physical objects, about their causes and effects? Ultimately, science is what tells you that, natural science. Presumably, ultimately, physics tells you how various things move and how energy levels are set and so on. So physics already explains this.
6.58: Now she says, there's a problem of too many causes. You're saying something mental affects something physical. But actually, physics says it's a self-contained system. The physical moves in the way that it does on the basis of physical law due to physical causes. So you're going to say there's a physical cause, but also a mental cause that's in some way distinct. It seems like now we have too many causes.
6.59: So what's going on with the motion of my hand? You could say that there's this nervous impulse that proceeds from my brain. You give me a neurophysiological account of all that happening. Now, you say, "But it was your intention to do it. That also causes it." She says, now I've got not only the firing of certain neurons as the ultimate cause, but also an intention. You could identify the firing of the neurons with the intention. But then they seem to be different in these ways that you've just explained. You don't want to identify them. So now we have two things causing it. That's too many. We only need one thing causing it. The neurons are enough. You don't need this additional mental intention.
6.60: Descartes's answer, I've got to confess, is really disappointing. He just says, "We perceive the interaction of mind and body." It's known very clearly by the senses. I intend to raise my hand, and I do it. Yay me. But it seems like that utterly misses the point. She's not saying, "I don't think they interact." She's saying, of course, they interact. The question is how they do it.
6.61: This thing you're claiming is the cause—first of all, it seems superfluous because we already have an account of the causes. Secondly, it's outside of space and time. Well, at least it's outside of space. How is it affecting things in space? Descartes really has no answer.
6.62: At one point, later, he says that maybe there's a gland in the body where it happens. But that's like saying, it happens somehow in the brain. That would be our modern version of that. But I now want to know how. I mean, stuff's already happening in the brain. That's purely physical stuff. Where does this mental intention come in? It seems like saying that it does is no answer at all.
6.63: So Descartes leaves us in a position that, in a way, is very encouraging. He says, you might be worried about the skeptical arguments, and in fact, I'll take them, and I'll put them in an even more powerful form. Looks like we have reason to doubt absolutely everything. But then he says, not really. I can't doubt that I think. I can't doubt that I am. In fact, I end up concluding everything I clearly and distinctly perceive as true.
6.64: But now I end up also in the position of saying that minds are different from bodies. They're separable from bodies. They're quite distinct. But I can't really tell you how they connect, how they have this apparent intermingling. And so in the end, I've got to say that God somehow makes it all work out.
6.65: I'm not going to talk here about his arguments for God's existence, but to put it in a quick nutshell: "I've got this idea of God, didn't come from the world. It must have come from God." That's the third meditation argument in a very cheap and reduced form. But then I've got to argue that God is good because God has all perfections, and all of that takes me pretty far away from the "I think, I am." Many people think that path doesn't quite work.
6.66: In any case, I want to turn now to a different version of rationalism, a version you find in Leibniz. Leibniz wasn't really a professional philosopher at all. He was a diplomat and also a very deep thinker in logic and mathematics, a co-inventor of the calculus with Isaac Newton. Leibniz, too, like Descartes, was a first-rate mathematician and also had this career as a diplomat on the side, as it were.
6.67: He gives us a version of rationalism that is maybe closer to things we want to think about today. Here's the distinction that I think he begins to draw very clearly for the first time between rationalism and empiricism, as I've been putting it between that Platonic tradition and the Aristotelian tradition. The empiricist stemming from Aristotle says, "All of our knowledge of the world comes from experience. We have no other source than experience."
6.68: The rationalist says, "I grant that most of our knowledge of the world comes from experience, but some of it is independent of experience. Some of it is inborn. It is innate." So there are certain things that our mind is just structured know. It might be part of our biological heritage. I could give an evolutionary account, maybe—we've evolved in such a way that certain things are simply built into the mind from the beginning. We don't have to learn it afresh from experience. But however you try to understand that, we're born with our mind having a certain structure that gives us some basic knowledge independently of experience, and that's true both at the level of concepts and at the level of judgments.
6.69: Avicenna was an Islamic philosopher who was also in the rationalist tradition, and he draws that distinction between the knowledge of concepts and the acquisition of concepts, and then the acquisition of knowledge and judgments of the world. He says that, really, the rationalists and the empiricists can disagree about both. There are two forms of rationalism, two forms of empiricism, but almost all rationalists advocate both forms. Almost all empiricists also advocate both forms of empiricism. They go together.
6.70: The empiricist says, "All my concepts come from experience, and all my knowledge comes from experience. After all, my knowledge is based on my concepts, but I'm getting all my ideas from experience. None of them are really built into the mind from the start." So my building blocks—this is Locke's idea—the building blocks of knowledge are all coming from experience, and then the ways in which I can put them together to get knowledge also come from experience.
6.71: The rationalist denies both of these. At the level of concepts, says some concepts don't come from experience. They are innate. Those are ideas that are simply built into the structure of the mind. And then judgment, too. There are things we can know about the world that don't come from experience. They are, in philosophical terms, a priori. They are independent of experience. Prior to experience, not so much in the sense that they come first, but in the sense that they are independent. They could come first. That's rationalism as Leibniz understands it. There are innate ideas or concepts, and there is a priori knowledge of the world—knowledge of the world independently of experience.
6.72: What are these innate concepts? What do you think we're born knowing? And what do you think we're born having as our conceptual apparatus? Leibniz says, "Can it be denied that there's much that's innate in our mind since we are, so to speak, innate to ourselves, and since in ourselves, there are being, unity, substance, duration, change, activity, perception, pleasure, and a thousand other objects of our intellectual ideas?" In other words, he thinks all of these are built in. Being—notice, I can think, I am. That is something that doesn't, in his view, really depend on experience.
6.73: Avicenna, in fact, has this thought of the flying man. He has a thought experiment. Imagine somebody who is born and immediately has all their sense organs plugged up or is in a sensory deprivation tank. He imagines this person just flying through the air, incapable of learning anything from experience. Could that person nevertheless be aware that they exist? And his answer is yes. They could think "I am" even without any experience of the world.
6.74: So Leibniz here is saying things like existence or being, things like unity, in other words, the concept of an object, substance, and unification of something, the idea of dividing the world up into things, he says that's just built into the structure of our minds.
6.75: Here, there are two views. You watch a child, and at first, they don't really seem to divide up the world into distinct objects, but at a certain point, they do. Then they start seeing causal relations and recognizing the continuity of objects. And by the time they're nine months old, let's say, they've got all of that. The empiricist says that they're learning all that from experience. If they were in a situation where there were nothing but swirling colors and no objects of any distinct kind, they wouldn't come to those ideas.
6.76: But the rationalist says, no, no, no. They're built into the structure of the mind. It may be that the mind has to develop and has to acquire a certain amount of experience for these structures to become fully there and to become triggered and relevant. But nevertheless, those structures are part of the structure of the brain. We divide the world up into objects.
6.77: Even if you imagine an experience of swirling colors, we're going to start thinking of the swirls as things, the idea of dividing the world into objects, substances, and thinking of them as unified in some way and as existing and as enduring through time, and then one enduring object changing or doing things or having things done to them. Notice the Aristotelian category is in the background here. He's saying all of that is built into the structure of the mind.
6.78: There are modern rationalists who have a very similar view. Noam Chomsky, for example, in his approach to linguistics, is thoroughly rationalist. He says that there is a universal grammar and these basic structures of subject and predicate, substance and quality and relation and so on—basically, the Aristotelian categories are built into the structure of the mind, the innate grammar that we all have. Then, when we learn language, we're figuring out how that grammar gets expressed in English or French or Spanish or Swahili or some other language. But the basic grammar is already there in the mind at birth.
6.79: Leibniz is giving us a view something like that. Those basic categories, he says, are just part of the structure of the mind. They are built in, and yes, they might take time to develop, maybe only at nine months does the child fully have these, but they're not being all derived from experience. The child is taking experience and actually using these to organize it, and the ability to do that is already there.
6.80: Here is how he frames the issue between himself and Locke. This is from his New Essays Concerning Human Understanding, which is a response to Locke's empiricist essay, Concerning Human Understanding. He says, "There's a question whether the soul in itself is entirely empty, like a writing tablet on which nothing has been written, a tabula rasa, which is the opinion of Aristotle and the author of the Essay,"—namely John Locke—"and whether everything that's inscribed upon it comes solely from the senses and experience,"—that's the empiricist position—"or whether the soul originally contains the principles of several notions and doctrines, which are merely roused on certain occasions by external objects, as I hold, along with Plato and even with the Schoolmen."
6.81: The schoolmen, in other words, medieval philosophers, Aquinas is clearly in the Aristotelian empiricist tradition, but most of the other medieval philosophers are on Leibniz's side, certainly, Anselm is, Bonaventure is, a variety of others. Leibniz is saying here that the mind can either be viewed as this blank slate, this purely white sheet of paper on which experience writes, and everything written on it is coming from experience, or you can see it as something that has a built-in structure, and then it organizes experience according to that structure.
6.82: So either you've got this blank sheet of paper, nothing on it, nothing yet organized, or you've got something like marble, where there is already a structure there, and the sculptor approaching the marble has to recognize the structure of the marble and has to carve it in the right way. That already organizes, you might think, what then the sculptor can produce out of that block of marble.
6.83: Leibniz thinks the brain, the mind, is more like marble than it is like a blank sheet of paper. It's already got a structure. So he says, now we can move from that idea about concepts, notions, ideas, to the question of whether all truths are dependent on experience, on induction and instances, or whether there's some that have yet another foundation, a foundation independent of experience, where, again, knowledge of these truths is simply built into the structure of the mind itself.
6.84: Here is one way of framing the issue. Philosophers have distinguished analytic from synthetic judgments. Kant is maybe the first person to do that explicitly, but the idea is already there in several earlier philosophers. The idea is that an analytic judgment is true just by virtue of the meanings of its terms. An example from Locke: "a soul is a soul." You don't have to know what a soul is to know that's a true sentence. It's just logically true. Or if I say, "Bachelors are unmarried," it's true by virtue of the meanings of the terms.
6.85: A synthetic statement actually says something about the world. It is not true just by virtue of the meanings of the terms. If I say, "The floor on which I'm standing is white," that's something that actually is about the world. It's not just that I can think "this floor, white"—think about the meanings of the terms and conclude just from that, independently of experience, that it is true.
6.86: A posteriori judgments come from experience; they depend on experience. A priori ones don't. Can we have analytic and a priori judgments, like bachelors are unmarried or a soul is a soul? Sure. Can we have a posteriori and synthetic judgments, ones that say something about the world and depend on experience, like the floor is white? Yes.
6.87: The question is: Can we have things that are really about the world, not just verbal truths, but really about the world, so synthetic truths, that are also a priori, independent of experience? Those would be synthetic a priori. That's exactly where the rationalists and the empiricists disagree.
6.88: By the way, nobody thinks there can be analytic a posteriori judgments. After all, if the meanings of the terms establish it, like bachelors are unmarried, who needs experience? I don't need to survey bachelors to find out. It's already true by virtue of the meanings of the terms. So the empiricist says, no, there are no a priori synthetic truths. Everything is either purely a verbal truth or it's really a truth about the world, dependent on experience. But the rationalist says that no, there is this third category. There are things we can know truly about the world that are independent of experience.
6.89: Leibniz puts it this way. He says, "If some events can be foreseen before we've made any trial of them, it's manifest we contribute something of our own. The senses, though necessary for all our actual acquiring of knowledge, are by no means sufficient to give us the whole of our knowledge. The senses never give us anything but instances, particular or individual truths. We've got to be adding something of our own."
6.90: Here's the idea: we infer general truths from particular cases. I say, "Wow, lightning, thunder, lightning, thunder, lightning, thunder." I think that lightning and thunder always go together. Or I notice this cat makes this sound, meow, and this cat makes that sound, meow. And then I start concluding that all cats meow. Somehow, I go from these particular instances to a universal claim. What enables me to do that?
6.91: He says the argument from those particular cases is not valid. No matter how many cats I examine, no matter how many storms I see, I've just looked at finitely many particular cases. Nothing there allows me to conclude that this is always true. But nevertheless, I do, and I seem to have real knowledge of the world in doing that. What makes that possible?
6.92: Something's got to be added other than the experience because the experience is just going to add more of those particular cases. I think this cat meows, that cat meows, that cat meows— is there anything that will allow me to conclude that all cats meow? No matter how many I survey, I'm never going to get to all. He says that tells us one thing that's very important: we're adding something.
6.93: Now, let's turn to a different sphere. Think about logic. I think, "Aha, here's a valid form of argument: If P, then Q. P. Therefore, Q. Modus ponens." Do I gain that from experience? No, I must use that in organizing the data of experience. What about metaphysics? I think the world consists of substances, objects, that they have properties and stand in relations. Have I learned that from experience? No, that's something I'm deriving from the structure of my mind. That's how I think about experience. It's not like I have to then survey more things and I find, "Oh, over here, there's this bowl of oatmeal, and it's really mushy now. I don't know. Where are the objects?" It's not like that. My mind is organizing things into objects of this kind. That's happening independently.
6.94: What about ethics? Do I learn that, for example, murder is wrong on the basis of experience? Well, the empiricist would say yes, but Leibniz is going to say, no, this idea of wrongness, I don't get that from experience. That's something I bring to experience. Yes, I may learn that these things have really bad effects and so on, but what enables me to supply this is not something I find in the experience itself. It's something I am contributing, my mind is contributing.
6.95: Anyway, you don't have to accept all of these arguments, all of these points. But he's saying that even if I'm looking at experience, it's always particular. I never get to the universal. I'm adding something. Then, in math, it's not even clear where the experiences would be. Or, in a basic metaphysical claim, there are substances that stand in relations. Where's the experience? Or in "this is wrong, that's wrong, that's unjust," where's the relevant experience?
6.96: So he's saying, "All the instances that confirm a general truth, however numerous, aren't sufficient to establish the universal necessity of the truth." Here, he's adding necessity. He says it doesn't follow that what's happened will happen in the same way. So maybe all the cats I've seen meow. Maybe there are cats I haven't met that don't.
6.97: Indeed, in the history of science, sometimes things like this have happened. All the swans we've observed have been white, and then in the middle of Australia, we find black swans. So it could be that all the ones we've seen are not indicative of the entire class and that we're making a mistake in saying all on the basis of those.
6.98: Notice here, he talks about the universal necessity. It's not just going from the particular instances to this universal claim: all. It's also going from contingent things to universal things and necessary things. He says, I look at this cat, it meows. This cat, it meows. Well, all of those are contingent things. Nothing made it necessary that that cat meow or even that that cat existed. But now I want to say, no, there's some really law- like relationship between cats and meowing or between lightning and thunder.
6.99: Where do I get this idea of necessity? I'm seeing contingent and particular things. I'm concluding something that is law-like and necessary, and also universal. Where's the necessity coming from? Where's the universality coming from? It's not coming from experience. Something is in between.
6.100: Somehow, I go from particular facts to a universal conclusion. Somehow, I go from contingent facts to a law-like, necessary conclusion or one about causation. I say lightning causes thunder, and that implies there's some necessary connection between them. But none of that follows from the mere instances. My mind has to be supplying the necessity. It has to be supplying the connections. It has to be the universality. The idea of things being organized in regular patterns according to the laws, that's not coming from experience. That's coming from me. That's got to be innate. That's the idea.
6.101: There is an ambiguity here. What is the necessity? If I'm talking about causation, lightning causing thunder, does the necessity attach to the conclusion? Like, okay, I've seen lightning, there must be thunder. Or is it the connection? Surely it's the connection. Last night, in fact, I saw lots of lightning that wasn't accompanied by thunder, at least here, because it was too far away. Presumably, there was thunder somewhere, so I could investigate that. But we might say, really, it's something about the connection, presumably, that is being supplied here, where the necessity attaches. I want to say there is a necessity.
6.102: One way of thinking about this is to imagine dropping something—this is fragile and valuable, so I don't want to drop it. But the idea is, if I were to let this go, what's going to happen? You've seen people drop things before. They fall, right? So you'd say, "It's going to fall." How do you know? Have you seen clickers fall? Probably not. I've seen other things fall. So how do you know it applies to clickers?
6.103: You've just seen particular cases, and now you're going to include, "Oh, there's some causal link. There's something like gravity, and when you let this go, it's going to fall." Well, you're right, it is going to, and you're right to think there's some necessity to it. It's not just that it will fall; it's got to fall. There's some necessity to that. But the necessity isn't coming from the experience. There's just been a bunch of stuff we've seen. No necessity comes from that.
6.104: If I see a bunch of cars drive by one evening, and I tabulate them—once, my daughters and I did this just for a little lesson in statistics: How many of the things driving by are passenger cars? How many are SUVs? How many are pickup trucks? How many are other kinds of trucks? We tabulated all this. Does that mean tomorrow it's going to be the same mix? No, of course not.
6.105: So there is something about a certain experience that allows us to attribute some necessity to it. Think it's law-like. What is that coming from? It's not just coming from the experience. It's coming from something else that we use in organizing our experiences.
6.106: Leibniz says that the universal and necessary premises that are missing here somehowhave to come from somewhere. They're not coming from experience. They must be innate. They must be a priori. They've got to be synthetic because, after all, they're allowing us to draw conclusions about the world. It's not just a verbal truth that events in the world happen due to certain causes, that causal relations exist between the events in the world.
6.107: In fact, it seems like something that doesn't really have to be true in a broader sense. We see lots of things in the world that seem to be random. And so the idea that the world is more than random, that it's law-like, that's something that is being contributed by us. It's not necessarily there, in our experiences. It is not something that is just a verbal truth, like events always have causes. That's not verbal. That's a real claim about the world.
6.108: Now, if there are these synthetic a priori truths, what on earth are they? You might think, okay, great. You've convinced me that we're contributing something of our own, but what? The rationalist is going to tell you something. For example, Avicenna says, "Here are some examples I'll give you: the whole is greater than its parts," or "things equal to the same thing are equal to each other."
6.109: I remember in my high school geometry class, a girl in the class who could not understand that. She kept saying, "Why? Why?" The coach, who was our geometry teacher, would be getting very red-faced because he was like, "Look, A is equal to B. Is that right? B is equal to C. Therefore, A is equal to C." "But Why?" "Things equal to the same thing are equal to each other." "Why?" Leibniz would say that, actually, it's a really good question. Why? I can't point to experiences that convince me of this. Instead, I've got to say that this is just part of the basic structure of the brain.
6.110: The empiricist will say, "I beg to differ. I think it's a definition of equality, and it's the meaning of equality that tells me this." An empiricist is going to say, "I've got another explanation for all of these." But in any case, Leibniz would say that Janie, who was raising these questions in that class, was raising a good question: Where is that coming from?
6.111: The answer is it's not coming from experience, and in his view, it's not just coming from the meanings of the terms. It is something that is this synthetic a priori judgment. It's a deep axiom, as it were, that we know intuitively, and she was having trouble recovering that bit of knowledge. What the coach was saying was not triggering that and activating it for her. But he would say, it's nevertheless a really good question. Where is it coming from? It's got to be somewhere else. That's what my theory means to say.
6.112: In Descartes, well, it's certain things like the "I think" and the "I am." Also, anyone who thinks has to exist while thinking. Nothing's made from nothing. He thinks that's an important synthetic a priori truth. It's impossible for anything to be and not be at the same time. What's been done can't be undone. You can't change the past—I think that's an especially interesting one.
6.113: Leibniz has the principle of sufficient reason, which says there can be no fact without a sufficient reason why it's so and not otherwise. One form of that is that every event has a cause, but this is deeper. He's saying everything has an explanation. Everything has some reason why it's that way and not some other way.
6.114: In Immanuel Kant, who was also a rationalist, every event has a cause; this is his version of this. He thinks the truths of arithmetic are synthetic and a priori in this way. His example is 7 + 5 = 12. And by the way, earlier in Augustine, his example is 7 + 3 = 10. So I don't know if Kant is explicitly thinking of that one or whether he's coming close to it by accident. But why would you think that the truth of arithmetic is something that is actually synthetic and really true about the world, not just a verbal truth, and also, is independent of experience, is a priori?
6.115: Well, what are you thinking? Kant explains it this way. You are imagining seven things— sadly, I don't have seven fingers on my hand to illustrate—but you're thinking of seven things and then adding five, and then you put them together to get 12. That idea you can put them together, he says, is not just a verbal truth.
6.116: I think in set theory, he would put it this way: the union of any two sets is a set. I can take this group of seven things, this group of five things, and I can put them together to get a larger group. That is not just a verbal truth. It's not just by the meaning of union or set that we know that the union of any two sets is a set. That's something that is another assumption: a basic axiom of set theory, maybe.
6.117: But it's also something that makes us say, wait a minute, that idea of unifying two things into one is a claim about the world; it's not merely verbal. On the other hand, we don't go around taking groups of things and putting them together to do research. If I said, "I'm going to apply to the National Science Foundation to do research on whether you can actually combine groups in this way," they would laugh at me. It would be ridiculous, right? So We're saying that's synthetic, but it's also a priori. It doesn't depend on experience.
6.118: Geometry—between any two points lies one and only one line. Well, that seems to be true, but it's not a verbal truth. It also doesn't seem to be derived from experience. What enables us to say that? It is something that is synthetic and a priori.
6.119: In medieval philosophy, there are all sorts of other candidates: "God exists." Or, "The soul is immortal." Or, "The world consists of substances and their attributes," something that is really implicit in Leibniz and would be part of Chomsky's universal grammar. "The will is free." "Every substance has an essence." Or, "You ought to seek the good. You ought to avoid evil. Happiness is intrinsically good. Courage is a virtue." All of these would be potential candidates for being this synthetic and a priori truth.
6.120: The upshot of all of this is that the rationalist is looking at our experience of the world and saying, "I don't see how we get from that experience of the world, which is always particular, always contingent, to saying anything that is universal, that is necessary, that is law-like, that involves causation." It's in its purest form, maybe in mathematics, where you think, I don't even see how experience is relevant to this, and yet we claim to have a lot of mathematical knowledge. We're right to think we do have that. The skeptic is wrong.
6.121: On the other hand, what makes it possible for us to have that knowledge where we're adding something independently of experience? It must be because our minds have certain innate concepts and are able to put them together to have certain innate bits of knowledge. Next time, we'll look at the empiricist alternative. Lecture 7: On Empiricism At a glance — On empiricism.
7.1: I've said that there are two great traditions in Western philosophy. One of them, really a series of footnotes to Plato, and the other, a series of footnotes to Aristotle. We've already looked at the tradition that stems from Plato, the rationalist tradition that extends through Descartes, Leibniz, and a variety of other figures. Today, I want to talk about the footnotes to Aristotle, this other grand tradition, which is an empiricist tradition.
7.2: Last time, we already talked some about what empiricism is, but here I want to look at the two really most important figures, at least since the medieval period, of that empiricist tradition, the followers of Aristotle. That's John Locke and David Hume, both of them writing in English, so they're more accessible in a way than the people who are writing in Latin or French or other languages.
7.3: But from another point of view, their thought is, well, while utterly commonsensical, also tricky in ways that are not evident on the surface. We're going to have to think carefully about why Locke and Hume, for example, end up in different places despite the fact that they start out in the same way. The fact that they write in English and the fact that they write in common-sense terms can actually mislead us and make us think that this is very simple.
7.4: Indeed, as a student, I thought, this is simple, these guys are getting everything right. I was thoroughly convinced. Now I see that it's a little more complicated than the language suggests. They can lure you in with the seeming simplicity. That's not to say I now think they're wrong. I think these arguments are very serious arguments, but we have to watch them carefully.
7.5: John Locke is a 17th-century philosopher. He was, by trade, a medical doctor who attached himself to the Earl of Shaftesbury. He was the private physician of the Earl, which gave him a lot of time to get involved in politics, among other things, but also to write a series of works. Our own Declaration of Independence and Constitution is based on his work in political philosophy, but today I'm going to be focusing on his thinking about the philosophy of mind and more broadly about his philosophical approach.
7.6: We've said empiricism is the idea that, first of all, all of our ideas, all of our concepts come from experience. Secondly, that all of our knowledge of the world comes from experience. There is some knowledge that is purely analytic, as the empiricists tend to have it, or is a trifling proposition in Locke's terminology.
7.7: The idea is certain things like "a soul is a soul," or logical propositions, or "bachelors are unmarried"—those are just verbal truths. If you understand the language, you know that they're true. But if we're talking about truth about the world, all of that comes from experience. If all of the building blocks come from experience, we can't really have knowledge of the world built out of them independently of experience. That, too, has to come from experience.
7.8: Locke puts it this way, and here we have to be careful because he says thatmost of our experience is experience of the world outside of us, but we also have internal experiences through reflection. I am aware of my own states of mind. So yes, I can perceive the world: I can hear things, I can taste things, I can see things. But I also can reflect, and I'm aware of my own mental states. That means there are two sources, really. There is sensation of the outside world, but then also reflection, this awareness of my own mental states.
7.9: So he says, "Let's suppose the mind to be white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas. How comes it to be furnished? Whence comes it by that vast store, which the busy and boundless fancy of man has painted on it with an almost endless variety? Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge?" In other words, we seem to know a lot about the world, but where are we getting all of this? It seems as if all we have is sensation, perception of the world around us, and then the awareness of our own mental states.
7.10: Is that enough? He says, yes, it is enough. "I can answer the question with one word: experience." In that all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself. The only source I have is experience, perception of the outside world, but then also reflection, awareness of my own mental states.
7.11: Now, you can also recognize that the thought that I have not only an awareness of the outside world, but an awareness of my own mental states, is going to enable him to respond to certain arguments that the rationalists give. For example, what about the "I think, I am" of Descartes? Well, that's reflection. Descartes is reflecting on his own mental states.
7.12: Avicenna's flying man, having no perception of the outside world, he's still got experience. He's got experience of his own mind. And so Avcenna is right that the flying person in a sensory deprivation situation could be aware that he exists. However, it's because he has this internal experience. He's not experiencing the outside world, but he's experiencing the inside world.
7.13: We do have these two kinds of experience. Perception: vision, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and it's now argued that there are some other senses as well. If that's true, like an awareness of motion and so on, then fine. We have that awareness of the world. But we also have reflection: the notice the mind takes of its own operations. I can be aware of my own mental states. I know when I am seeing things. I know my own thoughts. I know when I'm afraid. I know my own feelings, in other words. All of those are internal kinds of perception.
7.14: Now, what is an idea? Descartes, I've said, pioneered this new way of ideas, and Locke goes along with that completely. But what is an idea? It's a term that's a little bit slippery. Here is what he says about it, the objects of understanding. He says that an idea is "whatsoever is the object of understanding when you think." It's "whatsoever it is the mind can be employed about in thinking." It's "that which his mind is applied about while thinking." One way of putting this is that these are first-order cognitive abilities.
7.15: What do I mean by that? It's a cognitive ability. That is to say, if I have an idea of a cat, then I have the ability to recognize cats, for example, maybe identify when this cat is the same cat, again. I've got a certain set of abilities that go along with having that idea of a cat. But it's first order, that is to say, it's not an idea about an idea; it's an idea about a cat. So these first-order abilities are abilities to recognize things in the world and maybe internally, to recognize things about my own mental states, to recognize fear, to recognize something I see as opposed to something I taste or something I hear. Those are first-order abilities.
7.16: The reason I want to stress that first-order part—and I think it's important—is that Locke and other empiricists do not deny that there are higher-order abilities, that the mind does come equipped with the ability, for example, to combine ideas or separate ideas or perform logical functions. We'll come to that more in a moment, but think of this as an ability to recognize and identify things in the world or things in my own mind, things that are my own mental states.
7.17: Well, I generally refer to these as concepts rather than ideas because I think it's clearly tied to abilities, maybe in a way that idea isn't. Idea suggests an image to a lot of people, and that's really not an accurate way. It's tied to abilities, not to little mental pictures.
7.18: But here's the idea: all of our concepts come from experience; none of them are innate, none of them are inborn, at least these first-order ones. What that means is that my mind comes something like a blank sheet of paper, a blank slate. On the other hand, paper does have certain characteristics, and it can, for example, receive writing, or at least most paper can. Take a page out of a magazine—it's slippery, and if you try to write on it with a pencil, it won't work. That's a good example of a higher-order ability that something might have. The mind has the ability to absorb information from its surroundings. It has the ability to reflect on itself.
7.19: Anything that is innate in a mind is like that. It's this higher-order thing, the ability to manipulate these other abilities, the ability to actually do things with the raw material of experience. For example, we can abstract ideas, we can combine ideas, we can negate them, and we can perform other kinds of logical operations—I'll say a little bit more about that in a minute, and how we build bigger ideas out of the ideas that we receive from experience.
7.20: But here is how Locke expresses it. "Men, barely by the use of their natural faculties, may attain to all the knowledge they have without the help of any innate impressions. All ideas come from sensation or reflection." Hume says the same thing. He says, "All our ideas are nothing but copies of our impressions,"—those are the basic units of sensation or reflection—"or in other words, it's impossible for us to think of anything that we haven't antecedently felt either by our external or internal senses." Hume talks about external senses and internal senses. For Locke, it's sensation and reflection, but it's the same distinction.
7.21: Let's move on to judgment empiricism. The idea is that all of our knowledge of the world comes from experience. There are no synthetic a priori truths, no truths that are synthetic in the sense that they're really about the world, they're not just verbal, but are also a priori, independent of experience.
7.22: Last time, I defined things this way in terms of this little chart. The empiricist says, "Yes, we have some knowledge that is analytic a priori." That is to say, I know it independently of experience. It's just verbal truth. "A soul is a soul," or "bachelors are unmarried," or the empiricist typically says "mathematics: 1 + 1 = 2," that is something that is analytic and a priori, according to the judgment empiricist.
7.23: Then, there are all sorts of things. The vast majority of our knowledge is synthetic and a posteriori. It is really about the world, but it's something that comes from experience. "The floor is white," that's something I learn from experience. I can't deduce that independently. If I think—what? Istanbul—actually, that's not true. Istanbul is not the capital of Turkey. Okay, that's a good example. It's an example of a synthetic proposition. It's about the world, but in that case, it's false. We know that it's false on the basis of experience. It should be Ankara, not Istanbul.
7.24: But that's the idea: we get that from experience; we have to learn that from the world. If I simply say: Which of those is the capital of Turkey? And I'm basing that on just verbal things, I can't know that. But now the empiricist says, rationalists, you think you're so smart. Figure it out without experience. Obviously, you can't. So we're going to have to examine the things that the rationalist takes to be inborn in us because the empiricist is going to say that there's no such thing. They have to fit into one of those two boxes. Either they're things like "bachelors are unmarried," in which case they are analytic and a priori, or they're synthetic and a posteriori.
7.25: Hume puts it this way. He doesn't use that language of analytic-synthetic and a priori-a posteriori, but he distinguishes matters of fact and relations of ideas. I think in a way, it's the same distinction. He's saying a matter of fact is dependent on experience. In other words, it's a posteriori. It's dependent on experience. There are lots of things like that that are dependent on experience; they are synthetic. They're not just verbal truths.
7.26: But then there are things that he describes as relations of ideas. That's his language for the things that are analytic and a priori. That is to say, they can be known by a mere operation of thought, and in the end, they turn out to be just verbal truths. Locke describes those as trifling propositions, and he thinks of them as trivial. But once you get to the point of thinking that it includes all of mathematics, it no longer feels as trifling, which is part of the reason that, after Locke, people say, "Let's not call them trifling. Let's call them relations of ideas or analytic propositions" or something like that.
7.27: Now, what's wrong with these synthetic a priori judgments, the kind of thing that Plato or Leibniz or Descartes would have thought has to be introduced to explain how we get knowledge of the world. Here's the problem. Locke says synthetic a priori judgments would have to contain certain concepts. After all, judgments are about propositions. Propositions are made up of concepts or ideas.
7.28: But if we don't have any concepts independently of experience, we can't have any knowledge independently of experience. So he says that concept empiricism actually implies judgment empiricism. If you don't have any building blocks, you can't build anything. You have no ideas, then you can't have any knowledge because knowledge would have to involve ideas. Hume has this distinction I've already alluded to between impressions and ideas. It's more explicit in Hume than it is in Locke. Let me say a little bit about that.
7.29: His idea is that I have sensations, awarenesses of the outside world that are raw. Later philosophers refer to these as sense data. They are things that are sensations. They're purely perceptual. They're independent of ideas. I just have the way the world appears to me at a certain time. Now, already that's complicated because I'm seeing things, I'm hearing things, I may be smelling things, feeling things. All of those are happening at the same time. But somehow I take that array of sensations and construct this perception of the world. I've got simple sensations here, simple impressions, Hume calls them, but they fit together to form a complex impression, a complex perception of things.
7.30: These are things, these impressions that are received from the senses, either external senses like vision and hearing and so on, or from the internal sense, what Locke calls reflection. So awareness is of my own mental states. And what are ideas? He says, Ideas are just copies of these things. So I have an awareness of something that is gray for example, and then I am able to abstract the idea of gray from this. The idea of the clicker, let's say, is just a copy of the impression that I have. The idea of gray is just a copy of the impression of gray that I have.
7.31: Now, there are, as I mentioned, simple and complex impressions. Correspondingly, there are simple and complex ideas. Here, I get into one of the trickier questions in Hume because he thinks, Okay, I've got this perception of the world. I am seeing things right now. I'm looking at people, I'm looking at cameras, I'm looking at screens. I'm seeing all sorts of things around me. So I've got this highly complicated impression or perception of my surroundings.
7.32: Does it consist of simple parts? Hume's answer is yes. There are certain components. We might imagine this on a computer screen, let's say, and examine it pixel by pixel to see what's going on. Or we might think of the various cells in the retina, the rods, the cones, and so on, and think about each one of those as giving us a simple impression of what's taking place in vision, for example. So he thinks all of those can be broken down into these simple components.
7.33: That turns out to be very important in his view. Why? Because these complex ideas and complex impressions are compounds of other ideas and impressions. But the simple ideas and the simple impressions are not. They are the units out of which everything else is built.
7.34: So we have two rather bold claims here. One is that we can break our perceptions down into these simple components and see it as a combination of the simples, but then also say that the ideas corresponding to things can similarly be broken down into these simple units that are the copies of simple impressions.
7.35: So we've got this structure of complex things built out of simple things at the level of sensation. Then corresponding to that, more or less one to one, is this idea of ideas, also complex, breaking down into simple ideas that relate directly to those simple impressions. This gives us a method. If we want to know what somebody's talking about and really understand an idea or understand a claim, understand a theory, we figure out what impressions it traces to.
7.36: So Locke has that method, and Hume picks up the same method. The thought is we trace the origins of our ideas. You have an idea, let's figure out where it comes from. It's probably a complex idea, so we can say, "It's complicated. Let's break it down into its simple components and then see what impressions those components correspond to." We trace knowledge to the ideas that it's made up of, trace those ideas to their simple parts, and then relate the simple parts to impressions. In that way, we can understand things.
7.37: Sometimes we'll find that there's this very nice tracking. We break things down into the simples. The simples correspond to these simple impressions. There they are in the world. That justifies what we said. And so, yay, we've got knowledge.
7.38: But sometimes it's not going to correspond quite so easily. Locke says that now we're in the realm of faith or opinion, belief, but not really knowledge. Hume is going to say something much more radical, because if we can't trace it back to these simple impressions, Hume is going to say that it's utter nonsense. Locke will say that you don't really have knowledge. Maybe that's faith, maybe that's opinion, it's belief, but it's not knowledge.
7.39: Hume will say that it's garbage. Get rid of it. That's a difference. It's the same method, but as it were a different conclusion. If Hume says that you can't trace it back to any impressions, then what's the content? It's not even that what you're saying is false. It's more likely that what you're saying is utter nonsense. It doesn't correspond to anything.
7.40: Here, in general, is the empiricist method. We analyze complex ideas into the simple ideas of which they're made up. We find the origins of these simple ideas in experience —that's going to be simple sensations or reflection, simple impressions. Then we say, what is the content of the idea? Well, it lies in the simple impressions from which it comes. We not only have this tracking method to say we get back to the impressions, but then we say that's the content, that's the real content of the idea.
7.41: Here's a picture of how we might do that. We get a vision of something that is complex. In this case, it's nine different squares of different colors, and it's not that hard to think, we've got different colors here, so we can divide it into those nine squares. Actually, we have the idea of a square, so we're going to have to talk about the origin of the idea of the square as well as of the colors.
7.42: But then we trace each of those back to some origin. We can abstract particular colors out of this. We can do it one by one. Here's one of those higher-order abilities that the mind has. I can look at complexes, whether of ideas or of impressions, and start splitting them up into their simple components. So I can abstract things.
7.43: I can go into an animal shelter, for example, or into my house and see a bunch of cats. When I do that, I think, "They're different in various ways, but I can abstract the idea of a cat." Or I go into a furniture store, I see a lot of tables. I can abstract the idea of a table. That itself is not simple, but then I can say, "Flat surface, legs"—that's a bit simpler. And then, I can start tracking those back and breaking them down into their simple parts. What I'm doing throughout all of that is I'm abstracting certain components from this complex.
7.44: Here's an example. We have a bunch of clowns. They are dressed differently, but nevertheless, we can recognize them all as clowns. We can abstract something from the appearance of all of those strange beings and say they have something in common. The Platonist will say that yes, they have being a clown in common. They have this abstract form. But the empiricist says, that no, no no, they have funny noses and funny hair and funny lips, and so on, and start breaking it down into the simple components.
7.45: We can also combine things. We can take different shapes and put them together. The idea of combining ideas is something that is built into the mind itself. We don't have to learn that from experience. That is one of those higher-order things the mind is equipped for.
7.46: Now, it's not an idea that applies directly to the world, but it is an idea about ideas or about impressions.
