It's a way of having an ability to do things with our other abilities, combining them to form complexes. So I can have the idea of a golden mountain. I don't experience a mountain made of gold, but I can think gold plus mountain, and I can put them together in a way that makes sense. I can envision that and have an idea of it.
7.47: The idea does have content. I can say that it's a combination of gold and mountain. Then I can trace those back to the impressions that constitute them ultimately and constitute their content. I can say that that is an idea that actually does have content. So Hume is not going to say, "That's just nonsense." He's going to say, "I understand exactly what you mean. There's no such thing, but I can understand what you mean well enough to actually verify and experience there is no such thing."
7.48: That's the same thing with a unicorn. I can say, "Imagine a horse with this one horn sticking out of its head." I can take the idea of a horn and the idea of a horse, put them together to form the idea of a unicorn. It's not hard to do that combination. It's entirely meaningful. I can say that I understand horse, I understand horn, I understand what it is for something to be poking out of somebody's head. I can do all of that and it has content, but then I look for that content in the world and I don't find it.
7.49: Similarly, with a flying car or all sorts of other things, I can take ideas—indeed, in a sense, this is what any inventor does. They take ideas, put them together in new ways, and then create an object corresponding to it. They say, "Nothing like this really exists in the world, but I'll make it exist. I will form it." That's how a lot of innovation happens.
7.50: I can negate ideas. I can say that I understand what clowns are, for example. So what about people who aren't clowns? I can think that's a clown. So I'm looking for somebody who is not a clown in this context. I can put in a negation. Here, what I've done is go to complementary colors. That's not really exactly negation. But nevertheless, I can say, "I want something that is not blue. I want something that is not red. I want something that's not brown, not yellow," and so on. I know what it would mean to be yellow, so I know what it means not to be yellow. I know what it is to be a cat, so I know what it is not to be a cat.
7.51: In general, that ability to negate is something that's built into the mind, too. It's not something that applies directly to the world. If I say, "Not—are there any nots around here?" I mean, N-O-T, nots. Well, no, it's not something that's first order. It doesn't apply to the world. It applies to our ideas. It's an ability to do something with another idea.
7.52: I can actually extend things like this to infinity. Even that is something that is a mental operation. I can think, "What if you just kept going?" Indeed, that's part of the empiricist account of arithmetic, for example. I can say 1, 2, 3, 4, and I can recognize I could just keep going, and I could extend that infinitely, so I can have as many numbers as I want. That thought that I can do that in an unlimited way is part of how I recognize that I've got an ability to do things. In this case, I can't complete the task. I can't say that I will now count all the numbers for you—it would be a very long video; I can't do that—but I can, and I could just keep going.
7.53: I can do other logical functions. I can disjoin something. I can say, "What about something like that or something like that?" Some ideas we build disjunctively out of that. We say, "We're looking for this or that." It can be hard to think of intuitive examples like this, but there are examples. Jade, for example, is something that is recognizable and tends to look the same. But actually, there are two kinds of jade that have very different chemical compositions. They just happen to look alike. You could say what jade is. It's really this or this. It's two different kinds of things we call jade.
7.54: Something similar applies to certain family terms like uncle. What's an uncle? Well, it could be the brother of a parent, or it could be somebody married to a sister of a parent. Those are two different things. In a lot of languages, they would be separated out. One, after all, is a blood relation, and the other is just a relation by marriage. But in English, we lump them together. It's this or that, really, that's an uncle. There's no one thing exactly.
7.55: Then we can have conditionals: if this, then that. That, too, is a mental operation that the mind has. We can take ideas and combine them. We can think, for example, "What is it for something to be soluble? If you put it in water, it dissolves." So if we have the idea of dissolving, the idea of placing something in water, we can have the idea of solubility. That's, by the way, controversial, but I think it's right. In any case, that's something that enables us to say that we can build complex concepts out of things that are really given in experience or complexes built out of those. We can start performing all these logical operations on them.
7.56: That thought, that that's how we build ideas and that's how we build knowledge, in some sense, is wonderful because we can now construct all sorts of things out of what you might think is pretty limited raw material of the impressions that we actually receive and experience. But it does place limits on what we can do as well because we're limited to those raw materials. We're limited to these tools and these abilities in building them.
7.57: Locke says, "All those sublime thoughts which tower above the clouds and reach as high as heaven itself, take their rise and footing here;"—in experience, in other words. "In all that great extent wherein the mind wanders in those remote speculations, it may seem to be elevated with, it stirs not one jot beyond those ideas which sense of reflection has offered for its contemplation."
7.58: So we start here with experience. We have simple ideas. We start making more and more complex ideas. We form propositions out of those. We can gain lots of knowledge, but we can construct that tower, and that's all we have. We cannot get anywhere else. All of it traces back to experience. So it does impose a limit.
7.59: Now, we can abstract, we can combine, we can negate, we can disjoin. Doing that allows us to have ideas that don't correspond to anything in experience, and to form propositions that don't relate very closely to experience. They can be highly abstract, and their connection to experience can be highly indirect.
7.60: But Locke says, be careful about that, because now we can diverge from experience and from the structure of the world in pretty radical ways. To have knowledge, our ideas have to match the structure of the world, and what we say has to match what's really true of the world. It's easy for us to start talking about unicorns and golden mountains, and all sorts of things that don't really exist. The more abstract our terms get, the greater danger we're in of saying something that really has no real relation to the world anymore.
7.61: This raises a certain question. Let's go back to Descartes and his demon. I was talking about the demon who would trick us utterly by filling our minds with things that don't match the world. Now, both Locke and Hume think that's not a problem because we've got these ideas coming directly from the impressions. But wait a minute. In Descartes, it's what if our innate ideas are all inadequate? That is to say, what if they don't match reality? What if it really is square pegs that we're trying to insert in round holes? If we're thinking about building ideas, what if they're all inadequate?
7.62: Locke is concerned about that. He thinks it's a real problem. What if the ideas that I have in my head actually don't match the world at all? They don't adequately describe its structure. So, I've got this set of ideas to apply to something, and they don't match the world at all.
7.63: If you want examples of this, think about the history of science, where people talked about things like phlogiston, for example, and it doesn't correspond to anything in the world. Or go back further, they were talking about bodily humors and so on. Now we look at that, and we think that that doesn't match anything in the world.
7.64: It's not a trivial point. What if all our ideas are like that? What if at every point we're saying things that people in the future will say, that's a bunch of punk. None of those ideas match the way things really are. But of course, they're destined to be similarly dismissed by future generations. So what if it's just the case that our minds are not built to deal with the world? Locke says that we can be assured because some ideas do perfectly represent the archetypes, which the mind supposes them taken from, to which it refers them. So sometimes our ideas really do match things.
7.65: In particular, all our simple ideas are adequate. What's an example of a simple idea? I hear a sound, for example, and I form an idea of that sound. That idea is adequate. Let's say it's a simple sound. Most sounds we hear aren't like that, but let's say it's a pure tone [sings a tone] or something. We have an idea of that, and that idea matches it exactly. Or a particular color patch. We have an idea of that color, and that matches the impression exactly.
7.66: So he says, "Here's the key to defeating Descartes's demon." It isn't some fancy argument. It isn't proving God's existence and all of that. Instead, it's just a matter of saying, "Where are you getting the simple ideas that you're using to describe the world? Oh, from experience?" Well, that idea does match that impression. It's why Hume says, "These are mere copies." We've got a copy. It's true, it's a copy, and you might worry the copy machine is not very good or something, but really, there is that direct tie, the level of simple ideas and simple impressions.
7.67: So all our simple ideas are adequate. They're nothing but the effects of certain powers and things, he says. Here, he does bring in God. He says, "They're fitted and ordained by God to produce such sensations in us." So, of course, they correspond. But I think it's not like he puts great stress on that religious idea. It's more like, "Hey, look, I've got this idea of white, and I'm looking at a certain patch of white. How could things go wrong? My idea is of that, and I've got direct experience."
7.68: So he says, at the level of simple things, of course, it's adequate. When I think about certain kinds of primary qualities, he calls them, then yes, they are adequate. I think about something being solid. I think of this, and I think, "Oh, yes, it's solid. It resists pressure." Or, "It's extended. It's this long," for example, "and this wide." Well, then those things are directly adequate to it. I can measure it, you can measure it. We can say, "Yes, this is the way this object is." And so those ideas are adequate.
7.69: But now, other ideas, he says, maybe not so much. For example, ideas of substances, as referred to real essences. Here he's thinking about Aristotle in the background. We've got substances, things like this [holds up a clicker]. They have certain essential properties. He says that our ideas of substances aren't really adequate. Why? Well, because we're imagining a bunch of qualities, a bunch of relations here in this thing. But if we say, "What is it that is actually the thing that has those properties and stands in those relations?" We don't know how to answer it. He says, "It's something I know not what."
7.70: What is it that's gray and extended and this long and this wide? He'll say, "Something I know not what." He says that's a problem. These aren't really adequate. In other words, we've got a bunch of qualities here, a bunch of relations, and we don't really know what holds them all together. We have these ideas of particular features of this thing, but what is the thing that has all those qualities? We're not sure. We don't experience it directly. We experience its qualities.
7.71: I've said that Hume is a bit more radical than Locke. Locke will say, trace it all back. If you can't quite trace it, maybe you're wrong because you're saying something about the world that can't be traced back to experience. Or maybe this is just a belief of yours, but it can't consist of knowledge because, after all, we cannot trace it back and really assign it a place in experience.
7.72: Hume is more radical. He has the same method. He's going to similarly trace the complex ideas we have back into the simple ideas, look at the simple impressions they came from and say, that's the content of that complex idea. But if he can't do it, he's going to say, there's something really wrong with that idea. Maybe it has no content at all, or maybe its content turns out to be something radically different from what we would have thought.
7.73: He expresses these ideas in a book he wrote when he was 23, A Treatise of Human Nature. He was very disappointed that it didn't make much of a splash when it came out. He later wrote that it fell stillborn from the press. And so he wrote a short version later so that people would actually read it and get interested in the original. But that's my well-loved copy there. And you can see that it's something that now is considered one of the great works of Western philosophy. It's a very long and very important book, but also in a way, a very radical book.
7.74: Here's one way of looking at the contrast between Locke and Hume. Locke has these empiricist starting points, these empiricist convictions. But when it comes to hard cases like causation or God or other things that motivated rationalists, Locke says that, of course, things cause other things. Of course, things have powers. Of course, there are necessary connections. Of course, there's a God. And he gives us a long argument, borrowed from Aquinas, about God's existence. But it's much worse than Aquinas's argument, partly because he's trying to be a strict empiricist. Aquinas was, too, but he's forgetting about some of the background in Aquinas and trying to fill it in himself and doesn't do a great job.
7.75: But here's the thought. He is actually saying, "These things seem to make sense, so I've got to explain how these actually do relate to experience." Hume says, "I've got this hard-headed method, and if I don't see how this relates to experience, it's gone." So he never got a university position, partly because he was suspected of being an atheist, which Locke certainly was not. He did support himself by writing histories, so he did fine. But nevertheless, these were somewhat scandalous works when they came out because he was willing to discard anything that couldn't be traced back.
7.76: Here's, as I mentioned, the core of his method, the simple ideas into which we break down the complexes, come from simple impressions. They represent them exactly. They are, strictly speaking, copies, adequate and accurate copies. He says, "All our simple ideas in their first appearance are derived from simple impressions, which are correspondent to them, and which they exactly represent."
7.77: We don't have any problem at the base level. There we've got an exact correspondence between idea and impression, sensation of the world. So we analyze the complex ideas just as Locke would. We find the origins of these simple ideas and experience just as Locke would. The content of the idea lies in those simple impressions, again, like Locke.
7.78: But now, he's more skeptical than Locke because he says, "All ideas, and especially abstract ones, are naturally faint and obscure. The mind has but a slender hold of them. They're apt to be confounded with other resembling ideas." When we've often employed any term, though without a distinct meaning, we're apt to imagine it has a determinate idea next to it. So he thinks the further we get from experience, the more confusion arises, the more you might be building that idea in a way that's different from the way I built it.
7.79: If we're talking about our idea of white or specifically like that white color, then we're going to be in agreement; there's an exact match. The moment we move even to the generalization of white, for example, you go into a paint store, and somebody says, "Is that white or is that off-white? Is that cream? Is that vanilla?" All of a sudden, you start thinking, "I don't know what white is anymore." You start realizing that different people can draw the line in different places.
7.80: My wife and I draw the line between blue and green in different places. It's not that we disagree about the color. We both have, Hume would say, a completely adequate idea of that color. It's just that we build blue and green out of things in different ways, so that what I call blue, she calls green. We're differing on the borderline cases.
7.81: Ideas get weaker and weaker, and the ties to experience become more and more remote, and it makes it easier to have these disagreements. You get highly abstract to something about, I don't know, communication or democracy or whatever. Now we're far from those simple impressions, and people can have very different ideas about them. He says that sometimes we have such different ideas or such puzzling ideas, you might wonder whether there's any content at all. Maybe people are just talking garbage.
7.82: Indeed, I've spent my life in universities. I can tell you that half the time I get these emails that tell me there's a talk coming about blah, blah, blah. I think that just sounds like complete and utter nonsense. Hume would say, guess what—it probably is. He would say, "When we entertain any suspicion that a philosophical term is employed without any meaning or idea, as is but too frequent, we need but inquire from what impression is that supposed idea derived? And if it be impossible to assign any, this will serve to confirm our suspicion. By bringing ideas into so clear a light, we may reasonably hope to remove all dispute, which may arise, concerning their nature and reality."
7.83: So he says that by the time we get up here, it's not like now, the realm of opinion. He says, no, it's now the realm of nonsense. So we trace the origins of these ideas. Sometimes we find impressions, and we have real content. Sometimes, though, there is none. We find out there is no impression underlying this. Sometimes it's contradictory. We find out that actually, this is built in a way that makes no sense. Sometimes it's just not at all what it seems. That turns out to be the case for a lot of instances.
7.84: If he looks at these synthetic a priori judgments that the rationalists talk about, he sometimes says that they're analytic and a priori, they're just verbal. Sometimes they're synthetic and a posteriori. We're getting them from experience. Sometimes they're nonsense. We have knowledge of logic, definitions, mathematics—that's the analytic a priori part, the relations of ideas. Then we have the matters of fact, the synthetic a posteriori— that's natural science, history, and so forth.
7.85: But he says that a lot of times we're not going to find it to be either one. "When we run over libraries, persuaded of these principles, what havoc must we make? If we take in our hand any volume of divinity or school metaphysics, for instance, let us ask, does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames, for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion." So go through the library, you're going to find all sorts of nonsense. Commit it to the flames.
7.86: Let's apply it to some of those things that the rationalist said were synthetic a priori truths. "The whole is greater than its parts"—that's from Avicenna. He would say, that's by definition. What is a whole? It's made up of parts. That's just a matter of the meanings of the terms. "Things equal to the same thing are equal to each other"—that just comes from the meaning of equality. "Nothing's made from nothing," that is to say, if you start out with nothing, things don't pop randomly into existence. That's a claim about the world. If that's true, it's coming from experience.
7.87: "It's impossible for anything to be and not be at the same time"—that's just logic; that's analytic. So it's a verbal truth. "What's been done can't be undone"—that's a matter of our experience of the world. We realize we can't change the past, and that's something we learn from experience. "Every event has a cause"—that, too, comes from experience, and we can imagine an experience that would defeat it. Something just happens at random, and we can assign it no cause. That could happen. So it's something that arises in experience.
7.88: What about things like "God exists?" Here, Hume says, existence is no problem, but what about the idea of God? Where does that come from? And now, a question mark. Can I trace that back to experiences in the world? Well, maybe I can, maybe I can't. He's dodgy about this. But in any case, that turns out to be a tricky question. Or "the soul is immortal." I can easily get the idea of mortality from death. And immortality, I just negate that, so that's not a problem.
7.89: But the "soul," do I have an idea of a soul? That, too, is going to be a question mark. "The will is free." What is the will exactly? What is freedom in this sense? Question mark. "Every substance has an essence," as Aristotle would think. Well, we've already seen in Locke, substance is a problem. What is it that holds all these qualities together? We don't really know. "What makes something essential?" He thinks that we don't really know that either. "You ought to seek the good." I don't know where that comes from. "Courage is a virtue." A lot of question marks are going to arise.
7.90: Yes, a lot of things are going to flunk the test. We're going to say it doesn't belong here; it doesn't belong there. It's not that we're not sure what to do. We're sure what to do: it's nonsense. So get rid of it. Commit it to the flames.
7.91: Let's go back to Leibniz's arguments for rationalism. Leibniz said, wait a minute. All experience can give us our contingent truths, and particular contingent truths. But somehow we get universal conclusions, and we think we get law-like, necessary conclusions. We think we can infer things about causation. So there must be a synthetic a priori principle that is operating there that allows us to get to universality, and causation, and laws, and necessity. And Hume says, no. There's nothing like that.
7.92: Here's what's happening. These inferences are simply induction. We see particular cases, we infer a general principle. All the observed ravens have been black; we infer that all ravens are black. I've eaten bread, and I've found it nourishing, so I infer that when I eat bread, I will find it nourishing. When the sun sets, it rises the next morning, so I infer that the sun will rise the next morning. But it's not as if there's some a priori principle lurking behind. It just seems to be working out. Let's go with it.
7.93: Here's the scandal that he points out. He says, I want to find the origin of this. Leibniz says that it's something that is built into the mind. In a funny way, Hume actually agrees with that, but it is a funny way because he says, if I'm looking for a rational justification for these moves, like the sun will rise the next morning or I'll be nourished by this bread, he realizes this isn't a priori. It could go wrong. The next raven I find might be white. The next bread I eat might be poison. Maybe the sun will go nova, and actually it won't rise the next morning.
7.94: So wait a minute. It can't be a priori. It isn't really strictly necessary in that sense. I can imagine things going wrong. But also it's not a posteriori. I can't justify induction on the basis of experience. Why? I'd be appealing to experience. I'd say, I've been making these inductive moves going from particular to general all the way along, and it seems to be working out, so I guess it will continue to work out. That's to say, I've been doing it in these particular cases, so it will continue. That's itself a move from particular to general, so that would be circular. So in short, he says, "I can't justify these moves."
7.95: It's not that Leibniz says that you can't justify them logically, so there's got to be some hidden thing that justifies them." Hume says, no, there's nothing that justifies them. It couldn't be a priori because we can imagine it going wrong. It couldn't be a posteriori because that would be arguing in a circle. So we tend to assume that the future will be like the past. But why do we think that? It's not built into the mind. It's just, in the end, we say it's worked up to now. It has been. But that's just to appeal to the very thing at issue. It's a circular argument. We can't very well say, "Why will the future resemble the past? It has up to now."
7.96: That leads him to say that there is no rational foundation for this. We don't have a synthetic a priori principle that supplies the rational foundation, but there is no rational foundation. That's not going to do it. It can't do it since things could go wrong, and we can't justify things in circles. In the end, it can't be rational. He concludes that all these inferences from experience are the effects of custom, not of reasoning. In other words, we just do it. We're in the habit of doing it, but there is no justification.
7.97: He says, look at how this actually works. If I put my hand in a flame and I go, "Oh, it's hot," and I say that all flames are hot, well, that seems like a pretty radical jump from one instance to a generalization. But if I keep doing it, then it seems like I have a very good reason for thinking this. "Oh, that was hot. That's hot, too." The more I do this—I mean, in this case, it seems like one would be enough, actually. But in a lot of cases, that's not true. You can't find that one patient is helped by administering this drug, for example, and conclude that all patients with that symptom are going to be helped by that drug. But the more you test, the more acceptable it seems.
7.98: But Hume says, that's weird, isn't it? There's no rational justification. In one case, it would seem like a ridiculous leap, but in another case, it seems to make sense. That tells us that there is some difference between the one case and the multiple cases, and it's evidence that it is based on habit or custom, not on reason. Why? Because I actually have a difference. Here's why it's different. I think in one case, I can't draw this conclusion, but in multiple cases, I can. And yet I've just got the same type of thing. "This flame is hot, that flame is hot, that flame is hot"—why would the repetition of that make any difference?
7.99: He says, here's why it matters. It affects my feeling of expectation. If something happens once, I'll think, "Whoa, look at that." But if it keeps happening, I start expecting it to happen. At that point, I realized there's a difference, but it's not a rational difference. It's a difference in my feeling of expectation. I see lightning and then thunder, lightning, thunder, lightning, thunder, and eventually, I see the lightning, and I expect the thunder. I conclude that there's a causal relationship, that the lightning causes the thunder.
7.100: What justifies it? The answer is my feeling of expectation is the source in experience. It's not a priori. We can imagine it otherwise. I can imagine that lightning occurs and there's no thunder, or the thunder just occurs without any lightning. Easy to imagine that. I've experienced it. But wait, he said, in this case, do I experience the causal link? No, I see the flash of lightning. I hear the thunder. I don't see the connection between them. I don't experience the connection between them. It's just one thing and then another thing.
7.101: And that is generally true. He says, we've got contiguity, in other words, this then that, and succession, this then that. But there's no connection. We never experience the connection between events like this. So if we're looking for the simple idea of causation, and then we say, "Where is the impression from which it's derived?" There's nothing in the world that we experience corresponding to the causal link itself.
7.102: If we think, but what happens in one case, first time a child, let's say, witnesses a storm, lightning, and then thunder, they think of those as two separate events. After a while, they start linking them. The difference is not a rational one; it's not a matter of logic. It is a matter of the feeling of expectation. The child sees the flash of lightning and expects the thunder.
7.103: So he says, "When we look about us towards external objects and consider the operation of causes, we are never able in a single instance to discover any power or necessary connection, any quality that binds the effect to the cause and renders one an infallible consequence of the other." We never see the necessary connection. We never experience the causation. It's just one thing happens, and another thing happens. I hit the billiard ball, it hits another ball, that one moves. We see that happening, but we don't see the causation. We just see one motion followed by another motion.
7.104: So he says that if that's right, it doesn't look as if in the world we find any impression that corresponds to our idea of causation. "One event follows another; but we can never observe any tie between them. They seem conjoined but never connected." We don't see the connection. It's just one thing, another thing. So in the end, we've got to trace this back to an impression. That's the whole method. But how can we do it?
7.105: Well, he says, it looks like somehow we get from this constant conjunction to causation. But we don't find anything in the world. There is no impression. There's no sensation of any connection in the world. In the end, Leibniz would say, there must be some reason then that supplied a priori. But he says that can't be right. Because that would mean it was just a priori, that is to say, necessary and independent of experience, that the world just keeps following in the same pattern. And that's just not true. In fact, it's certainly the case that we can imagine things going differently.
7.106: So we can't prove on the basis of logic that the world has to keep going in the same way and that the same causal patterns have to apply. We can imagine a change in the course of nature. Indeed, sometimes there are changes in the course of nature. Sometimes, let's say, the magnetic pole of the Earth might shift, and then, wow, things are different, and the patterns that used to exist don't exist anymore. We, again, get led into that circle if we think it's experience that justifies this.
7.107: We've got to find something that makes the repetition actually give us an idea that we didn't have before. He says, Here's the thing: it's just the feeling. The child experiences the lightning and thunder and starts having a feeling of expectation. So there is a new impression in the mind, but it's not an external impression. It's not an impression of something out there. It is internal. I start feeling something. I start expecting the thunder when I see the lightning. That is the origin of the idea of causation. From one instance, we infer nothing. From multiple instances, we do infer a causal link, but nothing in the world really changes. Where is that coming from? It's coming from our feeling of expectation.
7.108: That implies something pretty dramatic. The idea of necessity, the idea of causation, it isn't something that we find in the world. It comes from an internal impression of the mind. So it exists in the mind, not in objects. The necessity is in us. It is not in the world. Here's a case where it's not as if we find that causation is nonsense. We find an origin, but it's purely subjective. It is a subjective origin. It's not an objective thing in the world. So the source is not in the world. The source is in us.
7.109: Leibniz would agree, yes, and from a rational part of us, it's a matter of these synthetic a priori principles. But Hume says, no, no, no, it's not rational at all. It comes from this feeling of expectation. It is a matter of custom and habit, but that implies it's a social thing. He thinks it's just a matter of us starting to have an emotional response. So the origin is within us. We project this regularity onto the world, but actually it's just a matter of our own feeling and reaction to the world.
7.110: So he says, "The mind has a great propensity to spread itself on external objects, and to conjoint with them any internal impressions, which they occasion, and which always make their appearance at the same time as the objects." So this is something we simply project onto the world. Well, all sorts of things are going to turn out to be like this. It isn't just necessity. It isn't just causation. It turns out to be substance. What is it that actually holds these qualities together that stands in certain relations?
7.111: Locke would say, "Something I know not what." He would say, I guess, the idea is fuzzy. Hume says that it's just that these qualities go together. We project that this is an object, but it's us saying this is one thing. It's not really one thing in the world. The idea of unity, the idea of substance is something we project onto the world. Matter—that's something we are projecting onto the world.
7.112: The self, that I am I. It's part of the reason I worried about the "I think" and" I am" in Descartes. Hume would say, "Who is this I? I don't know where you're getting the idea of yourself. Where's the impression of yourself?" He says, I look inside myself and all I see are thoughts, feelings, perceptions. I don't find a little me. And so in the end, I'm projecting this idea of a self onto the world. That's true of the identity of all sorts of objects.
7.113: It's true also of morality because, actually, I call murder wrong, let's say, and I call generosity good. I look for the wrongness in the world. I look for the goodness in the world. I don't find it. What do I find? My own reaction, my own emotional reaction. I see a murder, and I'm horrified. I see an act of generosity, and it pleases me. He says, in the end, the source of all of those moral ideas is my own feelings of approval and disapproval. In the end, there's no rational way to get from the "is" to the "ought." It's purely a matter of feeling.
7.114: To say "that is wrong" is really a way of saying, "I disapprove of that." To say "that's good" is a way of saying, "I approve of that." In all cases like this, the source is an internal impression. We're imposing everything onto the world. In the end, he says, all our reasoning is concerning cause and effect, but also concerning substance, concerning the self, concerning identity of objects, concerning goodness and badness and other moral qualities, all of that is derived from nothing but custom or our own internal reactions, our feelings. It's part of our sensitive nature, not our cognitive part. It's a matter of feeling.
7.115: Let me just say a few words at the end here about how this works with objects, because it's maybe not quite so intuitive. Heraclitus said, "You can't step into the same river twice." In some intuitive sense, that seems wrong. Yes, the water is flowing by, and there are different stages of this river, but we think of the river as something that has a unity, even though it's different water and the boundaries may change a little.
7.116: On the other hand, as soon as you think, "Is the Missouri the same river as the Mississippi? Is that all one river or is it two rivers?" You start realizing that seems a little bit arbitrary. Indeed, the same is true with the Colorado. You could say it's a matter of river stages, but you have a sense we're calling it that river. It's the same with all objects. Really, we are defining the boundaries of the objects.
7.117: Here's the classic case I will finish with, because it's so beautiful in illustrating the point. It's the Ship of Theseus. The example comes from Plutarch. Theseus sets out to sail, and he is on long journeys in the ship for many years. Well, some planks start to deteriorate, they start to rot or they get broken, and so they're replaced as they go sailing along. Eventually, it turns out there is not a single plank left of the original ship. Is it still the same ship?
7.118: Interestingly, in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, there's an article on the Ship of Theseus problem, and it's been revised many times, and not a single sentence remains unchanged from the very first version. So it is itself an example of the Ship of Theseus problem.
7.119: Now, Hobbes actually makes this problem even more interesting because he says, imagine there's a collector who has been following Theseus around. He's a big Theseus fan. He gathers up all these old discarded planks, and he actually recreates the ship in the original form, the original shape, with the original planks. Now, Theseus is still sailing along in the boat, and now this guy has reconstructed it and put it in a museum saying, "Here is the ship of Theseus." Theseus, meanwhile, says, "What do you mean? Here's my ship." We can get into complicated questions of ownership here, but which is truly the ship of Theseus? Is that the original shape, the original matter and planks and so on, reconstructed? Or is it the one that he's still sailing, even though no individual part is the same as a part it had at the beginning?
7.120: What should we really say? Hume says in the end that it's not a question about the world. It's a question about language. This is a grammatical rather than a philosophical difficulty. There is no truth of the matter, no fact of the matter, about which is really the ship of Theseus. It's how we choose to talk.
7.121: He says, in this case, I think we would choose to say it's the ship that Theseus is still sailing around in because it's been a gradual process. But if it had happened fast, if Theseus had said, "I'm done with this ship, just tear it apart," and somebody then quickly rebuilt it, then we'd be inclined to say that now maybe that one is the ship. So he says, at the end, it's not a question about the world. There is no fact of the matter. It's just how we choose to talk.
7.122: That's going to be true of identity, of causation, of moral qualities, and in the end, of the self, which is a pretty scary thought. Next time, we'll look at the idea of the idealists who say that actually, that idea that we're projecting things like this onto the world, can be taken even further. Maybe we project the world itself.
7.123: How does science play into this argument? How far along is science while Hume is talking about these ideas, especially causation?
7.124: Okay, excellent. John Locke thinks that science plays into this in a pretty fundamental way because he thinks there is a distinction— and we'll talk a little bit about this next time—between the nominal essence of something and the real essence of something. In Aristotle, there are certain properties that are necessary to being a thing, and those are the essential properties. Aristotle thinks it's not that hard to identify what they are.
7.125: Hume thinks it's all nonsense. It's a matter of us projecting things because it's a matter of necessity. "Oh, this is necessarily that?" I'm necessarily a human being, but not necessarily, let's say—what? A certain height. He would say that you're talking about certain properties being necessary, but there's no identity to anything, including me. When you say that property is necessary to being me, that necessity is something you're supplying. So in the end, I can't really talk about this. It's a matter of how we project our concepts onto things. That's it.
7.126: Locke says, wait a minute, wait a minute. Yes, it is true that I associate certain things with a term. So some necessities are purely verbal necessities. So I might just conclude a human being has the following properties necessarily. If it doesn't have those properties, I'm not going to call it a human being. That's a verbal matter. Those are the nominal essences. This is just part of what it is to call something that.
7.127: But then, he says there's also a real essence which has to do with the real internal constitution of the thing. That's where science comes in. So what is water? You might think it's this tasteless, odorless liquid that is necessary to life. You find it in rivers and lakes. That's part of the nominal essence of the thing. Those are things that we associate with the word. But he says, really, what is water? It's H₂O. That's the real internal constitution. That's the real essence of it. That's what makes it water.
7.128: Aristotle says at one point, "What is the essence? It's what's necessary for being the thing." It's something like the definition or what the definition would correspond to. The essence is what really makes it what it is. Locke, I think, says, "Hold on a second. Those are two different things." What we associate with the word and what thereby is in some sense true by definition, that's different from what makes it what it is. What makes water what it is is being H₂O. And then these are the things we associate with the word. But those are two different sets of things.
7.129: Whereas Hume says, "All this is just projected on the world by us. There's no fact of the matter." Locke says, "Yes, there is, and is revealed by natural science." Locke is writing right at the beginnings of the chemical revolution. So he is not yet in a position to talk about this in much detail. In fact, he's pessimistic about it. He says that maybe we'll never know the real essences of things. If only he had been alive a century later, he could have said that now we do know the real essences of a lot of these things. So I think he's unduly pessimistic, but he recognizes that that's the role of science to uncover those real essences.
7.130: Some things are purely artificial kinds, and so there probably is no real essence. For example, what makes something a tie? I don't know that there's a scientific answer to that. It seems to me something that isn't really scientific; it's a matter of social convention. And so there, maybe it is a matter of verbal truths, or maybe it's, as Hume says, just something we project onto the world.
7.131: But when you have a natural kind like water or gold or jade—well, jade is really one of those disjunctive things of two different natural kinds—but in any case, there, we do have a scientific answer we can give. Locke would say that it's not projected on the world. That's not a verbal matter. That's really the way the world is. And that's the thing that Hume can't really say.
7.132: Even though they start in the same place and start with the same method, they end up exactly on questions of science in a really different place. The Humian ends up making all this subjective—we're projecting all of this. But for Locke, no, there's a real objective matter. There is a real internal constitution that answers questions like, "What is this thing? What makes it what it is? What is its essence?" Lecture 8: On Idealism At a glance — On idealism.
8.1: We're going to be talking today about idealism. Idealism is the view that there really isn't a mind-independent world. That is to say, everything really, in some sense, depends on the mind. The world, as we think of it, is really something like a construction or a projection of the mind. Now, that might seem a really bizarre sort of view.
8.2: It emerges very early in Indian philosophy and very early in Chinese philosophy. Interestingly, it doesn't really emerge until the 17th and 18th century in Western philosophy. But for several centuries, it becomes the dominant view. And today, it competes with realism. I think the realists are slightly ahead if you took a poll of philosophers, and believe it or not, people do that. But nevertheless, there are lots of idealists, or as they tend to call themselves these days, "anti-realists," around. I want to talk some about that tradition and why some people embrace it and, in fact, think it's inevitable, why other people reject it.
8.3: The key figure is Immanuel Kant, who really shifts things around. He is not the first idealist in the Western tradition; Bishop Berkeley probably deserves that honor. But we're not really going to talk much about Berkeley, essentially because I think his reasons for being an idealist are not very compelling reasons, except for one. And that is, it is, in his view, the only way we can really defeat the skeptic. The skeptic says there's no reason to believe one thing or another. From one point of view, the skeptic sees this huge gap between our minds and the world and says, "I do not see how to get across that gap.
8.4: And Berkeley says, "Well, what if the world were a projection of my mind?" If my mind's task is to actually represent the world accurately, I don't see how I could be short of doing that. But if my mind is projecting the world, not a problem. It's as if I'm the author of a story. If I'm writing a work of non-fiction, I've got to try to get things right. But if I'm creating a work of fiction, I'm making up what's right, and it's not a problem anymore. So the idealist, like Berkeley says, "I know how to defeat the skeptic, make the world my own construction. And then, of course, it matches my ideas because I built it out of those ideas." Now, Kant, as we'll see, is not quite that simple an idealist, but that is one of the motivations for taking this turn. Let's talk about the contrast in a little more detail.
8.5: The realist says, "Some things are mind-independent." Now, it's important that there's a "some" there because presumably, there are all sorts of things that are mind- dependent. The whole branch of science known as psychology is mind-dependent. After all, it's the study of the mind. If I'm telling you something about my own thoughts, my own dreams, my own emotions, then of course all that I'm talking about is mind- dependent because I'm talking about my own mental states and mental episodes.
8.6: In fact, I might be a realist about a particular thing. I might say, "I'm a realist about this. I think those things really exist in a way that's independent of the mind." So a scientific realist, for example, is someone who says, "I think the basic entities of science are things that really exist independently of us." But a realist, as such, just says, "Some things are independent of the mind. Not everything is like psychology."
8.7: The idealist says, "Everything is mind-dependent," and that is a sweeping universal claim—everything is really a projection of the mind. Now, you could be an idealist about a particular thing without being a sweeping idealist in this way. You could be an idealist about, let's say, ethics. You could say, "Well, I think actually Hume is right, that we're just projecting good and bad, right and wrong, and so on in the world. That is a mental construction. But of course, I think electrons really exist." You could be a realist about some things and an anti-realist or an idealist about certain other things.
8.8: But we're going to be talking for the most part about idealism as a sweeping view that says everything is dependent on the mind. Everything, including the objects of science, including the objects of everyday life, all of those things are really constructions of the mind. Now, one way of thinking about this, given what we've been doing already, is to go back to Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities.
8.9: Locke is a realist. He's somebody who thinks that certain things really are independent of the mind, even though his theory is really thoroughly within the new way of ideas. You could interpret Locke as a kind of idealist because everything is built out of ideas. But I think in the end, he thinks, "No, no, no. Some of our ideas actually match the world." Not all of them, of course. Horse, that matches the world. They're really our horses. Unicorn, that doesn't match the world. There aren't really unicorns. And he thinks that's true of our terms for qualities as well. So adjectives, some of them really describe qualities of things in the world and other things don't.
8.10: Let's go back to the argument from comparison that the skeptics used, saying, "Here's why I don't think we can have any reasonable beliefs about the way the world really is." We have no way of telling what is really in the world and what is being supplied by our own sensory and cognitive apparatus. I have faculties that allow me to sense the outside world, but they shape it in certain ways. I'm sensitive to certain things about the outside world and not sensitive to others. There are fish, for example, that can sense magnetic fields. I can't do that. I can sense things, visually, for example, that a bat cannot sense, but a bat has sonar that I don't have. In short, I'm contributing a lot just by the faculties I have for perceiving the world.
8.11: But also then the brain processes all of that and produces out of what is, after all, a two-dimensional array on the retina, a three-dimensional representation. And so how does that work? I am, in a sense, constructing that three-dimensional representation of things around me. I have no way, the skeptic says, of telling what the world really contains and what is being supplied by all of those levels of processing in my sense organs, and then in the transmission of the brain, and then in the brain itself.
8.12: Well, I can't tell—like the colors of the dresses. This was a few years ago, a famous online controversy. Is the dress really blue and black or is it really white and gold? It looks one way in some lighting conditions and a different way in other lighting conditions. And yet, as you can see from that little strip of fabric that somebody has put along helpfully, it's actually the same thing. It all depends on the background. It depends on the other things around it. And so is the color really in the dress or is it being supplied by our own faculties of cognition and sensation?
8.13: That's actually a pretty good argument that our color perceptions are being supplied by us. They're not really there in the world. If they were really there in the world, why would it matter what the background is, whether it's light or dark, what the lighting conditions are? And so on. You might think, okay, color is a good example of the kind of thing that we seem to be supplying. It isn't there really in the world. Well, what if everything's like that? That's the idealist worry. What if everything turns out to be like that?
8.14: Now, Locke does not think everything is like that. He says, wait a minute. He was before the main part of the chemical revolution, but already the atomic theory of matter was starting to predominate in science. Locke was aware of that. He spoke of perception for example, in terms of little tennis balls bouncing off objects and entering the eye. You could think of a photon, I guess, as something like a little tennis ball. So he's not completely off base. But he sees that the atomic theory, on the one hand, seems to suggest the world really is made up of certain things like atoms or whatever their components are.
8.15: But from another point of view, poses a real challenge because it seems to imply that the world is not at all what it seems to us. In other words, it's not just the color of the dress, let's say, that we think, "Oh, we must be supplying that—that isn't really in the world. It's not really in the object." We start thinking, "Wait, most of the things we perceive are not at all what they're like or what they seem to be like."
8.16: For example, it's not just color; things seem to have a certain texture, they seem to be solid. This lectern seems to be solid. I can't put my hand through it. And yet, according to the atomic theory, it consists of these tiny particles vibrating rapidly. It seems to be still, but no, it's vibrating rapidly, or at least the parts are. And most of it is empty space. It doesn't seem like it's empty space. Well, actually, in this case, being translucent, it sort of does. But in general, that's not true of solid objects.
8.17: And so maybe solidity, maybe motion, maybe texture, all sorts of things are like color in that respect. Maybe they are being supplied. And if we could see things with a true scientific eye, we'd just see atoms and fields of certain kinds, we wouldn't see the objects that we perceive at all. So from one point of view, you can say, "Look, things are radically not as they appear." And that's a scary thought.
8.18: Aristotle tends to not even consider that. There are ancient Greek atomists, but he's not one of them. He thinks, "Look, objects like the lectern caused my perception of it and are represented in my perceptions. The cause of what I'm perceiving and my representation and the object of that representation are just the same thing. And so I can perceive the qualities that it really has."
8.19: But once we have the atomic theory, we start realizing, "Wait a minute, what if the cause of my perceptions is radically unlike the object of the perception?" What if, in other words, the cause of this is really the atoms that make it up, and what's represented in my mind is this object that actually isn't very much like that collection of atoms at all? The objects might be mere appearances, and the things in themselves, those are the atoms. They're the real things. This, then, is some combination of those. But the qualities it has are radically unlike the qualities of the things that really exist.
8.20: It introduces this skeptical scenario that Zhuangzi and Philo and others talked about, and suddenly makes it real and dramatic. Wait a minute, if modern science is right, and actually, the succession of relativity theory and then of quantum mechanics makes this even worse. Study the objects of quantum mechanics, and you can think, "I don't even know what the world consists in anymore. I have no idea what the reality is." The fact that certain things like waves collapse when you perceive them but are different when you don't—the Schrödinger's cat experiment and so on—those things are terrifying. You start really—wait, what if there is no reality until I perceive it? What if it's all a construction? What if it all has a certain structure purely because I'm perceiving it?
8.21: Arthur Eddington saw this problem pretty early. He was, by the way, one of the key figures that actually worked to verify and confirm Einstein's theory of general relativity. But he says, "In the world of physics, we watch a shadowgraph performance of the drama of familiar life. The shadow of my elbow rests on the shadow table as the shadow ink flows over the shadow paper." Notice the echo of Plato here. All these things that seem to be the objects around us, what if they're just shadows? In this case, not shadows of the abstract Forms, but shadows of the atoms.
8.22: He says, "It's all symbolic, and as a symbol, the physicist leaves it. The frank realization that physical science is concerned with a world of shadows is one of the most significant of recent advances." So he's worried about the fact that there is not really one table, as Aristotle thought—the table causes my perception of the table and is represented in that perception in a way that's pretty accurate. What if there are two tables there? Eddington says, "One of them is the table as understood by physicists, and it's not at all like the table that I actually perceive." So the table in my representation has one set of qualities, but the physicist says, "Well, here's what's really going on," and it turns out to be radically unlike the table as I perceive it.
8.23: Well, here's one way of thinking about this: maybe some of the qualities match; it's maybe not different in every single respect. There are qualities, let's say, that according to atomic theory, the atoms have. Call those the primary qualities. Then there are qualities that only the thing has as it's represented by me as an appearance. Those are the secondary qualities. Locke says the primary qualities are the qualities that are really in the thing itself. They're possessed by the thing itself, and they are the ones that ultimately are described by physics and could be given a mathematical representation. But the other qualities are being supplied by us.
8.24: Here is how Locke puts it, "Take a grain of wheat, divide it into two parts, each part still has solidity, extension, figure, and mobility; divide it again, and it retains the same qualities; divide it on till the parts become insensible, they still have those qualities. These I call the original or primary qualities of body"—they include things like —"solidity, extension, figure, motion, or rest, and number." Now, even the special theory of relativity says that collection might be a lot smaller than you'd think.
8.25: For example, motion or rest, Einstein is saying that it depends on my frame of reference. I'm on the train, and it seems like you're just sitting there beside me on the train; you're stationary. But of course, to somebody outside the train, we both seem to be moving along rapidly. So are you in motion or at rest? Well, it depends on your frame of reference. What is the shape of your motion? What does it look like? From my point of view, you're just going forward like this. But from the point of view of somebody outside the train, maybe the track is curving and so on. So maybe your trajectory looks quite different.
8.26: So certain things that Locke would have said that's part of what physics takes as basic, those are really in the object. After relativity, we might say, "Oh, at least some of those are different." Now, not all of them, maybe. Rest mass, for example, might still be something that is really there in the object. But inertial mass is going to depend on velocity, and that's going to depend on a frame of reference. Maybe only a few of these survive once we move to relativity theory.
8.27: But in any case, that doesn't change the basic point. Locke is saying the primary qualities are inseparable from the objects. The atoms have them. Those things are had by the thing itself. It's not relative to an inertial frame; it is not relative to a perceiver. Those, he says, produce simple ideas in us that exactly match what they are. In that respect, at least, we're seeing the world as it is.
8.28: The secondary qualities are different. Descartes says, yes, these are the mathematical properties of things that are described in physics. They reflect the true natures of things. But the secondary qualities aren't like that. The secondary qualities aren't things like solidity, and extension, and mass and so forth. Instead, they involve the sensations these things produce in us. They depend on the primary qualities, and so there's something about the object that determines our color perception of it. But on the other hand, that color or the sound of something, the taste of something, all of that is a secondary quality. That's a matter of it producing a certain sensation in us.
8.29: Those are things that can differ. They can differ with the setting. We're going to see the dress as different colors in different settings. They can differ person to person. People might perceive color differently. A person could be colorblind, for example. People can perceive sounds differently. Somebody might find a sound really loud, and another person might find it fine.
8.30: Taste is like this. In fact, cilantro is a good example. Some people think it tastes soapy. Some don't. I don't. But that means, it turns out, I lack a gene that enables me to taste a certain compound in the cilantro. Durian is a much more outrageous example. To most people, including me, it smells like rotting garbage. But some people actually eat it because they lack the gene that enables them to smell that. If you get past that smell, it apparently tastes delicious. I have never gotten past that smell, so I don't know from experience, but in that case, it's rather unfortunate to have the gene that allows you to taste it. The point is that the taste and the smell aren't in the durian or aren't in the cilantro. They are a matter of how that affects a certain perceiver, and people differ in the way they respond.
8.31: We look at something like red, and that's a matter of the effect of the object on our nervous systems. The redness is not in the object itself. Go down and it's not like red things are made up of red atoms, blue things are made up of little blue atoms and so on. It's not like that. It's a matter of the fabric or whatever it is, the surface, reflecting certain wavelengths of light and then us perceiving those in certain ways.
8.32: These are sometimes described as response-dependent. That is to say, to be red is just to be something a standard perceiver perceives as red. It's to have the power to affect a standard perceiver in certain ways. That does get determined by certain primary qualities of the thing, but the redness isn't that set of primary qualities. It's not in the atoms, it's not in the shape and so on. It's a matter of how it affects people.
8.33: We could put it this way: Descartes and Locke are realists about the primary qualities— they think they're independent of the mind. But the secondary qualities of things are dependent on the mind. They're idealists, basically, about the secondary qualities, but realists about the primary qualities of things. Once you start making that move, you start realizing, let's see if we can squeeze that group of primary qualities. What if that disappears altogether? Then it turns out we're idealists about everything. The secondary qualities, in some sense, they just exist in the mind, but the primary qualities exist in the things.
8.34: According to Descartes and Locke, our ideas of the primary qualities are adequate. But we are supplying these others, and so the secondary quality ideas are inadequate. They're not really in the thing, even though we perceive them as being in the thing. We perceive those colors as really being in the thing, but in fact, the thing is what it is. It's just different lighting conditions, different backgrounds, and so on that make us perceive the colors differently.
8.35: Well, the first person to come along and really push this systematically in a direction that leads to idealism is Immanuel Kant. I've mentioned that Berkeley does this for a variety of reasons that I don't find very persuasive, but Kant comes up with deeper reasons. I want to talk for a while about Immanuel Kant's view. We've already discussed his views of ethics, but now I want to think about his broader view.
8.36: He calls what he's doing a Copernican Revolution in philosophy. Here's the way you might think about it. Rationalists like Avicenna, Descartes, Leibniz, think that universal and necessary conclusions—things about causation, for example, or all this or that, or necessarily blah, blah, blah—they all can't possibly be coming from a collection of purely contingent and particular bits of experience. We must be supplying something of our own. We've got to be adding something synthetic and a priori. That's knowledge of the world that's independent of experience at all.
8.37: Hume says, "Well, I agree with you that we cannot get, logically, from the particular and the contingent to the universal and necessary." So what's supplying it is not something from reason. It's just our own reactions to things. We are projecting that onto the world. It's a matter of custom or habit or feeling, not a matter of something that's in the world.
8.38: Kant's response is to say, "Hume, you're right that the source is in us. It's not really in the world. It's not a matter of synthetic a priori knowledge of things out there. But it is reason. It's not just custom or habit." It's not just a matter of custom, for example, that I react in a certain way, that I start thinking of lightning as causing thunder. That's not just the custom we have, like we say, "How are you?" or, "How do you do?" or, "Nice to meet you." When we meet a new person. It's not like that. It's something built into the structure of the mind. Admittedly, it's not a rational feature of the mind, but nevertheless, it is a tendency that is built into us. Kant says, wait a minute. What if it is rational? What if there is a reason behind it?
8.39: It looks as if the traditional rationalist, like Descartes or Leibniz, has a problem here because they've got to convince you that somehow you have this knowledge of the world independently of experience. We could be like Philo and saying that here's what's happening: God is stamping your mind and the world with the same stamp. The logos informs your mind, the logos informs the world. Yay, they match. That gives you synthetic a priori knowledge.
8.40: But as soon as we think about Descartes's deceiver, we realize, what if there isn't a being that's doing that? What if it's just random evolutionary processes that mean that my mind has no particular relation to the world? Or what if there's actually an evil deceiver that stamps my mind with the wrong stamp? Now, Kant says, as long as my concepts have to match the objects of the world, I don't see how to solve that problem. I think that Descartes's evil deceiver, or just the fact that it might be random, suggests that that's not going to work.
8.41: But what if the objects have to revolve around our concepts? So instead of saying, my mind has to revolve around the world and match it somehow—and I don't see how I can be confident that it does that—what if the world revolves around my concepts and I can be guaranteed it is as if I am the author of a fiction and I'm constructing this, I'm projecting it. So, of course, it matches the structure of my concepts because my concepts are building the world. Well, then great. I can solve this problem.
8.42: Now, Kant calls this his Copernican Revolution. I actually think it's his anti-Copernican Revolution. After all, Copernicus says that we aren't the center of things. It's not like everything else revolves around us. We're revolving around the sun. Here, I think Kant is trying to glorify himself by saying, "Hey, I'm part of the scientific revolution, too!" But I think he's going in the opposite direction. He's saying that, actually, the world has to revolve around me. Instead of the problem, I have to revolve around the world because I don't know how I can do that.
8.43: Here's how he puts it, "It's hitherto been assumed that our cognition must conform to the objects, but all attempts to ascertain anything about these objects a priori, by means of concepts, and thus to extend the range of our knowledge have been rendered abortive by this assumption. Let's make the experiment whether we may not be more successful in metaphysics, if we assume that the objects must conform to our cognition."
8.44: If I've got to match my mind to the world, that's a serious problem. Maybe I can do it. I don't know. I don't know how I can ever be in a position to have confidence that I can do it because I can never get outside my own mind to see what the world is like independently of the mind. But if the world has to conform to my mind, I'm home, right? Sweet. It's got to match me because I'm building it, I'm constructing it. My mind is responsible for it. So, of course, it has to match my mind. It's being built by my mind.
8.45: He says this is just like Copernicus. As I've mentioned, I think, no, it's just the opposite. He says, "If the object conforms to the nature of our faculty of intuition," which is his term for sensibility— he's borrowing that from Avicenna, by the way. It's confusing because intuition is a term we think of as this magical awareness of something, and we can't really explain how, but he just means sensation, or maybe sensation plus reflection. He just means experience, really. "I can then easily conceive the possibility of such an a priori knowledge." If the object has to conform to my faculties, then, of course, I can know something about it a priori, independently of experience.
8.46: The realist says, "My concepts have to revolve around the world." The idealist says, "No, the world of objects revolves around us. It has to conform to us." And so he says, "Yeah, I seem to have this a priori knowledge of the world." And by the way, he doesn't so much argue for this as just assert it. He says, "I do know certain things synthetic a priori." And his example, as I mentioned earlier, is 7 + 5 = 12. I can know truths of arithmetic. And he says, they are a priori. I don't need to do experiments to see if 7 + 5 = 12, or for that matter, 1 + 1 = 2. I don't have to test that. I don't have to look around and say, " Anybody have anything so I can put these together and count them?" No, it's just true by virtue of—
8.47: Now, Hume would say the meanings of the terms 1 + 2 or 7 + 5 = 12, et cetera, an equality. But Kant says, no, no, no. And I've already mentioned the reason: I can take this group of seven things, this group of five things, I can put them together in a larger group. I can combine groups. Where does that claim come from? That isn't true just verbally. It looks like something that must be true, on the other hand, but I don't know how I could test it in an experience. That's why he's convinced that that kind of truth is synthetic and it is a priori. We know it about the world. We can combine different groups of things into bigger groups. But that's not something we're deriving from experience.
8.48: So he says that that must be possible. But if it's possible, what would make it possible? First of all, there have to be laws of the understanding. The objects have to conform to me. If there ends up being a necessity to that, the necessity is coming from me. In that respect, he's agreeing with Hume. But there must be these laws in my mind, in my understanding, that are expressed in a priori concepts. I've got to have these innate ideas, and moreover, these laws connecting them that are built in and that are then built into the objects as I perceive them. So all the objects of experience necessarily have to conform to these concepts and to these laws.
8.49: So let's take it apart. I have to have these innate ideas. These a priori concepts, they are called the pure concepts of the understanding. He also calls them the categories. And then there are going to be the laws of the understanding, the synthetic a priori truths that are made up of these innate concepts. But there's a trick. So far, it might seem that we are now saying, "Descartes, you were right. Leibniz, you were right. I've got the same laws of the understanding."
8.50: But it's not quite so simple because he's saying, these are going to be laws of the understanding, and they're going to govern sensation as well, but they apply only within the realm of experience. In other words, I am faced with this world that I somehow experience. "I don't know," he says, "what the world is really like."
8.51: From one point of view, you could see Kant as somebody who takes the argument from comparison, from Philo and from Zhuangzi, and just runs with it and says that it's absolutely true. I cannot tell what in the object of my experience corresponds to what's really out there in the world. So can I conclude something about what's really out there in the world on the basis of how my processing works? No. But can I conclude something about the objects as I experience them? Yes.
8.52: So the laws of the understanding and the a priori concepts, the categories, are going to apply to the things as I experience them. They're going to apply to things like the lectern, and to human beings, and to neckties, and to cats, and to clowns, and a variety of other things. They're going to apply to all of that as I experience them.
8.53: But now you say, what's the real reality? What is the, as he puts it, the unconditional equal to X, the thing-in-itself that actually is pre-processing, the way the thing is independently of the way I perceive it and so on. He says, "That thing-in-itself, it's unknowable. I don't know." Now, the scientific realist says, "I know. Natural science is telling me it's the atoms and so on." But Kant says that that's just one more level of our building a theory. Actually, all I can talk about are the things I experience or the things I postulate on the basis of that experience. But they conform to these laws because I'm constructing them to make sense of what's happening to me.
8.54: But what's really out there and causing these? Oh, I said, "causing" these things to happen to me. In the first edition, he talks that way when he's writing the Critique of Pure Reason. In the second edition, he takes that out because he realizes, causation— that's one of the categories. I can't apply that to things themselves. They apply only within the realm of experience. So I actually can't say whatever's really out there is causing this. So maybe I can't even say that stuff exists because existence is also one of the categories, as we'll see.
8.55: Actually, he's in the position of now saying—and by the way, this is why a lot of idealists now call themselves anti-realists, because it's one thing to say, "There's nothing beyond my perceptions. There are only the objects of experience. There are no things in themselves behind any of that." Kant's saying, I can't really tell you there are, but I think actually there are. We'll get to that argument in a moment.
8.56: Because he has a section of the Critique of Pure Reason where he says—this is called the Refutation of Idealism. " I'm going to tell you I'm not really an idealist," because he does think there are things in themselves. It's just that he thinks it's impossible to talk about them and that, really, technically can't even say they exist. But on the other hand, he can't make sense of things without them. We'll get to that in a moment I'm jumping ahead of myself.
8.57: Kant is giving us here a transcendental argument. We've already seen this in Descartes, where he's getting from the "I think," and "I am," to the idea that he can trust his clear and distinct perceptions in general. Kant is the one who is really, maybe the first person to spell out the details of this and call it a transcendental argument, even though I think he's not really the first to use it. In fact, I think it's already in Plato, but nevertheless, it's something that is part of this entire rationalist tradition, and Kant is in that rationalist tradition. If we're talking about footnotes to Plato or footnotes to Aristotle, he's a footnote to Plato, but actually a pretty radical one.
8.58: Now, here is the idea. If something is a necessary condition for the very possibility of something else, so that that thing would be impossible if this weren't the case, and that other thing actually happens, well, then you can say, necessarily then, that condition must hold. If B is a necessary condition for the possibility of A, and A is actual, then you can say, then necessarily B.
8.59: Here is how this goes in Kant. He says, a priori concepts and these laws of the understanding are necessary conditions for the possibility of experience, for the experience of objects as we actually experience them. But we do experience them that way. We have that experience. So there must be these a priori concepts and laws of the understanding, and they have a kind of necessity to them. They apply necessarily to the things that we experience. But of course, I can only conclude that about the things that we actually experience, the objects of experience.
8.60: So he says, I can know about things a priori, but only what I am placing in them, only what they have to be like in order to be objects of experience for me. The laws that govern that realm are in us. They're these laws of the understanding, so I can know things as experienced by me, not as they are in themselves. Now, this means he is in a funny position, partly agreeing with classical rationalists like Descartes and Leibniz, partly agreeing with Hume. Is there such a thing as a synthetic a priori truth? Kant says, yes, there are these laws of the understanding. And so in that respect, he's agreeing with Descartes against Hume. He's a rationalist.
8.61: But can I have knowledge beyond the realm of experience? Descartes says, "Yes, I can know that God exists," for example, "and that God is good." Hume says, "No." And Kant says, "No, I can know the objects of experience. In fact, I can know them with a kind of necessity. But can I know what the things in themselves are really like? No. Can I know the world as it is? No." So in both of those respects, he's agreeing with the empiricist like Hume and not with Descartes or Leibniz.
8.62: Well, let's go back to Plato. Plato's philosophy of mind, I describe this way. When I have the thought that something is a triangle, I'm partly directed at that object, the particular contingent object, and I'm saying that's a triangle. I am linking that in some way to a Form, a general abstract Form like triangularity. I'm saying it exhibits triangularity, or in Plato's language, it participates in triangularity. And triangularity is what enables me to talk about triangles. It gives content to my claim that that's a triangle, and it corresponds in some way to my concept of triangularity. Somehow, the good makes sense of all of that. And that in Augustine becomes God that makes sense of all of that.
8.63: Kant is putting the Forms in my mind. He says, let's think of those as a priori concepts, as innate ideas in the mind, which is also what Descartes does. So here he's following Descartes's new way of ideas. And now, the other big change, the thing that makes him very different from Leibniz, is the connection between my concept and the object. In Descartes and in Leibniz, that object has to, in some way, trigger that concept, and the concept I have to be confident applies to the object.
8.64: But in this case, why should I have that confidence? Actually, the object, as I perceive it, is not the thing-in-itself. It's the thing as it's been processed by mysensory apparatus and by my cognitive abilities within the brain. And so the result of that is, well, I can know something about it and I can have confidence that that concept matches the object, but only in so far as the object is being constructed by my mind, is something that is a product of my sensory and my cognitive apparatus.
8.65: And so this, as an object of experience, I can know something about, and I can know something about it with necessity, but only because it's a mental construction. It itself is something that is mind-dependent. It depends, that is to say, it, as I perceive it, depends on my faculties of perception and of cognition in general.
8.66: Because if I get more careful about it, I realize the "cause" of my perception. Here I do have to put cause in quotes—because I can't officially apply it to this—but there's a thing-in-itself out there that must be in some way responsible for my having these sensations. Then I've got these a priori concepts, and I use those to organize these sensations. Then my mind produces an object as it appears, the appearance.
