8.67: What's the relationship between that "cause," the thing-in-itself, and then the thing as it appears to me? I have no idea. And so that is the puzzle. I can know something about the appearance and know it with necessity, know it a priori, but about the thing-in- itself, I am utterly in the dark.
8.68: So Aristotle doesn't have this problem. He says, "Hey, the "cause" is the thing that I perceive." The lectern is the cause of my perception of a lectern. God says, "Something is," probably, but does it really look like this? After Descartes, after Locke, we know that some aspects of it aren't really in the thing itself. We have no reason to think that anything that we perceive is in the thing itself. We don't know about that thing-in-itself at all.
8.69: So for Descartes, there is a match there, but only on the primary qualities. Locke would agree with that. But for Kant, we have no way of knowing. To what extent does this agree with the thing-in-itself that presumably underlies my perception of it? Who knows? We can't talk about that or even think about that at all.
8.70: Now, it's natural for the idealist. And by the way, this is why Kant says, "I'm not really an idealist. I'll call myself a transcendental idealist, but I'm not a real idealist because I still have these things in themselves floating around, even though I can't really tell you they exist." But the idealist says, "Wait, you can't tell me they exist, and you can't say they caused me to perceive things. What good are they?" You say, "There's this unconditioned thing—I'm just going to talk about the unconditioned = X, the "Ding an sich," the thing-in-itself.
8.71: Hegel and other idealists say, "If it's not playing any role in your theory, just get rid of it." But then, great, I can know about things, but the things are just the mental constructions. So from the strict idealist point of view, Kant is a guilty idealist. He's an idealist who feels bad about being an idealist. He says, "I think there must be a real world, but I don't know what it's like. I can't tell what it's like. I have no reason to believe anything I think actually is true of it." And the idealist says, "Well, just have the confidence of your convictions and just say, 'there is no such thing as the thing-in-itself, there is just the world of appearance.'"
8.72: I've talked about these categories, the a priori concepts. I haven't told you anything about what they are. So let me just say very quickly, before we move on to Hegel and the pure, strict idealists, what these things are supposed to be. What are those necessary conditions? Well, I perceive things as being in space and time. I can recognize something about things before I even experience them. I say, "I teach at the University of Texas at Austin." Before you know anything of what it looks like, you can know, "Well, I guess it exists in space somewhere." Actually, now that we're in an online world, maybe that's not even true. But nevertheless, we can say, "Well, at least it exists in time." I mean, there's a time when it started existing.
8.73: And so we know something about it. And that sort of thing is possible because we tend to perceive objects in space and time. Are the things in themselves really in space and time? Kant says, "I don't know," but those are part of our faculty of sensibility. We perceive things in space and time. Are they really like that? We're not sure.
8.74: That's true of other things. We can say, yeah, something like the White House is extended in space. It exists in time. It has a certain character. It's being a house, stationary. It's the kind of thing that we can know about, even if we've never seen it. Similarly, I can ask you about other things. I can say, "Oh, yes, I met someone yesterday." Before you know anything about this person, you can know something about it, and not just the verbal things about a human being, let's say. You can actually know that person exists in space, that person exists in time, blah, blah, blah.
8.75: We have all sorts of experience of the world, but all of those experiences are extended in space and time, and all of them have certain kinds of qualities, and we can know about that in advance. Oh, there's my kitty cat who just died recently. She was my companion for many, many years. I don't know why I went on and on with all of these material objects. I got fascinated by this. But the point is, all of those objects have something in common. Pizzas and cats and sunsets and buildings and institutions like universities, they all have some things in common, just as objects of experience. They're all extended in space and time.
8.76: Moreover, not only are they extended in space and time—because those are simply forms of sensibility, everything we can perceive is perceived in space and time. Things exist in space and time, that's something that is a synthetic a priori truth. But now there are all sorts of other categories and a priori concepts we use. Like unity, we call things objects. We just use the term "thing." We describe things as one. I point to things and say, "this," or, "that," "the." All of those are basic logical functions built into the mind.
8.77: The same thing with plurality, recognizing a group of things as, "some," or, "several." And totalities, "all," "every," "each." Those things are just built into the logical structure of the mind. The same thing is true for certain qualities. The concept of reality or negation or limitation. Yeah, that's true, that's false. I don't know. Like the infinite, it's the not finite. Maybe it's just a negation. On the other hand, I think he has in mind here that sometimes I'm putting a different kind of boundary on there. Unhappy, for example, might just not—it seems stronger than just not happy. Maybe it's a different kind of opposition that's at stake there.
8.78: Then, there are all sorts of relations. The relation of being a substance or having a quality, standing in a relation. There are relations like "if/then," "causes," "depends on," "determines," "grounds." Then, "if and only if," type relations or other logical relations among things, "being part," "being whole." All of those are built into the mind, he's saying, as a priori concepts. We're not getting them from experience.
8.79: And indeed, Locke would say, I think that many of these are just those second-order or higher-order abilities that, of course, the mind has. So I don't have to build them in as a priori. They are inborn, but on the other hand, they aren't the kind of thing we're really fighting about between the rationalists and empiricists. So some of these are like that, but some of them aren't. And notice this one, this is a big one and a way of trying to respond to Hume: possibility, existence, and necessity.
8.80: He says that those are just built into the mind. It is true, we don't get them from experience, but they are part of our mental apparatus. We can sense when something might happen, when something has to happen. And where are we getting that idea? Hume says that it's this subjective feeling in us. Kant is saying that no, it's not some subjective feeling. It is instead part of our mental equipment that we already have even at birth.
8.81: Now, maybe there are other categories that we could supply here of a logical kind, but the point is: these allow us to form some of these laws of the understanding. What are they like? Here are some examples. "Every object stands under the necessary conditions of the synthetic unity of the manifold of intuition in a possible experience." Now, that's a complicated way of saying that everything could be experienced. What we can talk about existing is only what we could possibly experience.
8.82: That's actually a bold claim. In fact, remember when I was talking about Fitch's paradox, it might also be an inconsistent claim in the end. But nevertheless, his idea is, "Look, to exist is to be knowable, to be perceivable." Berkeley had said, "To be is to be perceived." Kant is saying, "To be is to be perceivable." I can only talk about the things that are existent insofar as I talk about them as possible objects of perception.
8.83: Here's another one. "In all change of appearances substance is permanent." In other words, the world does consist of substances. Those substances change over time. They stand in relations. They have qualities. In other words, those Aristotelian categories, he thinks, are basic laws of the understanding.
8.84: "All alterations take place in conformity with the law of the connection of cause and effect." In other words, every change, every event has some sort of cause. That, too, is a classic rationalist synthetic a priori truth. He thinks that's just built into the mind. We automatically look for causes, and we assume there is a cause.
8.85: Then finally, "All substances [...] are in thoroughgoing reciprocity," which is another way of saying there's one universe. There is one collection of things in the universe. It's not like there are parts of the universe, or a multiverse, or this collection of objects that just can't be related to this collection of objects—there's no way to get there from here. No, it's all part of one universe.
8.86: In any case, that enables him to say that things like this really are synthetic a priori judgments, but they apply to the objects of experience, not necessarily to the things-in- themselves.
8.87: So he draws a distinction between phenomena—the appearances, the objects as we perceive them— the categories apply to them, the synthetic a priori truths apply to them, we can know them with universality and necessity. But the noumena are the things in themselves—they are unconditioned by our cognitive faculties. They're the way things are or would be independently of us; the categories don't apply to them. These a priori principles don't apply to them, and we can't know them at all.
8.88: This brings us to critics of Kant, like Hegel. Hegel was someone who existed in Germany, maybe a generation after Kant. He critiques Kant on a number of different grounds, but the basic one we've already mentioned. If you can't know anything about these things in themselves, what are they doing there? They play no role in the system at all. The pure concepts of the understanding don't apply to them. These principles, the laws of the understanding, don't apply to them.
8.89: Notice what that means. We can't talk about them being possible or being necessary or even existing. We can't talk about them having causal relations to anything. So they don't fall under any of these categories, including existence or causation. Well, then what are they doing? We can't say they cause things to appear as they do to us. We can't say they actually are the things that are the inputs to our sensory apparatus. We can't even say they exist. So let's get rid of them. They don't do anything.
8.90: But if we get rid of them, then we end up saying, "Great, now everything is a construction of the mind!" You at least had these shadowy things out there that were somehow responsible for all this stuff, but we've gotten rid of them, and now everything is a construction of the mind. Now, what about the mind itself? Hegel says, "Well, actually, I think the same thing is true of the self," because in Kant, there is something he refers to as the transcendental unity of our perception.
8.91: In Hume, the idea that all our thoughts, feelings, and perceptions are part of one's self is just kind of something imposed by us. He says, "At best, the mind is a kind of theater, and we imagine all this is taking place in the theater that is me." But he says, "I have no perception of myself. I have no real content to this idea of myself." And Kant says, "Well, then, but look, there has to be. I mean, it's my perception. It's my thought. It's my feeling. There's got to be a me." That's a necessary condition for the possibility of this kind of experience." Let's call that the transcendental unity of our perception.
8.92: But Hegel says, "Well, wait a minute. That's a thing-in-itself. That can't play any role. So let's get rid of it, too." We get rid of that noumenal self, that self-in-itself, that real thing. And now, how do I have a self then? What do you mean? I'm not like you. I just have a collection of thoughts, feelings, and perceptions. Hegel says, "Well, I gradually evolved this idea of a self, but that's an achievement." That's something I achieve in this process that is actually a kind of complicated process that he describes in the Phenomenology of Spirit. Notice "phenomenology," the study of the phenomena, the study of the appearances, because there's nothing beyond the appearances. And he traces the development of the self through all these stages. The last one is unhappy consciousness.
8.93: And finally, how do I overcome this sense of myself as disunified? I recognize you as a self. You recognize me as a self. I recognize that you recognize me as a self. You recognize that I recognize you as a self. And so that mutual recognition in society, in community with others, enables me to think of myself as a self. But that's an achievement. That's a result of all these appearances. That is not something that is presupposed as a given.
8.94: That, by the way, is something that inspires much of 19th-century philosophy. It's too bad I don't have time to go into it deeper here. But the idea is that the self is not something-in-itself. It is instead something that is achieved. It's not a fiction, as Hume thinks, but it's something that I gradually come to have as I interact with other people.
8.95: There is something else we can talk about in Hegel because Kant thinks you have these forms of sensibility. You perceive things in space and time, and everything is subject to the laws of the understanding and the categories, these a priori concepts. But Hegel says, "Why should I think that everybody, no matter when they exist or in what culture they exist, perceives things in the same way or uses the same set of concepts?"
8.96: He says that Kant thinks there's a universal and necessary set of these laws and concepts—they're constant, they're there for everybody in every circumstance. But he says, why should we think that's true? Maybe people don't always construct the world in the same way at all times and places, in all circumstances, in all cultures. What if they vary?
8.97: So Hegel is a historicist. He says, if you were in ancient Egypt, you'd use a different set of concepts in understanding the world. Some of them are likely to be in common with ours. You would also see things in space and time. But on the other hand, are the basic logical concepts you would use the same? Maybe, maybe not. What if you were in medieval Europe? Maybe you would have the same set of concepts we have as the really foundational concepts, but maybe not.
8.98: Maybe these things evolve over time. We know that other kinds of concepts evolve. Surely, the ancient Egyptians had no concept of electricity, and the medieval thinkers had no real concept of, let's say, quantum mechanics. So, of course, our concepts evolve over time. Why think there is this constant core of things that include things like, well, things being in community, causal relations, negation, and blah, blah, blah, all those other things that are in those categories. Maybe they evolved, too.
8.99: Imagine that you lived in the desert—not too hard in the current context. You might say, okay, you're going to have a certain set of concepts for understanding your environment. If you live in the middle of a city, you might have a different set of concepts you're going to use for navigating your environment. If you live in the jungle, still another one and so on.
8.100: Hegel says that the way we construct the world develops over time. It develops systematically. He thinks he can tell you some very high-level laws about how it does that. But in any case, philosophy varies with historical circumstances. Kant acts as if he can stand above all times, all cultures, and say, "Here are the concepts we all have automatically." Hegel says, "I'm not convinced there are any. Maybe there are, but you haven't convinced me there have to be." Maybe I have to have some concepts that are fundamental in order to process reality, in order to frame objects of the understanding and have knowledge, but I don't see why it always has to be the same set.
8.101: So he says, "Philosophy is its own time, raised to the level of thought." I think his view is, we should be careful about thinking that we have the key to being human or understanding anything, and that must be universal at all times and places. He says, maybe it changes, maybe there's some common core, but we need an argument for that. It looks like most of our concepts develop over time. Why not conclude that they all do?
8.102: Now, to be fair, Hegel does think things progress in fairly regular ways. This is the "march of Geist," the march of the Spirit, and it is progressing toward absolute knowledge. Now, why does he have this confidence, this idea that we're making at least progress and we're getting better and better concepts and better and better theories? Well, because we're getting more and more experience of the world. And so as we accumulate that experience, he thinks we are progressing in these stages toward absolute knowledge. But it's not a straight line. It comes with all sorts of bends and dips and so on.
8.103: But eventually, he imagines a future in which we attain absolute knowledge, where all possible experiences have been experienced by us, and yay, we know. And in that situation, maybe we could be like Kant. But he says, "No, we're not there." There are these dynamic principles that lead us toward that kind of knowledge, but we don't have it yet. And I'm not going to talk about the details of that. I'll skip past that. But throughout, all of this is informed by the social context, by the interactions between people, by our own communities.
8.104: There's nothing, he thinks, that is really just given to us in sensation. Everything is shaped by our concepts. In Kant, there's a pretty sharp divide between sensibility and understanding, between what happens in the sense organs and what happens in the brain. Hegel is not so convinced we can draw that distinction. He thinks what we see is in part shaped by our concepts. We're looking at the world looking for something. We have concepts we're looking to apply, and we identify those things. Sensibility is really being directed by the understanding, and so he's not convinced there is anything that's just raw data coming in in perception that then we work with conceptually. He sees them instead as intertwined and interacting.
8.105: Okay, well, it's that idea of Hegel's that actually leads to the American philosophical movement known as pragmatism. The pragmatic theory of truth is really that thought that we are progressing toward absolute knowledge. In one sense, the pragmatist says, "There's no difference in meaning without a difference in practice." The pragmatist is always looking for the practical payoff, the practical difference. That's one aspect of pragmatism.
8.106: But the other aspect is to say just as Hegel thought. We're heading toward this stage of absolute knowledge, we can think about these mysterious dynamic laws he talks about to give him this confidence and say, wait a minute, wait a minute. It's not some mystical thing. It's just scientific method.
8.107: Why do we have confidence that we're getting better at understanding the world? Because scientific method is a method that actually allows us to accumulate experiences, conduct experiments, and make revisions. In other words, it is empirically grounded based on observation, based on experience, but also it is self-correcting. That enables us to have some confidence that scientific method is leading us to better and better understanding of the world.
8.108: Moreover, instead of having this confidence that it's going to lead to absolute knowledge someday, think of the truth as just whatever the limit of that kind of scientific inquiry would be. Instead of saying science is inquiring after the truth, say truth is what science will produce at the end of time. In the infinite limit, if we can have all possible experiences, and do all possible self-correction.
8.109: What are we really interested in? The pragmatist says, stable belief, belief that we're not going to have to give up in the face of further information, in the face of further experimentation. That's the best we can do. For now, we don't know what the truth is. The truth is what the ultimate scientific community, the ideal scientific community, would agree on. We don't yet know what that is, but we can say we hope to find things that at least won't be overturned later.
8.110: What gives us the confidence is that science is self-correcting. It consists of a regular pattern of making observations, formulating hypotheses, testing consequences, and then revising our hypotheses—getting better and better. This really is the first test of a bulletproof vest. Okay, pretty dramatic test. "I'm wearing the vest, shoot me!" And he survived, proving this, right? But if somebody said, "Hey, this will protect you from a bullet," pretty scary. But we test it out, we find out, "Yes, it does." Okay.
8.111: Instead of defining science as the search for truth, we say, "I'll define truth as what science would ideally produce at the end of scientific inquiry." It's what would ultimately be agreed to by those who investigate in this way. It's the ideal limit of scientific inquiry. Now, anything we think along the way, we could be wrong about. We can't say these are necessary laws of the understanding we can have full confidence in now, but we can hope that they are stable and don't get revised. If they get revised, we can have confidence that ultimately they'll be revised for the better.
8.112: Okay, so notice that does allow him to reject some of Leibniz's arguments, saying, "Yeah, how do I go from these particular contingent truths to things that are universal and necessary? I do it very provisionally, recognizing I could be wrong. So let's inquire further and see if I need to correct all of that."
8.113: I'm going to conclude here with two thoughts. First of all, Nietzsche, who leads us in a radical direction that is somewhat pessimistic. Nietzsche says, "Look, Hegel thinks all of this leads ultimately to truth, whether it does now or not. Kant thinks we already have these ultimate truths there in the laws of the understanding. But what if there are no universal truths about the world? What if there is no such thing as absolute knowledge, absolute truth?"
8.114: Protagoras had said, "Man is the measure of all things." That's a relativist view, and he meant each individual person. But what if we think that truth is relative to, I don't know, a culture, a society, a historical era, an interpretive community, an individual person? We might think there is no ideal limit to scientific inquiry. There is no law of the understanding.
8.115: Maybe our understanding of the truth doesn't change in rational ways. Maybe Hegel and the pragmatists are wrong. Maybe in the end, science isn't even driven in this rational self-correcting way? What if it's driven in irrational and arbitrary ways? Then there's no reason to think it converges on the truth or converges at all, and that's pretty scary.
8.116: He concludes science needs to become more playful. Just try out interpretations because he's not convinced that scientists actually move in a direction in a rational way. There are contemporary philosophers of science who think that's right. In the end, he's left with authenticity. Be the person you are, become the person you are. There's no guidance outside yourself you can really look to. You're the only test.
8.117: And that leads him to say most dramatically, "God is dead." And here he really means just in any sense of absolute truth, absolute knowledge, absolute anything, is gone. That's a scary prospect. He said that we're now on the horizon of the infinite. In a way, it's exciting because there are no boundaries, but it's also terrifying. He says, "Hours will come when you recognize it's infinite, and there's nothing more terrible than infinity." You are out there on the sea. You don't have a compass, and there is no land to sail to. And so you're in trouble.
8.118: And he predicts that the 20th century will be a century of great wars as a result of this because nobody has anything to anchor, anything. But he hopes we can approach life as a child at play rather than as a warrior, hating all those who disagree with us.
8.119: I do want to finish with one other thought, though. And that is the objection that the realist has to all of this. Because you might think, okay, it's true that in Kant, there is no role that that thing-in-itself actually plays. And yet that leaves us with a kind of puzzle. It's a puzzle that I call the missing explanation argument. Here's why. I do something that is perceptible by all of you. I clap my hands, say. You all hear a hand clap. That's amazing from an idealist point of view. If we get rid of the thing-in-itself, then, wow, you have this mental episode. So do you. So do you. Now, it's not exactly the same one. People sitting in different positions are going to hear it a few milliseconds apart and so on. But nevertheless, it would be amazing to think of this.
8.120: It's as if we all had the same dream last night. We'd say that's so weird. How did we all have the same dream? If you get rid of the thing-in-itself, there's no reason to think that our experiences have anything to do with the experiences of anyone else. Or, for that matter, that my experiences at one moment of time are going to match my experiences at another moment of time. Dreams are such that there's sudden discontinuities.
8.121: But I look around this room, I cover up my eyes, I look again, you're still here. What explains that? Why are you still here? Well, the idealist has nothing to say. Once you get rid of the thing-in-itself, how can you answer that question? The thing-in-itself is what would give you an answer. There's still that same thing, whatever it is, that I'm actually perceiving.
8.122: And so Bertrand Russell, thinking about pragmatism, but also thinking about idealism more broadly, says, wait a minute. There is something about this view that cannot be right. Something must explain why the world seems continuous to me, why your experience seems to match mine, at least roughly. And the idealist, the pragmatist, has no such explanation. So in the end, he says, "Look, as far as I can tell, it is possible that the world could just end tonight. And I can't do anything to stop it." He says, "No matter what the idealist thinks, no matter what the pragmatist thinks, it is not I who made the world."
8.123: And that is Russell's plea in the end, I think, for realism. He says that there's got to be something independent of the mind. Otherwise, we have nothing that can explain why minds actually experience the world as continuous and why your mind in any way corresponds to my mind in what we're experiencing. I don't want to leave you with Nietzsche's pessimism. I'll leave you instead with Russell's claim, "Look, I am not God. I am not the one who is projecting this entire world."
8.124: May put you on the spot here. With all of the different philosophers, how would you define Bonevacism?
8.125: How would I define my own philosophy? That's a tricky question. I find myself drawn— and by the way, I did not know this at the time, actually. One of my teachers, Nicholas Rescher, was somebody I took some courses with and I knew quite well. But at the time that I was studying with him, he was mostly focused on the philosophy of Leibniz and a variety of other historical figures, and that's what he was teaching. I did not realize that in the end, my view of a lot of questions and his view were very much the same.
8.126: But after I left graduate school, he began writing a series of things, and I just recently published a paper describing that. And in doing that, I was not only describing his views, I was to some extent describing my own. I called it the Unfathomable World. Here is my picture of things, and I think Rescher's picture of things.
8.127: The world is real. It does exist independently of the mind, but it's also immensely complex. What we do in constructing ideas about it and theories about it and just common sense views of it, is that we have to simplify. We create these simple models of an incredibly complex reality. In doing that, we are at best approximating what's really going on out there. To some extent, I think the skeptic is right to say, "Hey, what if our ideas don't match reality?" Because I think we've got these simple models that only match reality partly.
8.128: Think about, for example, well, the kind of physics I studied. I found that I was hopeless at trying to help my daughter—who was in engineering—with her physics courses because I thought, "Oh, I know lots of physics." Then in engineering physics, there's stuff like friction. In theoretical physics that I studied, there's no friction. We're all just point masses in a frictionless universe and elastic collisions.
8.129: Anyway, there's something about Newtonian or even relativistic mechanics that's quite beautiful and oversimplified. I think that sort of picture of the world, that picture where, "Oh, yeah, all collisions are elastic and there is no friction and so on." It's a model. It's a model that doesn't match the reality, which is much more complicated. But I think that's what we're doing all the time. Even in engineering physics you're doing that. You're just adding in a few more things. I think that's true of all of our thinking about the world. We're constantly constructing these overly simple models.
8.130: Now, as we go on, I think we do get better at it. We replace inadequate models with more sophisticated models. Sometimes we go backwards and actually forget things. In fact, another teacher of mine, Wilfrid Sellars, said, "Philosophy starts with a certain set of simple models. They become more and more complex. Eventually, they get to the point where they can actually match reality pretty well. But they're now so difficult and so complicated that everybody looks at them and says, 'Oh, that's really boring,' and seeks to throw them out and start with a new set of insights."
8.131: In his view, that's roughly what happened to medieval philosophy. It got very sophisticated, very complicated, and got better and better at describing reality—at least before the scientific revolution, part of our understanding of reality—then people just dropped it. Why? Partly because the black plague and nobody knew Latin anymore, but partly because they said, "Oh, all these distinctions, it's complicated, it's boring, it's intricate, it's difficult." So they gave up. I think there's an element of that, too, which is why I'm not so convinced that it's this steady path toward improvement.
8.132: But I think that's, broadly speaking, what happens. I think it happens in ethics. I think it happens in all sorts of areas. I am a realist in one sense, thinking there is a mind- independent world, but also someone who thinks our models cognitively don't match it all that terribly well because we have tooversimplify it. It's not necessarily infinite in its complexity, but it's a very high degree of complexity, and we can only take fragments of it and understand it a bit by bit.
8.133: So part of what I see, and I think Rescher sees about this, is our theories are bound to remain local. I can have a theory of this, a theory of that. But if you're looking for a grand theory of everything, you're probably not going to get it.
8.134: Going back to the pulling ideas from experience, I was wondering if you had any explanation for ideas formed by people who may be undergoing drug use. In that case, would the idea, or would the drug itself, be the experience?
8.135: Okay, yes. It's an interesting question to ask about altered states of consciousness and what people are experiencing then and what that tells us about reality. Let me go back to Philo's On Drunkenness. We tend to assume that the world that you perceive when you're drunk is less accurate than your perceptions of things when you're sober. But some people have taken at least certain kinds of drugs and have thought it gives them a deep insight of the world. That's not just true of the Timothy Leary LSD 1960s set. It's true of a variety of traditions throughout the world.
8.136: In addition to drug use, or something like that, you've got these meditative traditions. For example, within Buddhism, you have a number of different schools who say that meditation is something that can give you a deeper insight into reality. The same thing is true in Hinduism. Within those contexts, you think, all right, there's this altered state of perception. The view is that somehow that altered state lets you see reality in a different way, gives you concepts to understand reality in a different way and gives you knowledge you couldn't otherwise have.
8.137: Now, one thing I find interesting about a lot of those traditions is that they say, yes, there's this deep insight and deep transformation that happens to you mentally. But you can't really put it into words. People will say, "I've had this experience and it is blissful and it is something like a breakdown between my own mind and the world. I feel this unity with the world, this harmony that I can't really describe or explain." That sort of thought, I'm not going to discount at all. I think that might be very important. But I think it's also revealing that people say, "I don't know how to put that into language."
8.138: That actually, I think, is maybe part of this idea of complexity that I have, where I think a lot of things we can't actually put into language. Suppose I'm trying to describe my own feelings Wassily Kandinsky, the painter, said, "What I'm doing in my paintings"— which after his early stages were highly abstract— he wrote a book trying to describe what he was doing concerning the spiritual in art. He said, "I'm trying to give you certain kinds of experience and create certain feelings, have a language in these paintings of feelings, and you're not going to have any words to describe those feelings. I am trying to give you a language for things you don't know how to express now."
8.139: At least when I look at those paintings, I get it. That painting will give me a certain kind of feeling and a certain state of mind. If you say, "What is it?" I can't tell you. That's why I'm not an art critic. I'd say, "Look at this!" I don't know how to express it, but I get that there are all these feelings and all these awarenesses, let me put it very broadly, that I don't know how to describe. I think there's a lot in the world that is really—I don't know if I want to say it's ineffable, absolutely—in other words, that you couldn't use language to describe it.
8.140: Maybe it's just that given any existing language, we don't have terms for that. We don't know how to describe it. I do find it really interesting when you look at terms for emotions or feelings in different languages, you find different kinds of things. In Danish, there are certain terms for states of mind that as soon as you learn the term, you realize, "Oh, I totally get it." Like feeling comfortable at home, we don't have a word for that in English, really. I can express it in some way. "Imagine yourself coming in on a cold winter's day, sitting there warm and having a nice cup of cocoa. That feeling, okay?" I don't have a word for that feeling, but the Danes do.
8.141: When you start realizing that, you think, okay, maybe there are all sorts of things that my language, and any given language won't have terms for, but that are really important. I think sometimes that's what people are recognizing through meditation or through drug use or something. They're having an experience they don't know how to describe, but it really is an experience. It's really a different king of thing. There might be a real insight into the world sometimes in this. It's just that they don't have the language to tell you what that is, really.
